Appendia A 


be satisfied before either party would be bound to close, 
among which was a condition that the holders of at least 
one-half of the outstanding common stock of Provident 
approve and adopt a proposal that Provident be wound up 
and dissolved and adopt a plan of complete liquidation of 
Provident and that the holders of at least one-half of the 
outstanding common stock and the holders of at least two- 
thirds of the outstanding preferred stock of Provident 
approve and ratify the execution of the Purchase Agree- 
ment. 

As early as September 3, 1969, the Board of Directors 
of Provident resolved to recommend to the shareholders 
dissolution and winding up of the corporation and adoption 
of a plan of complete liquidation and distribution of the 
corporate assets to the shareholders. 

Simultaneously with negotiations for this agreement 
Provident’s Board of Directors and shareholders began 
procedures necessary for winding up and dissolving the 
corporation. 

On September 29, 1969, Provident filed a certificate of 
election to wind up and dissolve with the California Secre- 
tary of State and mailed notice of intention to wind up and 
dissolve to all of its creditors and shareholders. 

On the same date, Foremost filed a Form S-1 registra- 
tion statement with the Securities and Exchange Commis- 
tion pursuant to the Securities Act of 1933 covering the 
$25,000,000 aggregate principal amount of the Foremost 
debentures pursuant to which the Provident shareholders, 
as sellers, would offer the $25,000,000 aggregate principal 
amount of debentures distributed to them as a liquidating 


35a 
Appendiaz A 


distribution by Provident. This S-1 form was amended on 
October 3, 1969. 

Early in October of 1969, Provident realized that there 
were several difficulties in having the shareholders them- 
selves make the public offering of the $25,000,000 aggregate 
principal amount of Foremost debentures following dis- 
tribution of the same to them. Certain of the shareholders 
were minors and one of the shareholders could not be con- 
tacted. The problem was discussed with Foremost, and 
Foremost orally agreed to a change in the Purchase -\gree- 
ment so that Provident itself, instead of its shareholders, 
might sell the $25,000,000 principal amount of debentures. 
This was really no more than a change in form since by the 
terms of the Purchase Agreement as originally drawn, 
Foremost was committed to enter into an underwriting 
agreement authorizing the immediate sale of $25,000,000 
principal amount of Foremost debentures. At a meeting 
of the Provident shareholders on October 15, 1969, Provi- 
dent obtained the consent of two-thirds of the preferred 
stockholders and a majority of the common stockholders 
to this change and on October 15, 1969, Foremost formally 
consented in writing to the alteration, and it Was ineor- 
porated in amendment No. 2 to the S-1 registration form 
filed on October 21, 1969. | 

At the closing on October 15, 1969, Foremost delivered 
to Provident a check for $4,250,000 and a debenture in the 
principal amount of $40,000,000. Pursuant to the agreement, 
$2,500,000 principal amount of debentures were delivered 
to Bank of American National Savings and Trust Associa- 
tion as an escrowholder. The remaining $7,250,000 prin- 


36a 
Appendix A 


cipal amount of debentures due under the agreement were 
delivered on October 20, 1969. 

After receipt of the debenture in the principal amount 
of $40,000,000, Provident had it split into two parts, one 
of $15,000,000 and the other of $25,000,000. Upon receipt 
of the final $7,250,000 principal amount of debentures on 
October 20, Provident executed bond powers to effect trans- 
fer of the $7,250,000 and the $15,000,000 aggregate principal 
amount of debentures pro rata to its shareholders pur- 
suant to a liquidating resolution of the Board previously 
adopted on October 13, 1969, Instructions to make this 
distribution were mailed to First National City Bank as 
trustee under the indenture covering the debentures on 
October 21, 1969, and the actual mailing of the debentures 
took place on October 24, 1969. After this distribution, 
there remained in Provident’s possession $25,000,000 ag- 
gregate principal amount of debentures. On October 21, 
1969, the registration statement under the Securities Act 
of 1933 covering the $25,000,000 aggregate principal amount 
of debentures became effective and in accordance with the 
Purchase Agreement of September 25, 1969, an under- 
writing agreement between Foremost, Provident and Dil- 
lon, Read & Co., Inc., as representative of the underwriting 
group, covering the $25,000,000 of debentures was executed 
by all parties. This underwriting agreement closed on 
October 28, 1969. At the closing, the underwriters de- 
livered $25,366,666.66 to Provident through New York 
clearing house funds, and Provident delivered the deben- 
ture in the principal amount of $25,000,000 to the under- 
writers, Shortly thereafter Provident distributed cash to 


37a 
Appendia A 


its shareholders in the amount of $29,623,500 ( ineluding 
the funds received from the underwriters). 

Throughout October of 1969, there were other liquidat- 
ing dividends paid to Provident’s shareholders consisting 
both of cash and of various securities as the process of 
liquidation and winding up proceeded. 

Section 16(b) provides: 


‘‘For the purpose of preventing the unfair use of 
information which may have been obtained by such 
beneficial owner, director, or officer by reason of his 
relationship to the issuer, any profit realized by him 
from any purchase and sale, or any sale and purchase, 
of any equity security of such issuer (other than an 
exempted security) within any period of less than six 
months, unless such security was acquired in good faith 
in connection with a debt previously contracted, shall 
inure to and be recoverable by the issuer, irrespective 
of any intention on the part of such beneficial owner, 
director, or officer in entering into such transaction of 
holding the security purchased or of not repurchasing 
the security sold for a period exceeding six months. 
Suit to recover such profit may be instituted at law 
or in equity in any court of competent jurisdiction by 
the issuer, or by the owner of any security of the issuer 
in the name and in behalf of the issuer if the issuer 
shall fail or refuse to bring such suit within sixty 
days after request or shall fail diligently to prosecute 
the same thereafter; but no such sut shall be brought 
more than two years after the date such profit was 
realized. This subsection shall not be construed to 
cover any transaction where such beneficial owner was 
not such both at the time of the purchase and sale, or 
the sale and purchase, of the security involved, or any 


38a 
Appendia A 


transaction or transactions which the Commission by 
rules and regulations may exempt as not comprehended 
within the purpose of this subsection.”’ 


Foremost contends for a starkly literal reading of Sec- 
tion 16(b), which would make Provident, by virtue of its 
short-lived position as holder of the convertible debentures 
of Foremost, accountable to it as provided in 16(b) for 
the relatively small profit resulting from the underwriting 
described above, without regard to the overall character of 
the transaction and its ultimate effect. It makes no claim 
that any of the evils against which 16(b) were directed 
were present in this, or that Provident derived inside in- 
formation, profit or advantage from its all-but-momentary 
status as an ‘‘insider’’ of Foremost. 

To require Provident to pay over to Foremost the 
amount the latter seeks under Section 16(b) would be to 
confer a complete windfall upon Foremost and would be 
utterly at war with any concept of equity known to this 
Court. 

Fortunately, the Courts, mindful of Justice Holmes’s 
oft-quoted canon of statutory construction, by which ‘‘[a 
word] is but the skin of a living thought’’, have not felt 
required to apply 16(b) in all cases regardless of con- 
comitant equities and circumstances. In the leading case 
in this Circuit, Judge Browning, speaking for a unanimous 
Court, enjoins us that in construing Section 16(b): 


‘*The initial inquiry must therefore be: What is the 
purpose of section 16(b)—what practices is the statute 
designed to prevent.’’ Blau v. Max Factor & Com- 


pany, 342 F.2d 304, 307 (9th Cir.), certiorari denied 382 
U.S. 892. 


39a 
Appendia A 


Likewise, the Eighth Circuit has said: 


‘‘There is, however, a very different and difficult 
problem when a transaction falls within the literal 
boundaries of the Act, by giving a broad interpretation 
of the definitions of purchase as ‘any contract to buy, 
purchase or otherwise acquire,’ and sale as ‘any con- 
tract to sell or otherwise dispose of,’ yet due to the 
particular factual situation which makes unfair specu- 
lation impossible it is clearly beyond the Act’s preven- 
tive purposes. In that situation the question arises, 
should the Act be literally applied without further in- 
quiry and without regard to the purposes, or should 
the broad and arbitrary rules be applied only to situa- 
tions which are capable of the abuse that the statute 
was designed to prevent? We believe that each case 
must be examined on its own facts and the -\ct only 
applied when these facts disclose the possibility of 
abuses that the Act were designed to prevent.’’ Petteys 
vy, Butler, 367 F.2d 528, 533 (Sth Cir.). 


It is sometimes said that Section 16(h) sets forth merely 
a ‘“‘erude rule of thumb,’’ the inference being drawn that 
if the facts, without regard to the purposes of the statute, 
the surrounding circumstances and the equities inherent 
therein, are such as are described in that section, the courts 
have no alternative but to impose liability. However, as to 
this, the Second Circuit has said: 


‘The description, ‘a crude rule of thumb,’ was first 
employed by Mr. Thomas Corcoran. - pokesman for the 
drafters of the statute, during congressional hearings 
on the bill which ultimately became section 16 b). 
Hearings Before Senate Committee on Banking & 
Currency, 73d Cong., 2d Sess. 6557 (1934). The parase 


40a 
Appendix A 


now serves to describe not only the statute but also one 
approach to its application. Under the ‘objective’ or 
‘rule of thumb’ approach, the statute is applied to all 
transactions which seem to fall within its terms, with- 
out regard to whether imposition of liability would 
further the purposes of the statute. See, e.g., Heli- 
Coil Corp. v. Webster, 352 F.2d 156 (3d Cir. 1965). 
We have rejected this interpretation, see Blau v. 
Lamb, 363 F.2d 507 (2d Cir. 1966), cert. denied 385 
U.S. 1002, 87 S.Ct. 707, 17 L.Ed.2d 542 (1967), in favor 
of the more ‘pragmatic’ approach of applying the stat- 
ute only to those situations subject to speculative 
manipulation. For a comparative analysis of the two 
approaches to application of the statute, which con- 
cludes that this Cireuit’s rule is preferable, see Note, 
Stock Exchanges Pursuant to Corporate Consolida- 
tion: A Section 16(b) ‘Purchase or Sale’?, 117 U.Pa. 
L.Rev. 1035 (1969). Newmark v. RKO General, Inc., 
425 F.2d 348, 350, n.1. 

‘‘The threshold issue raised on this appeal is 
whether the purchase and subsequent exchange of Cen- 
tral shares lent itself to the type of speculative abuse 
which section 16(b) was designed to prevent. Blau v. 
Lehman, 286 F.2d 786 (2d Cir. 1960), aff’d, 368 U.S. 
403, 82 S.Ct. 451, 7 L.Ed. 2d 403 (1962); Park & Til- 
ford, Ine. v. Schulte, 160 F.2d 984 (2d Cir.), cert. 
denied, 332 U.S. 761, 68 S.Ct. 64, 92 L.Ed. 347 (1947)”’ 
(emphasis added). Id., at p. 353. 


Even a cursory view of the facts presented herein are 
enough to show that to decide for Foremost would require 
application of an extremely crude rule of a most deformed 
and misshapen thumb. In all its essential details the form 
of the transaction was insisted upon if not dictated by 


stl Rte a AR NL OE AEA LNG He AE EOS 


4la 
Appendia A 


Foremost, often contrary to the plans and wishes of Provi- 
dent. If the matter had been handled as Provident wished, 
this case could never have arisen. To allow Foremost under 
these circumstances to recover the small profit of Provident 
(almost miniscule in terms of the total amounts involved) 
simply by a mindlessly literal application of Section 16(b) 
would be to perpetrate rather than correct an inequity. 
This the Court is unwilling to do. 

Summary judgment will accordingly be rendered for 
Provident.

Appendix B 
Statutory Appendix 


Sections 16(a) and (b) of the Securities Exchange 
Act of 1934 


Sec. 16. (a) Every person who is directly or indirectly 
the beneficial owner of more than 10 per centum of any 
class of any equity security (other than an exempted secu- 
rity) which is registered pursuant to section 12 of this title, 
or who is a director or an officer of the issuer of such 
security, shall file, at the time of the registration of such 
security on a national securities exchanuge or by the ef- 
fective date of a registration statement filed pursuant to 
section 12(g) of this title, or within ten days after he 
becomes such beneficial owner, director, or officer, a state- 
ment with the Commission (and, if such security is regis- 
tered on a national securities exchange, also with the ex- 
change) of the amount of all equity securities of such issuer 
of which he is the beneficial owner, and within ten days 
after the close of each calendar month thereafter, if there 
has been a change in such ownership during such month, 
shall file with the Commission (and if such security is reg- 
istered on a national securities exchange, shall also file 
with the exchange), a statement indicating his ownership 
at the close of the calendar month and such changes in his 
ownership as have occurred during such calendar month. 


(b) For the purpose of preventing the unfair use of 
information which may have been obtained by such benefi- 
cial owner, director, or officer by reasons of his relationship 
to the issuer, any profit realized by him from any purchase 
and sale, or any sale and purchase, of any equity security 
of such issuer (other than an exempted security) within any 
period of less than six months, unless such security was 
acquired in good faith in connection with a debt previously 
contracted, shall inure to and be recoverable by the issuer, 


2b 
Appendiz B 


irrespective of any intention on the part of such beneficial 
owner, director, or officer in entering into such transaction 
of holding the security purchased or of not repurchasing 
the security sold for a period exceeding six months. Suit 
to recover such profit may be instituted at law or in equity 
in any court of competent jurisdiction by the issuer, or by 
the owner of any security of the issuer in the name and in 
behalf of the issuer if the issuer shall fail or refuse to bring 
such suit within sixty days after request or shall fail dili- 
gently to prosecute the same thereafter; but no such suit 
shall be brought more than two years after the date such 
profit was realized. This subsection shall not be construed 
to cover any transaction where such beneficial owner was 
not such both at the time of the purchase and sale, or the 
sale and purchase, of the security involved, or any transac- 
tion or transactions which the Commission by rules and 
regulations may exempt as not comprehended within the 
purpose of this subsection. 


3b 
Appendix B 
Rule 16b-2 


Rule 16b-2. Exemption from Section 16(b) 
of Certain Transactions Effected in 
Connection with a Distribution. 


(a) Any transaction of purchase and sale, or sale and 
purchase, of a security which is effected in connection with 
the distribution of a substantial block of securities shall be 
exempt from the provisions of Section 16(b) of the Act, to 
the extent specified in this rule, as not comprehended within 
the purpose of said section, upon the following conditions: 


(1) The person effecting the transaction is engaged 
in the business of distributing securities and is partic- 
ipating in good faith, in the ordinary course of such 
business, in the distribution of such block of securities; 


(2) The security involved in the transaction is (A) 
a part of such block of securities and is acquired by the 
person effecting the transaction, with a view to the 
distribution thereof, from the issuer or other person 
on whose behalf such securities are being distributed or 
from a person who is participating in good faith in the 
distribution of such block of securities, or (B) a secu- 
rity purchased in good faith by or for the account of 
the person effecting the transaction for the purpose 
of stabilizing the market price of securities of the class 
being distributed or to cover an overallotment or other 
short position created in connection with such distribu- 
tion; and 


(3) Other persons not within the purview of Sec- 
tion 16(b) of the Act are participating in the distri- 
bution of such block of securities on terms at least as 


4b 
Appendia B 


favorable as those on which such person is participat- 
ing and to an extent at least equal to the aggregate 
participation of all persons exempted from the provi- 
sions of Section 16(b) of the Act by this rule. How- 
ever, the performance of the functions of manager of 
a distributing group and the receipt of a bona fide 
payment for performing such functions shall not pre- 
clude an exemption which would otherwise be available 
under this rule. 


(b) The exemption of a transaction pursuant to this 
rule with respect to the participation therein of one party 
thereto shall not render such transaction exempt with re- 
spect to participation of any other party therein unless 
such other party also meets the conditions of this rule.

PROCEEDINGS 


Entered Summary Judgment, filed Sept. 29, 1971, 
that Provident Securities Company has no liability 
under Sec. 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 
1934 for the sale of Foremost-McKesson, Inc. con- 
vertible subordinated debentures in 1969; the 
motion for partial summary judgment of Foremost- 
McKesson, Ine. is denied and the motion for sum- 
mary judgment of Provident Securities Co. is 
granted and Plaintiff and Counter-defendant shall 
receive its costs of suit.

Complaint for Declaratory Judgment Under the 
Federal Securities Exchange Act of 1934 


IN THE 
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT 
For tHe Norruern Disraict or CaurrorNia 


No. C-70 460 SAW 
$$$ 


Provivent Securities Company, a California corporation, 
Plaintiff, 


v. 


Foremost-McKesson, Inc., a Maryland corporation, 
Defendant. 
Ee 


Plaintiff Provment Securirms Company, a California 
corporation (hereinafter called ‘‘Provident’’), complains 
of Foremost-McKesson, Inc., a Maryland corporation 
(hereinafter called ‘‘Foremost’’), and avers as follows: 


1. This action arises under Section 16(b) of the Secu- 
rities Exchange Act of 1934, 15 U.S.C. §78p(b) (hereinafter 
called ‘‘Section 16(b)’’), and this Court has jurisdiction 
under said Section 16(b) and under Section 27 of said Act, 
15 U.S.C. §78aa, as amended. Most of the acts and trans- 
actions involved in this action occurred in the Northern 
District of California. In addition, Foremost is licensed 
to do business and is doing business in the Northern Dis- 
trict of California. 


2. An actual controversy has arisen, and now exists, 
relating to the rights and duties of the plaintiff and the 
defendant, and this is an action for a declaratory judgment 


OO 


A4 
Complaint 


pursuant to 28 U.S.C. $2201, for the purpose of determining 
the rights and duties of the parties in said actual contro- 
versy, as hereinafter more fully appears. 


3. On or about September 25, 1969, Provident entered 
into a Purchase Agreement with Foremost (hereinafter 
called the ‘‘Original Purchase Agreement’’), whereby cer- 
tain of Provident’s assets were to be sold to Foremost in 
exchange for cash and 6% Convertible Subordinated De- 
bentures of Foremost, due June 15, 1994 (hereinafter called 
the ‘‘Debentures’’). On or about October 15, 1969, the 
parties re-negotiated the Original Purchase Agreement and 
executed a Supplement to Purchase Agreement (the Sup- 
plement to Purchase Agreement and those provisions of 
the Original Purchase Agreement not changed by said 
Supplement to Purchase Agreement are hereinafter called 
the ‘‘Final Purchase Agreement’’) which materially altered 
and reduced the purchase price of the Original Purchase 
Agreement. On October 15, 1969, after the parties agreed 
to the Final Purchase Agreement, Provident transferred 
its assets to Foremost and received (i) $4,250,000 cash; 
(ii) $15,000,000 principal amount of Debentures ; and (iii) 
the right to the proceeds from the public sale of $25,000,000 
principal amount of Debentures, the legal title to such 
Debentures being transferred to Provident on October 15 
1969, for the purpose of a public sale as is hereinafter more 
fully set forth. In addition, $2,500,000 principal amount 
of Debentures were placed in escrow to cover claims of 
Foremost, if any, arising under the Final Purchase Agree- 
ment prior to April 15, 1970, after which time the remain- 
ing Debentures in escrow will be delivered to Provident. 
On October 20, 1969, pursuant to the Preliminary Adjusted 
Balance Sheets as provided for in the Final Purchase 
Agreement, an additional $7,500,000 principal amount of 
Debentures were delivered to Provident. 


A5 


Complaint 


4. At the same time Provident and Foremost entered 
into the Original Purchase Agreement, said parties also 
approved a form of underwriting agreement whereby the 
shareholders of Provident would sell to the public some 
$25,000,000 principal amount of Debentures as soon as 
possible after receipt of said Debentures from Foremost. 
However, after Provident experienced some difficulty in 
reaching each of its selling shareholders and obtaining their 
consent to the public offering of their pro rata share of 
the $25,000,000 principal amount of Debentures, which diffi- 
culty it was felt might delay the proposed public offering, 
and because a few of the shareholders of Provident were 
minors who could not consent to a public offering of their 
respective pro rata share of the Debentures, the parties, on 
or about October 15, 1969, agreed to a transfer of the legal 
title to said $25,000,000 principal amount of Debentures to 
Provident who would then proceed with a public sale of 
said Debentures for the direct benefit of its shareholders. 
Consequently, under the terms of the Final Purchase Agree- 
ment, Foremost agreed to register said $25,000,000 prin- 
cipal amount of Debentures under the Securities Act of 
1933 so that a sale thereof could occur as soon as possible 
after legal title to said Debentures was transferred to 
Provident. 


5. Thereafter, on or about October 21, 1969, Provident, 
Foremost and the Underwriters executed an Underwriting 
Agreement whereby the Underwriters agreed to purchase 
the $25,000,000 principal amount of the Debentures at a 
net price to Provident of $101.25 per $100 face amount of 
the Debentures, or a total net price of $25,366,666.66. The 
Settlement Date for said purchase occurred on October 28, 
1969. 


6. On the basis of the afore-mentioned transactions, 
Foremost contends that Provident was a 10% beneficial 
owner of a class of equity securities of Foremost as a 


A6 
Complaint 


result of the afore-mentioned transactions, that Provident’s 
purchase price of said Debentures was their face amount, 
and that Provident is liable to Foremost under Section 
16(b) for alleged profits arising out of said transactions, 
such alleged profits being the amount Provident received 
for said Debentures over their face amount. 


7. Provident, on the other hand, denies that said trans- 
actions resulted in any liability under Section 16(b), and 
contends that Section 16(b) is not applicable to said trans- 
actions for the following reasons, among others: (i) Provi- 
dent did not purchase, within the meaning of Section 16(b), 
the $25,000,000 principal amount of Debentures which were 
sold at the public offering and sale; (ii) even if Provident 
did purchase said $25,000,000 principal amount of Deben- 
tures, no profit was realized since the purchase price of 
said Debentures equalled or exceeded the selling price of 
said Debentures; (iii) even if Provident did purchase said 
$25,000,000 principal amount of Debentures Provident was 
not a 10% beneficial owner of a class of equity securities 
of Foremost within the meaning of Section 16(b) at the 
time of the sale of the Debentures; (iv) even if Provident 
did purchase said $25,000,000 principal amount of Deben- 
tures, the purchase and sale of said Debentures was for 
the direct benefit of Provident shareholders who were not 
10% beneficial owners of a class of equity securities of 
Foremost within the meaning of Section 16(b); (v) even 
if Provident did purchase said $25,000,000 principal amount 
of Debentures, both the acquisition and disposition of the 
$25,000,000 principal amount of Debentures by Provident 


did purchase said $25,000,000 principal amount of Deben- 
tures, at no time did, or could Provident have access to 


| ia 


A7 
Complaint 


any confidential information of Foremost as a result of 
said transactions. 


8. Because Provident is in the process of dissolving, 
having elected to wind up and dissolve on September 26, 
1969 (the same date it anproved the Original Purchare 
Agreement), and because Provident, on September 26, 1969, 
adopted a Plan of Complete Liquidation whereby all of its 
assets, after having paid off or made provision for all 
claimants, are to be distributed to its shareholders by 
September 25, 1970, it is necessary for Provident to com- 
mence this action for declaratory judgment so as to extin- 
guish the afore-mentioned Section 16(b) claim of Foremost, 
which claim, in the absence of this action, can be asserted 
by Foremost or on its behalf by any of its shareholders, 
at any time within two years of the sale of the Debentures. 


Wuererokre, plaintiff demands that the Court adjudge : 


1. That plaintiff has not violated Section 16(b) as a 
result of the afore-mentioned transactions ; 


2. That plaintiff is not liable to Foremost for any 
Section 16(b) profits as a result of the afore-mentioned 
transactions; and 


3. That plaintiff have such other and further relief as 
the Court shall deem just and proper. 


Dated: March 2, 1970.

Stock Exchange but is listed on any other recognized stock exchange in the United States, the average 
of the closing prices of such security on all suc: other recognized stock exchanges on which such 
Security is listed on such day, or, if there shall h: ve been no sales on the appropriate such exchange 
on such day, the average of the bid and asked prices of such security on such day as published in The 
Wall Street Journal for such day or, if the security shall not be so listed on any recognized stock 
exchange in the United States, the average of the bid prices of such security on such day as reported 
by the National Quotation Bureau, Incorporated.

EXHIBIT C 


ESCROW AGREEMENT 


AGREEMENT dated as of October 15, 1969, between Foremost-McKesson, Inc., a Maryland 
corporation (herein called the “Purchaser”), Provipent Securities ComPany, a California corporation 
(herein called the “Seller”), and Bawx or America, Nationat Trust & Savincs AssociaTion, a 
national banking association (herein called the “Escrow Agent’), 


WiITNESSETH: 


Werereas, the Seller and the Purchaser are parties to a Purchase Agreement (herein called the 
“Purchase Agreement”), dated September 25, 1969, providing for the sale of certain properties and 
assets of the Seller to the Purchaser; and 

WHEREAS, pursuant to the Purchase Agreement certain securities are to be deposited in escrow with 
the Escrow Agent; 

Now, THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual covenants contained in the Purchase Agreement 
and in this Escrow Agreement, the parties hereto hereby agree as follows: 

1. The Purchaser shall deposit with the Escrow Agent on the date hereof its 6% Convertible 
Subordinated Debentures due June 15, 1994 in the aggregate principal amount of $2,500,000 to be held 
by the Escrow Agent subject to the terms and conditions herein contained (herein, together with any 
interest or other moneys received in respect thereof, investments made hereunder and any income received 
thereon pursuant hereto, called the “Escrow Fund”). 

2. While held by the Escrow Agent pursuant to this Escrow Agreement, the Escrow Fund shall, 
subject to the terms and conditions of this Escrow Agreement, be applied (i) to adjust the purchase 
price set forth in the Purchase Agreement in the manner provided herein and (ii) to indemnify and 
hold harmless the Purchaser against and in respect of the entire amount of any loss, liability or reasonable 
and actual expense incurred by the Purchaser as a result of any misrepresentation or breach of warranty 
or agreement of the Seller contained in Section 3(b) (as to Crocker only), the last sentence of Section 
3(c) (as to Crocker only), the last sentence of Section 3(¢) and the first sentence of Section 3(f) (as to 
Crocker only) of the Purchase Agreement (herein called a “Loss”). As used herein the term “Loss” 
shall also include 38.9% of the amount of any loss, liability or reasonable and actual expense incurred by 
Crocker in excess of $300,000 as a result of an event or fact the existence or occurrence of which would 
constitute a misrepresentation or breach of warranty or agreement of the Seller contained in Section 
3(b) (as to Crocker only), the last sentence of Section 3(c) (as to Crocker only), the last sentence of 
Section 3(e) and the first sentence of Section 3(f) (as to Crocker only) of the Purchase Agreement 
or from any contingent obligation reflected in the Closing Balance Sheet of Crocker referred to in the 
Purchase Agreement. Anything herein to the contrary notwithstanding, there shall be no recovery from 
the Escrow Fund as a result of any misrepresentation or breach of warranty contained in the last 
sentence of said Section 3(c) due to the fact that the facts or events specified in Section 3(d) of the 
Purchase Agreement as to Crocker or any of its subsidiaries are untrue. The liability of Seller, and 
Purchaser’s sole recourse, in respect to any adjustment of the purchase price provided for in the Purchase 
Agreement and herein and in respect to any Loss or any other obligation under the Purchase Agreement 
or this Agreement shall be limited to the Escrow Fund provided for herein. 

3. If the aggregate Preliminary Adjusted Purchase Price (as defined in Section 2(f) of the 
Purchase Agreement) exceeds the aggregate purchase price as finally determined pursuant to the Purchase 
Agreement, the Seller and the Purchaser shall certify such excess to the Escrow Agent. The Escrow 
Agent promptly thereafter shall deliver to the Purchaser an aggregate principal amount of Debentures 
equal to such excess, except that if such excess is not an integral multiple of $1,000, the Escrow 
Agent shall deliver to the Purchaser an aggregate principal amount of Debentures equal to the next 
higher integral multiple of $1,000 and to the extent such next higher integral multiple of $1,000 


{1} 


exceeds the amount otherwise due to the Purchaser, the Purchaser shall deliver to the Seller a check 
for such amount. Any interest or other moneys theretofore received by the Escrow Agent on the 
Debentures delivered to the Purchaser (together with interest at the rate of 6% per annum thereon 
from the date of receipt thereof) shall at the same time be paid by the Escrow Agent to the Purchaser. 
At the time of such delivery to the Purchaser, the Escrow Agent shall also deliver to the Seller Debentures 
(and any interest or other moneys theretofore received thereon) in an aggregate principal amount equal 
to $1,000,000 less (i) the aggregate principal amount of any Debentures then being delivered to the 
Purchaser, (ii) such aggregate principal amount of Debentures as is equal to the aggregate amount of 
Losses theretofore paid to the Purchaser from the Escrow Fund, and (iii) such aggregate principal 
amount of Debentures as is equal to the aggregate amount of Losses theretofore asserted by the Pur- 
chaser and not yet certified to the Escrow Agent by the Seller and the Purchaser. 


4. (a) If the Purchaser is of the opinion that any Loss has occurred, and desires to have the 
Escrow Fund or any part thereof applied thereto pursuant to this Escrow Agreement, the Purchaser 
shall promptly so notify the Seller in writing at the address provided in paragraph 14 hereof and shall 
transmit a copy of such notice to the Escrow Agent. Any such notice shall contain a detailed statement 
specifying the circumstances and computation of such asserted Loss. Notice of any claim of Loss with 
respect to the Escrow Fund must be given on or prior to April 15, 1970. 


(b) The amount of any Loss asserted by the Purchaser by notice given pursuant to subparagraph 
4(a) hereof shall be certified to the Escrow Agent in writing jointly by the Purchaser and the Seller if 
they agree on said amount. If they cannot so agree within a period of 30 days after notice is given 
pursuant to subparagraph 4(a) hereof, either the Purchaser or the Seller shall be entitled after 30 days 
following the giving of such notice to direct submission of the matter or matters in dispute for decision to 
an Arbitration Committee initially composed of one person designated by the Purchaser and one person 
designated by the Seller. If such arbitrators fail to agree upon the settlement of any dispute submitted 
to them within 30 days, they shall designate a third arbitrator whose individual determination of the 
matter in dispute, based on a complete review of the matters in dispute, and on such information as 
either party may choose to present, shall be in lieu of the determination by the two named arbitrators. 
In the event the two arbitrators fail to choose a third arbitrator within 20 days after said 30 day period, 
either party hereto may apply for resolution of the dispute to the American Arbitration Association in 
San Francisco. The Purchaser and the Seller shall promptly notify the Escrow Agent of such submission 
to arbitration. As promptly as possible thereafter the arbitrator(s) shall certify to the Escrow Agent, 
and to the Purchaser and the Seller, that there is no Loss or, if there is a Loss, the amount thereof. 
Such certification shall contain a detailed statement specifying the circumstances and computation of any 
Loss. The determination of the arbitrator(s) as to the amount of the Loss shall be conclusive and 
binding upon the Purchaser and the Seller. Such determination may be deferred pending the time 
when any Loss which is uncertain or contingent becomes fixed. The Seller and the Purchaser shall 
each bear its own expenses, including legal and accounting fees, if any, with respect to any disagreement 
hereunder. If the matter is submitted to arbitration, the arbitrator(s) shall designate the party or parties 
to bear the other expenses of such determination and/or the respective amounts to be borne by each. 
Promptly after the certification to the Escrow Agent of any Loss pursuant to this subparagraph (b), 
the Escrow Agent shall pay to the Purchaser from the Escrow Fund an aggregate principal amount 
of Debentures equal to the amount of the Loss so certified. Any interest or other moneys theretofore 
received by the Escrow Agent on such Debentures (together with interest at the rate of 6% per annum 
thereon from the date of receipt thereof) shall at the same time be paid to the Purchaser. 


(c) In the event that the Escrow Agent shall not have received on or prior to April 15, 1970 
a copy of any notice of a Loss asserted by the Purchaser pursuant to the provisions of subparagraph (b) 
of this paragraph 4 (or if each Loss asserted has been satisfied prior to such date), then promptly after 
such date the Escrow Agent shall deliver the Escrow Fund still retained by it to the Seller. In the 
event that at April 15, 1970 the Purchaser shall have asserted any Loss or Losses hereunder and 
the amount of such Loss or Losses has not been certified to the Escrow Agent pursuant to subparagraph

(b) of this paragraph 4, then the Escrow Agent shall deliver to the Seller only such aggregate principal 
amount of Debentures, if any (and any interest or other moneys theretofore received thereon), as

or Losses claimed by the Purchaser. Promptly following the certification of any Loss or Losses referred 
to in the preceding sentence to the Escrow Agent pursuant to subparagraph (b) of this paragraph 4, the 
Escrow Agent shall deliver to the Purchaser an aggregate principal amount of Debentures equal to 
the amount of such Loss or Losses. Any interest or other moneys theretufore received by the Escrow

refrain from doing in connection herewith, except its own wilful misconduct. 

11. The Escrow Agent may seek the advice of legal counsel in the event of any dispute or question 
as to the construction of any of the provisions of this Agreement or its duties hereunder, and it shall 
incur no liability and shall be fully protected in respect of any action taken, omitted or suffered by it in 
good faith in accordance with the opinion of such counsel. 

12. If a controversy arises between one or more of the parties hereto, or between any of the parties 
hereto, and any person not a party hereto, as to whether or not or to whom the Escrow Agent shall

deliver the Escrow Fund or any portion thereof or as to any other matter arising out of or relating to 
this Agreement or the escrow deposits deposited hereunder, the Escrow Agent shall not be required to 
determine the same and need not make any delivery of the Escrow Fund or any portion thereof but may 
retain it until the rights of the parties to the dispute shall have finally been determined by agreement or 
by final order of a court of competent jurisdiction, provided, however, that the time for appeal of any 
such final order has expired without an appeal having been made. The Escrow Agent shall celiver the 
escrow deposits or any portion thereof within fifteen (15) days after the Escrow Agent has received 
written notice of any such agreement or final order accompanied by an affidavit that the time of appeal 
has expired without an appeal having been made. The Escrow Agent siiall be entitied to assume that 
no such controversy has arisen unless it has received a written notice that such a controversy has arisen 
which refers specifically to this Agreement and identifies by name and address the adverse claimants 
to the controversy. 


13. The Seller agrees to pay for the services of the Escrow Agent hereunder and to reimburse the 
Escrow Agent for all reasonable expenses, disbursements and advances incurred or made by the Escrow 
Agent in the performance of its duties hereunder, including but not limited to reasonable fees, expenses 
and disbursements of its counsel.

Q. [By Mr. Austin] Mr. Haskell, would you explain 
please the relationship of your firm to this transaction and 
what you were employed by Provident to do and what you 
have done in that employment. A. Certainly. We were 
employed starting approximately one year ago as financial 
advisor to the Provident Securities Company to first deter- 
mine what should be done today with this company and sec- 
ondly to try to implement whatever recommendation we 
came out with. 

We spent approximately six months making a thorough 
review of the past history of the Provident Securities Com- 
pany and came to a conclusion—and I made a recommenda- 
tion to the board of directors and to the shareholders of 
Provident—that the Provident Securities Company should 
no longer continue to exist as it has in the past. 

To give you a little bit of background: The Provident 
Securities Company was organized and formed in 1915 by 
Mr. W. H. Crocker. 

The shares of this company— 

Q. I believe you meant ‘‘the children of W. H. Crock- 
er’’. A. That’s right. 

Q. The four children. A. That’s right. 

And it was organized as a personal holding company at 
that time. And the purpose basically of the company was to 
keep together for the benefit of the children and their heirs 
the (8) capital that had been put together in the family 
and to keep it as a central pool of capital for investment 
purposes. 

Today the Provident Securities Company has as its 
shareholders, with one exception, all descendants of Mr. 
W. H. Crocker. The one exception is the San Francisco 
Foundation, which acts in trust for Mrs. Helen Crocker 
Russell, I believe. 

Q. The bank is the trustee? A. Right. 


A40 
Exhibit D Annexed to Affidavit of Wayne D. Hudson 


Q. I think one modification might be in order. 

I think in several instances spouses of decedents own 
shares, too. A. That’s right. 

The share capital of the Provident Securities Company 
consists of the following: 111,720 shares of outstanding 
preferred stock and 87,000 shares of common stock. 

. Now in the process of our investigation and study of 
this company it became clear that for several reasons this 
company no longer could continue to exist in its present 
form. There were some adverse tax implications under 
present tax laws of the personal holding company. It was 
also quite clear that as generation after generation had 
come into being as the principal shareholders of this com- 
pany, that the same uniformity of outlook on investment 
objectives and objectives for the company no longer were 
true. You had, for instance, certain members of the family 
who were far more interested in income; others who were 
far more interested in capital gain. 

The more we studied the situation the more we realized 
that (9) whatever advantages had existed at the time 
that the decedent had first set up this company in 1915 no 
longer existed today. We therefore made a recommenda- 
tion as the result of our study in about December of last 
year in which we suggested that the Provident Securities 
Company either be liquidated or sold to a purchaser or 
merged with another corporation, but that it go out of 
existence and a way be found as soon as possible for each 
. = yap get their proportionate share of the

through various forms of either merger or purchase of

We explored all the various possibilities. During the 
period from approximately the Ist of January until the

approximately twenty major corporations in this country 
—all who had indicated some interest at some point or other 
in some kind of relationship with Provident. 

Now having gone into great detail with a number of

This proposal consisted of the purchase from Provident of

On the ten business days prior to the closing of this 
transaction we will take the closing prices on each of those 
business days on the New York Stock Exchange of the 
Foremost-McKesson shares. Then having those ten prices, 
we will take an average of those ten. And this fifteen per- 
cent premium will (13) then be placed on that average 
that would come after those ten trading days. And that 
will then be the conversion price of these debentures. And 
that presumably will take place— Well, those ten business 
days prior to the closing—

CHARLES DE Limvr, being first duly sworn deposes and 
says: 


I make this sworn statement in opposition to Foremost- 
McKesson, Inc.’s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment 
on its counterclaim in the above-entitled action and in sup- 
port of Provident Securities Company’s Motion for Sum- 
mary Judgment on its complaint for declaratory relief in 
said action. I am over 21 years of age, and if sworn to tes- 
tify at the trial of the above-entitled matter, can testify 
competently to the following facts, all of which are within 
my personal knowledge. 

I served as president of Provident Securities Company, 
a California corporation (hereinafter referred to as ‘‘ Prov- 
ident’’) from 1967 until the company was dissolved by 
court order on August 31, 1970. Provident was a family 
holding company created in 1915 by the four children of 
William H. Crocker for the purpose of managing the vari- 
ous assets of the Crocker estate. The Crocker descendants 
and heirs were the shareholders in the company. 

When it acquired the Foremost-McKesson, Inc., six per 
cent convertible subordinated debentures, Provident had 
no legal or beneficial interest in any security of Foremost- 
McKesson, Inc. Neither I nor any of my fellow officers or 


A74 


Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


directors were or ever have been directors or officers of 
Foremost. 

The assets of Provident consisted primarily of market- 
able securities and real estate, art works and cash. In 
1968, Provident hired Dillon, Read & Co. Ine. as its financial 
advisers to assist its directors and shareholders in deter- 
mining the future course of the company. After investiga- 
tion of all relevant considerations, Dillon, Read recom- 
mended that Provident should be liquidated either by means 
of a sale of its assets and distribution of the proceeds or 
by distribution of its assets if kind. This recommendation 
was founded on anticipated adverse changes in the tax 
laws and upon the fact that after several generations of 
operation, the investment goals of the shareholders had 
diverged. 

Provident and its shareholders accepted this recom- 
mendation, and in early 1969, Dillon, Read & Co., Ine., as 
agent for Provident simultaneously proceeded to prepare 
a plan of liquidation and to look for a purchaser for Provi- 
dent’s assets. 

During the first six months of 1969, Dillon, Read & Co., 
Inc. investigated possible purchase offers from approxi- 
mately twenty companies scattered throughout the United 
States. After sifting all of the possibilities, Provident 
determined that a proposal by Foremost-McKesson, Inc. 
(hereinafter referred to as ‘*Foremost’’), appeared the 
most promising. There followed throughout the late sum- 
mer and early fall intense negotiations between Foremost 
and Provident. 

Because Provident was selling its assets with a view to 
liquidation of the company, it was primarily interested in 
receiving cash for its assets, but Foremost for various rea- 
sons, including its desire to acquire liquid assets to finance 
further acquisitions, insisted on paying the major portion 
of the purchase price in securities of Foremost to be issued 


- So ee ee eee 


So TE a eR 


A75 
Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


for the purpose of financing the purchase of Provident’s 
assets (namely Foremost six per cent convertible subordi- 
nated debentures due June 15, 1994). Provident argued 
that Foremost should sell said securities to the public itself 
and then use the proceeds to pay Provident in cash, but 
this Foremost refused to do. 

Because Foremost was unwilling to pay cash, Provident 
finally agreed that it would accept Foremost debentures in 
lieu of cash, but insisted that Foremost agree that following 
the closing of the purchase agreement, Foremost would use 
its best efforts to ensure a public sale of the Foremost 
debentures as soon as possible. Again Foremost was un- 
willing to so commit itself, and after extensive negotiations, 
a compromise was reached whereby Foremost agreed to 
effect registration under the Securities Act of 1933 of up 
to one half of the debentures to be delivered as payment 
for Provident’s assets and to enter into an underwriting 
agreement as promptly as possible following the closing 
whereby up to one half of the debentures could be publicly 
sold through an underwriting group headed by Dillon, Read 
& Co., Ine. 

In late August of 1969, negotiations resulted in a tenta- 
tive understanding. Foremost would purchase most of 
Provident’s assets for a combination of cash and Foremost 
debentures which were to be issued expressly for this pur- 
pose. 

Various draft memoranda were prepared by Dillon, 
Read & Co., Inc., and Glore Forgan, Wm. R. Staats, Ine. 
(investment banker for Foremost), incorporating the basic 
terms. Negotiations continued thereafter and resulted in 
various adjustments to the terms and the purchase price. 
True copies of these draft memoranda of August 26, 1969, 
August 27, 1969, and two dated August 29, 1969, are at- 
tached as Exhibits A-1, A-2, A-3 and A-4 to this affidavit. 


— 


A76 
Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


Negotiations between the two companies continued 
through September of 1969, and finally culminated in the 
execution of a Purchase Agreement dated September 25, 
1969, which provided that Foremost would purchase ap- 
proximately two thirds of Provident’s assets for $54,000,000, 
consisting of $49,750,000 aggregate principal amount of 
Foremost debentures which were to be issued expressly for 
the purchase of Provident’s assets. This purchase price 
was subject to adjustment depending on the value of as- 
sets actually delivered by Provident. A true copy of the 
Purchase Agreement is attached hereto as Exhibit B. 

The Purchase Agreement further provided that, follow- 
ing the closing, Provident ‘‘as part of its plan of liquidation 
and dissolution may distribute to its stockholders the 
[Foremost] debentures’? (Exh. B, par. 5(c)), and that 
Foremost would use its best efforts to have up to $25,000,000 
aggregate principal amount of said debentures registered 
pursuant to the Securities Act of 1933 and to enter into an 
underwriting agreement whereby the Provident sharehold- 
ers would sell the debentures so registered at a public offer- 
ing (see par. 5(k)(i) of Exh. B hereto). 

It was contemplated that all of the debentures delivered 
by Foremost would be distributed in kind to the Provident 
shareholders who would in turn be named as selling deben- 
ture holders in the underwriting agreement. 

The Purchase Agreement set the closing date as October 
15, 1969, (see par. 2(a) of Exh. B hereto) and contained 
numerous conditions which had to be met before that date 
(see pars. 6 and 7 of Exh. B hereto) among which was a 
condition that the holders of at least one half of Provident’s 
common stock elect to wind up and dissolve Provident and 
that the holders of at least two thirds of Provident’s pre- 
ferred stock and one half of Provident’s common stock 


ratify and approve the Purchase Agreement

Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


A trne copy of the minutes of said Board of Directors’ 
meeting is attached hereto as Exhibit M and accurately 
reflect what took place at the meeting. 

This latter statement is of particular relevance here. 
For sometime prior to this meeting, we had been wrestling 
with the problem of how to effect a public sale of a portion 
of the Foremost debentures to be received at the closing 
of the Purchase Agreement on October 15, 1969. The 
Purchase Agreement, as executed, provided that the share- 
holders of Provident would make the public offering after 
distribution of the debentures to them, but we became 
increasingly aware that this was virtually impossible be- 
cause of the difficulty in obtaining the necessary consents 
to sell from minor shareholders and because one of the 
shareholders, William Crocker, was at places unknown in 
the Brazilian jungles and could not be contacted. We de- 
termined that it would be best if Provident as agent for its 
shareholders sold the debentures at public offering and 
then distributed the cash received from those sales to its 
shareholders. This required a change in the form of the 
Purchase Agreement to provide that Provident would be 
the selling debenture holder rather than Provident’s share- 
holders. 

Accordingly, on October 9, 1969, I sent a telegram re- 
questing that the various shareholders of Provident attend 
a selling debenture holders’ meeting on October 13th at 
2:00 P.M. A true copy of the telegram is attached hereto 
as Exhibit N. That meeting was, in fact, held on Ovtober 
13, 1969, and I explained the various alternatives and 
problems to the shareholders. Attached hereto as Exhibit 
Ay A, ne copy of the agenda of the meeting on October 

Amendment No. 2 to the form 8-1 registrati - 
ment (Exh. K hereto) reflects this change rsa ie 
of October 15, 1969, to the Securities and Exchange Com-

mission pursuant to Item 43 of the Commission’s guides 
for preparation and filing of registration statements. A 
true copy of that letter is attached hereto as Exhibit P. 

The necessary consents to the change in the form of 
the Purchase Agreement were obtained at the time of that 
meeting. A true copy of the consent form used for this 
purpose is attached as Exhibit Q hereto. 

On October 15, 1969, the Purchase Agreement between 
Provident and Foremost closed simultaneously in New 
York and San Francisco. At that time, Foremost consented 
to a change in the agreement so as to allow Provident 
rather than the Provident shareholders to sell up to $25,- 
000,000 aggregate principal amount of Foremost debentures 
to the public. A copy of Foremost’s consent is attached 
as Exhibit R hereto. 

The remainder of the closing procedure was completed 
on the same day. Foremost delivered to Provident $4,250,- 
000 in cash and $40,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 
Foremost debentures. Pursuant to paragraph 2(a)(ii) of 
the Purchase Agreement, Foremost delivered an additional 
$2,500,000 aggregate principal amount of Foremost deben- 
tures to The Bank of America, National Trust and Savings 
Association as escrow agent. Pursuant to paragraph 2(f) 
of the Purchase Agreement, the remaining $7,250,000 ag- 
gregate principal amount of debentures due under the 
Purchase Agreement were withheld by Foremost until 
October 20, 1969, at which time they were delivered to 
Provident. 

On October 16, 1969, I instructed First National City 
Bank, as trustee under the indenture for the Foremost 
debentures, to split the $40,000,000 aggregate principal 
amount Foremost debenture issued on October 15, 1969, 
into two certificates, one evidencing $25,000,000 principal 
amount and the other evidencing $15,000,000 principal 
amount. A true copy of my letter of October 16, 1969, so 
instructing the bank is attached hereto as Exhibit S.

Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


On October 20, 1969, pursuant to paragraph 2(f) of the 
Purchase Agreement, Foremost delivered the remaining 
$7,250,000 aggregate principal amount of Foremost deben- 
tures to Provident, and Provident executed bond powers 
to effect distribution of $22,250,000 worth of aggregate 
principal amount of debentures to its shareholders. By 
letter dated October 21, 1969, I ordered distribution of these 
to the shareholders. A true copy of my letter of October 
21, 1969, is attached as Exhibit T hereto, and the actual

debentures is attached as Exhibit U hereto. 

On October 21, 1969, Provident, Foremost and Dillon, 
Read & Co., Inc., as representatives of the underwriting 
group executed an underwriting agreement whereby Provi- 
dent was named as selling debenture holder of $25,000,000 
aggregate principal amount of Foremost debentures. A 
copy of the underwriting agreement is attached as Exhibit 
V hereto. This underwriting agreement closed on October 
28, 1969, and on that date, Provident delivered the $25,- 
000,000 aggregate principal amount of debentures to the 
underwriters, and the underwriters delivered to Provident 
cash in the amount of $25,366,666.66. On October 29, 1969, 
Provident distributed this cash to its shareholders. A copy 
of my letter dated October 29, 1969, distributing to the 
Provident shareholders cash including the sums received 
from the underwriters is attached as Exhibit W hereto. 

Meanwhile, liquidation had been proceeding on other

we Sacouhent the period from September 1, 1969, until 
dissolution of the corporation, I as President and a member 
of the Board of Directors and my fellow corporate officers 
and directors were committed to liquidating Provident and 
considered that our sole duty was to get the assets of Provi- 
dent into the hands of its individual shareholders as quickly 
as possible. All of our actions were directed to this end. 
We considered the change in the Purchase Agreement to 
provide for sale of the Foremost debentures by Provident 
in lieu of distribution to the shareholders and sale by them 
to be no more than a change in form to overcome legal 

icalities and simplify the liquidation process.

Provident Securities Company (‘*Provident’’), a Califor-

ings of Crocker National Corporation and Sierra Railroad 
Company stocks, and (iii) $12,000,000 worth of marketable 
securities in exchange for $5,000,000 cash and Convertible 
Subordinated Debentures of applicant in the principal 
amount of $49,750,000, subject to adjustment upward to the 
extent of $2,000,000 cash and the balance in Debentures, 
and downward by reduction in the principal amount of 
Debentures to be issued, all as more fully provided in the 
Exchange Agreement which, it is anticipated, will be ex- 
ecuted by applicant and Provident on September 24, 1969. 
The Exchange Agreement will be submitted as supple- 
— information to this permit application when avail- 
able. 

The exchange is not subject to the approval of the share- 
holders of applicant. It is contemplated that the proposal 
will be submitted to the shareholders of Provident on Sep- 
tember 26, 1969. Consummation of the proposed exchange 
is subject to approval by holders of a majority of the out- 
standing Common shares and by holders of two-thirds of 
the outstanding Preferred shares of Provident. There 
are approximately twenty-five shareholders of Provident 
who may vote on this matter. No proxies will be solicited; 
only notice of time, date, place and purpose of the meeting 
will be given to shareholders in the ordinary course of 
events as provided by law and the By-laws of Provident. 

The purpose of the plan of exchange is to facilitate the 
proposed liquidation of Provident. Prior to a vote on the 
Exchange Agreement, the shareholders will vote upon a 
voluntary liquidation of the Company. The consumma- 
tion of the exchange prior to the liquidation of Provident 
will give Provident the above mentioned Debentures for 
distribution to its shareholders, The Exchange Agreement

September 26, 1969 


Special Directors’ Meeting 


Upon notice duly given, a special meeting of the Board 
of Directors of Provident Securities Company, a California 
corporation, was held at 9:30 o’clock A.M. on September 
26, 1969, at One Montgomery Street, San Francisco, 
California. 

The following Directors, constituting a quorum, were 
present: 


Charles de Limur 
—  E. Merris-Cox 
Robert Homans 
Norton Adams 
Charles Crocker 
Donald C. Lahey 
Neil Carothers, II 
William H. Crocker 


The following Directors were absent: 


Emmett G. Solomon 


Charles de Limur, President of the Corporation, pre- 
sided as Chairman of the meeting, and Donald C. Lahey, 
Secretary of the Corporation, acted as Secretary of the 
meeting. 

The minutes of the last meeting of the Board of Direc- 
tors held on September 3, 1969, were read and unanimously 
approved as read. 

The Chairman stated that the first order of business 
was the approval of a plan of complete liquidation of the 


a 


A96 
Exhibit E Annexed to Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


Corporation for submission to the shareholders for their 
approval. 

After a full discussion of the foregoing matter, on mo- 
tion duly made, seconded and unanimously carried, the 
following resolution was adopted: 


Resotvep, That this Board recommends to the 
shareholders that the Corporation be wound up and 
dissolved and a plan of liquidation as presented to 
and considered at this meeting and attached hereto 
as Exhibit A is hereby approved for submission to 
and recommended to the shareholders for approval. 


The Chairman thereupon announced that Foremost- 
McKesson had agreed with the Corporation to purchase 
from the Corporation a substantial portion of the assets of 
the Corporation for Convertible Subordinated Debentures 
of Foremost-McKesson, Inc., cash and an assumption of 
liabilities. He noted that the Purchase Agreement was 
subject to shareholder approval and presented the Purchase 
Agreement to the meeting. 

Upon motion duly made, seconded and unanimously 
carried, the following resolution was adopted: 


Resotvep, That the form of Purchase Agreement, 
as presented to and considered at this meeting, and 
attached hereto as Exhibit B, is hereby approved, 
and the action of the President of this Corporation 
in executing the same on behalf of this Corporation 
subject to shareholder approval is hereby ratified, 
approved and confirmed. 


The meeting was thereupon temporarily adjourned until 
after the shareholder meeting. After such meeting the 
Board reconvened.

The Chairman proposed that authorization be given to 
transfer securities and property in connection with the 
liquidation. 


Resotvep Fvurtuer, That any two of the following

Special Meeting of Shareholders

meeting.

were present, constituting a quorum.

Plan of Complete Liquidation 


Pian or Compiere LiquipaTion oF PROVIDENT 
Securities Company 


This Plan of Complete Liquidation (the ‘*Plan’’) is 
intended to accomplish the complete liquidation and dis- 
solution of Provident Securities Company (‘‘Provident’’), 
a California corporation, pursuant to the following steps: 


A. The Board of Directors shall adopt a resolution 
stating that it believes that it is in the best interests of the 
shareholders that the corporation be liquidated. 


B. The Board of Directors shall recommend the adop- 
tion of a plan of liquidation by the Common Shareholders 
(‘Common Shareholders’’) of Provident at a special meet- 


ing of all Shareholders to be called by the Board of Direc- 
tors for that purpose. 


C. The Common Shareholders, by the affirmative vote 
of the holders of at least one-half of the outstanding Com- 
mon Stock of Provident, at a special meeting of all Share- 
holders called by the Board of Directors for that purpose, 
shall adopt the Plan. 

Unless the Plan shall receive the affirmative vote of the 
holders of at least one-half of the outstanding Common 
Stock of Provident, Provident shall not be wound up and 
dissolved and the Plan shall not be adopted. 


D. Provident shall file a Certificate of Election to Wind 
Up and Dissolve pursuant to §4603 of the California Cor- 
porations Code and shall give the notices to shareholders 


and creditors required by (4605 of the California Corpora- 
tions Code. 


E. If the holders of at least one-half of the outstand- 
ing Common Stock of Provident shall have voted in favor 


A103 
Exhibit G Annexed to Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


of the Plan and if Provident shall have entered into one 
or more agreements to dispose of a substantial part of its 
assets to a single purchaser, each such agreement shall be 
put to a vote of the Common and Preferred Shareholders 
at such special meeting of all Shareholders and if such 
agreement shall receive the affirmative vote of the holders 
of at least a majority of the outstanding Common Stock 
and two-thirds of the Preferred Stock of Provident such 
agreement shall be approved. Unless the affirmative vote 
of the holders of at least a majority of the outstanding 
Common Stock and two-thirds of the Preferred Stock shall 
be received, the agreement shall not be approved. 


F. If the holders of at least one-half of the outstanding 
Common Stock of Provident shall have voted in favor of 
the Plan, Provident shall as soon as practicable but in any 
event within the twelve-month period beginning on the date 
of the adoption of the Plan by the Shareholders: 


(1) Sell or otherwise dispose of its assets and 
properties in accordance with any agreement ap- 
proved as provided in Paragraph E above, to the 
extent therein provided; 


(2) Make payment of or adequate provision for 
all debts and liabilities of Provident not assumed 
by any purchaser and all expenses of the sales of 
assets and properties and of liquidation and dissolu- 
tion; 

‘2) Pay to the holders of the Preferred Stock in 
cesh their full liquidation preference; 


(4) Dispose of its remaining assets by sales to 
third parties or by sales or distributions to share- 
holders or the trust or trusts as provided in Para- 
graphs G through H. 


A104 
Exhibit G Annexed to Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


(5) Establish the trust or trusts described in 
Paragraph F below, if appropriate; and 


(6) After taking all other necessary and ap- 
propriate action to wind up, file a Certificate of 
Winding Up and Dissolution pursuant to $5200 of 
the California Corporations Code. 


G. Within the twelve-month period beginning on the 
date of the adoption of the Plan by the Common Share- 
holders (but only after the liquidation preference in respect 
to the Preferred Stock has been paid in cash), Provident 
shall distribute pro rata to the Common Shareholders pro- 
ceeds received from the sale of its assets and properties 
and all other assets of Provident then remaining, except 
for funds reasonably retained to meet claims against its 
assets or Provident (other than claims of Shareholders as 
such), including unascertained or contingent liabilities and 
expenses, and specifically set aside for that purpose, in 
complete liquidation of Provident and in exchange for the 
surrender for cancellation of all of the outstanding shares 
of Provident’s Common Stock. Liquidating distributions 
shall be made in such amounts, upon such dates and such 
manner, consistent with the foregoing, without further 
Shareholder action, as the Board of Directors may deter- 
mine, and any partial distribution shall be one of a series 
of two or more distributions in complete liquidation of 
Provident; provided that all distributions made by Provi- 
dent as such shall be made within the above-mentioned 
twelve-month period. 

Except to the extent that the Board shall determine 
that the plan set forth below in this Paragraph G shall 
be impraetical or inappropriate, it shall be followed in 
disposing of assets not sold pursuant to an agreement ap- 
proved as specified in Paragraph E above.

Exhibit G Annezed to Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


Prior to the sale or other disposition of any objets 
d’art, books, furniture and furnishings (excluding office 
furniture and furnishings) (‘‘ Art Works’’) held by Provi- 
dent at the time of the adoption of the Plan and within 60 
days after adoption of the Plan, Provident will cause all 
Art Works owned by it (other than those referred to in 
the paragraph immediately below) to be appraised by one 
or more appraisers of recognized standing. A copy of such 
appraisal shall be sent to each Common Shareholder within 
70 days after adoption of the Plan. Within 15 days after 
the sending of any such appraisal to the Common Share- 
holders, any Common Shareholder may purchase for cash 
any item at such appraised value less 10% ; provided, how- 
ever, that any Common Shareholder having physical pos- 
session of such item on the date of adoption of the Plan 
pursuant to written or oral agreement with Provident shall 
have the right (‘‘Possession Preference Right’’) to pur- 
chase any such item prior to any other Common Share- 
holder. If two Common Shareholders wish to purchase the 
same item and no Possession Preference Right applies, 
no Common Shareholder may purchase unless all but one 
Common Shareholder withdraws his bid to purchase. 

On or prior to October 21, 1969 any one or more of the 
Art Works described in the 1954 appraisal by Parke- 
Bernet (which is on file in the office of the corporation) 
and valued therein at $500 or less may be purchased by any 
Common Shareholder for cash at such appraised value, 
provided, however, that any Common Shareholder having 
physical possession of such item under written or oral 
agreement with Provident on the date of adoption of the 
Plan shall have a Possession Preference Right. If two 
Common Shareholders wish to purchase the same item and 
no Possession Preference Right applies, no Common Share- 
holder may purchase unless all but one Common Share- 
holder withdraws his bid to purchase.

entities who are not Shareholders.

agreements with any trustee or trustees. Provident may 
at any time transfer any assets (other than cash and mar-

the Common Shareholders. Not later than the expiration 
of twelve months following the date of adoption of the 
Plan by the Common Shareholders, Provident may transfer 
to a trust (a) any uncollected claims, contingent assets 
(including claims for refund of taxes or for proceeds of 
insurance) or other assets which may not be converted into 
cash prior to the expiration of said twelve-month period or 
which it is not practicable to distribute directly to the 
Common Shareholders within said twelve-month period, 
and (b) any funds of Provident reasonably retained to pay 
claims (including unascertained or contingent liabilities 
and expenses) and specifically set aside for that purpose 


which may not be disbursed prior to the expiration of said 
twelve-month period.

half of the outstanding Common Stock of Provident in 
favor of the Plan shall constitute full and complete author-

and to make, execute and deliver any and all agreements,

THE COMPANY

1967 of Foremost Duizics, Inc. (herein called “Foremosi”), whose busincss originated in 1931, and 
McKesson & Robbins, Incorporated (herein called “McKesson”), a corporation organized in 1928. The 
principal oflices of Foremost-McKesson, Inc. are located at 111 Pine Strect, San Francisco, California. 
Reference hercin to the “Company” includes Foremest-McKesson, Inc. and its subsidiaries unless the 


context otherwise requires. 


The Company is primarily engaged in the wholesale distribution of drugs; the processing and 


distribution of milx, ercam, ice cream and relat.:] dairy products; the wholesale distribution of wincs and 
liquors; and the wholesale distribution of industrial chemicals

THE COMPANY 


Foremost-McKesson, Inc. is a Maryland corporation which resulted from the merger on July 19, 
1967 of Foremost Dairies, Inc. (herein called “Foremost”), whose business originated in 1931, and 
McKesson & Robbins, locorporated (herein called “McKesson”), a corporation organized in 1928. The 
principal offices of Foremost-McKesson, Inc. are located at 111 Pine Strect, San Francisco, Califoraia. 
Reference herein to the “Company” includes Foremost-McKessoa, Inc. and its subsidiarics unless the 
context otherwise requires. 


The Company is primerily engaged in the wholesale distribution of drugs; the processing and 


distribution of milk, cream, ice eream ad related dairy products; the wholesale distribution of wines and 
liquors; and the wholesale distribution of industrial chemicals.

Competition 

In its domestic dairy business, the Company has active competition from national, regional 
a:d jocal dairy companies and from wholesale customers who may integrate their own dairy supply. 
In its distribution of drugs, chemicals and wines and liquors, the Company has active competitioa, both 
from regional and local wholesalers and from direct distribvtion by manufacturers. 


Employees

employees as satisfactory.

Supplemental Affidavit of Charles de Limur 
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT 


FOR THE NorTHERN District or CALIFORNIA 
No. C-70 460 RHS 


[Same Tit.e] 


State of California ) 
City and County of San Francisco ) ss.: 


Cuar.es pe Limvr, being first duly sworn, deposes and 
says: 


I make this sworn statement as a supplement to my ear- 
lier sworn statement in opposition to Foremost-Mc Kesson’s 
motion for partial summary judgment in the above-entitled 
action and in support of Provident Securities Company’s 
motion for summary judgment on its complaint for deciara- 
tory relief. 

As President of Provident Securities Company, I was 
directly involved in negotiations with Foremost-McKesson 
concerning the value of the assets to be transferred to 
Foremost by Provident and the aggregate principal amount 
of Foremost’s convertible debentures to be paid to Provi- 
dent therefor. The following facts are within my own 
knowledge and if sworn as a witness at trial I can compe- 
tently testify thereto. 

When in late 1968 Provident tentatively decided to liq- 
uidate, we had Dillon, Read & Co. prepare a memorandum 
dated November 6, 1968, evaluating the then current finan- 
cial structure of Provident in great detail. On January 
24, 1969, at my request, Dillon, Read prepared another up- 
dated and exhaustive evaluation of Provident’s assets. 
Both of these documents were made available to Foremost 


A138 
Supplemental Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


and to its financial advisors at the beginning of negotiations 
(the two evaluations are attached as Exhibits 1 and 2 to 
this affidavit and are incorporated herein by reference). 

Thereafter and throughout negotiations, we gave Fore- 
most free access to Provident’s books and records and to 
the various real property proposed to be transferred to 
Foremost. Foremost, with the assistance of Haskins & 
Sells and Coldwell Banker & Company, made a complete 
appraisal of all of the assets of Provident including mar- 
ketable and unmarketable securities and real estate. 

Following this, Mr. Purcell of Dillon, Read and I met 
with representatives of Foremost in Foremost’s board of 
directors’ room and went over with them the evaluation of 
each and every asset of Provident and the various values 
assigned were vigorously and exhaustively argued until 
agreement on their value was reached. 

Thereafter periodic reports were prepared updating the 
value of the various assets and the value of the sharehold- 
ers’ equity in Provident and were made available to Fore- 
most. The last of these reports was made immediately 
prior to the closing of the purchase agreement on October 
15, 1969. 

As evidence of the exhaustive investigation that Fore- 
most made, I point out that Schedule 1 to the purchase 
agreement lists various securities which were excluded 
from the purchase agreement because Foremost decided 
that they did not want them (see Exh. B to my earlier aff.). 
To further demonstrate the lengths to which Foremost 
went, on one occasion Mr. Boyce Smith, treasurer of Fore- 
most, visited Provident’s offices to determine whether there 
was any furniture in the office of value which Foremost 
might wish to take as part of the assets transferred under 
the agreement. 

In light of these facts, I was surprised in reading Fore- 
most’s reply memorandum to see them assert that Provi- 


5 emnputadiatiieat 


A139 
Supplemental Affidavit of Charles de Limur 


dent had information about the true value of the assets 
which was not available to Foremost. It is, I believe, fair 
to say that all information which Provident had about 
the value of any of the assets transferred to Foremost was 
made available to Foremost, was exhaustively evaluated 
and rechecked by Foremost and its advisors and was con- 
tinually updated until the time of the closing of the trans- 
action and even thereafter. 


Dated at San Francisco, California, this 17th day of 
August, 1971. 


Charles de Limur
