Study 
November 6, 1968 


Provident Securities Company 
(‘‘Provident’’) 


This preliminary study is made in response to a request 
by a committee appointed by the Board of Directors of 
Provident. Its purpose is to evaluate the current structure 
of Provident and suggest alternative directions Provident 
might take. 

Provident is an investment and real estate company with 
relatively liquid assets except for a 38.9% interest in 
Crocker Estate Company (‘‘Crocker Estate’’). Its port- 
folio of securities is diversified except for the Crocker 
Estate stock and three large holdings, Crocker-Citizens 
National Bank stock, Texas Instruments stock, and Gulf 
Resources & Chemical stock (formerly Bunker Hill Co.). 
Provident is a ‘‘personal holding company’ for tax pur- 
poses. (See Exhibit I) 

Crocker Estate Company is primarily a real estate 
company and owns a portfolio of diversified marketable 
securities. 

Although no Crocker Estate stockholder owns any Prov- 
ident stock and no individual Provident stockholder owns 
any Crocker Estate stock, three of the nine members of the 
Board of Directors of Provident are also members of the 
Crocker Estate Board of Directors which are eight in num- 
ber. (See Exhibit IT) 

A number of possibilities have been suggested as to 
Provident’s future. Without enumerating the many sub- 


variations of the various plans, the principal possibilities 
may be classified as follows: 


1, Provident to continue substantially as it is. 


~— 


ya a a eee ee oe 


A141 
Exhibit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


2. Provident to liquidate. 
3. Provident to merge: 


(a) Provident as the surviving corporation to ac- 
quire one or more other companies looking 
to the elimination of its personal holding 
company status with a view to subsequent 
issuance of shares to the public. 


(b) Provident not the surviving corporation 
merging into a large publicly-owned corpo- 
ration with a ready market for its securities. 


Possibility +1—Provident to continue as tt ts. 


The principal problems substantially with Provident 
continuing as it is lie in the areas of ‘‘nersonal holding 
company’’ taxation and the diverse interests and attitudes 
of shareholders, fiduciaries, and beneficiaries of trusts who 
do not have the option of selling their stock in the event 
of disagreement with a policy or policies adopted by a 
majority of the Board of Directors. ( See Exhibit IIT) 

‘‘Personal holding company’’ taxation forces Provident 
to distribute all its taxable income other than capital gains. 
There is imposed a corporate tax of 7.2% on dividend in- 
come and 48% on interest and other similar income. The 
balance of such income wher distributed as dividends by 
Provident is further subject to taxation at the full per- 
sonal tax rate applicable to the recipient. It is aarp 
apparent that this double taxation has a profound effect on 
what Provident can and cannot do, particularly in the area 
of investing in bonds or debentures convertible or — 

The corporate form of Provident has the get 
effect of taxing capital gains at the normal rate withou 
increasing the tax basis of the shareholders. sor “9 
capital gains realized by Provident would be taxed whe 


A142 
Exhibit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


taken, taxed again as ordinary income if paid out as divi- 
dends or taxed again as capital gain if Provident were 
subsequently liquidated. Reference is made to a memo- 
randum dated November 5, 1968, prepared by Shearman & 
Sterling with regard to the taxation of personal holding 
companies. 

The substantial unrealized capital gains of Provident 
are of course not taxable until realized. However, it should 
be recognized that not realizing these gains immobilizes the 
portfolio. Were Provident to diversify to a portfolio simi- 
lar to that of a representative investment company, it would 
have to realize large capital gains and pay substantial taxes 
estimated at about $4.7 million. (See Exhibit IV) 

In regard to estate taxes, there is no reason to suppose 
that Provident could not repeat the process of reclassifying 
its common stock into preferred stock and common stock, 
the preferred stock being redeemable with portfolio securi- 
ties which could be sold to meet the estate taxes. However, 
as the Provident stock becomes more widely distributed, 
this method becomes more impractical and cumbersome and 
could lead to problems with shareholders who had different 
interests, particularly as this process reduces liquidity. The 
principal advantage of Provident as it is with respect to 
estate taxes lies in the substantial discounts at which its 
shares have been valued for estate tax purposes. 

Provident’s ratio of expenses to total investment assets 
has not been out of line with other similar investment com- 
panies over the past six years. (See Exhibit V) 

Maintaining Provident in its present corporate form 
presents not only double taxation problems but problems 
in connection with investment opportunity and policy. 

A large pool of capital has many advantages under cer- 
tain circumstances. If the purposes of the shareholders are 
similar, a great many opportunities may be exploited which 
could not be done were the pool fractionated. Advisers, 


A143 
Exhibit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


technical and investment, etc. can be retained, influential 
positions could be taken in new enterprises, and substantial 
borrowing ability utilized. 

The effective use of a large pool of capital is, as stated 
above, dependent on unanimity of shareholder opinion. 
Suggestions as to expanding Provident’s activities in var- 
ious fields such as real estate or other businesses have not 
found w»ified support. Utilization of Provident’s credit to 
back projects entered into by Provident shareholders have 
met similar problenis as well as tax problems. Many share- 
holders, fiduciaries and beneficiaries have expressed a de- 
sire to enter ‘‘tax shelter’? deals because of their high 
personal tax brackets. With Provident in its present cor- 
porate form this form of investment is not a practical 
possibility. In addition, as long as the possibility of liquida- 
tion of Provident rests in the minds of a significant number 
of Provident shareholders, investment activity of Provident 
will be paralyzed insofar as investments of limited liquidity 
are concerned. 

Provident’s investment performance as far as its port- 
folio of marketable common stocks is concerned over the 
past six years as compared with other similar investment 
companies falls generally in the same range. The fact that 
Provident did not do better in this area compared to other 
companies and various published indexes could be due in 
large measure to the fact that Provident’s situation does 
inhibit investment mobility. (See Exhibits V, VI, VII) 

The continuation of Provident as a personal holding 
company would in our opinion tend to intensify the diver- 
gent view of its shareholders and fiduciaries. Remainder- 
men and life beneficiaries in some instances have different 
interests ; in some instances fiduciaries have different opin- 
ions than the beneficiaries of trusts and not all fiduciaries 
are agreed on a course of action or the status quo. These 
differences do not run only to the problem of investment 


A144 
Exhibit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental A fidavit 


objectives (e.g. income vs. capital gain) but also to the 
basic business philosophy which Provident should follow. 
These differences are so basic and so diverse that we do 
not believe that the present management or any other 
management which might be obtained would be accorded 
undivided support of its Board of Directors. Under such 
circumstances a clear cut policy line cannot be followed, a 
circumstance materially adversely affecting the value of 
Provident as a continuing organization. 


Possibility +2—Provident to liquidate. 


If Provident were liquidated, its shareholders would 
become subject to a heavy capital gains tax. Based on the 
average basis of the Provident shareholders the total tax 
payable would vary from about $12.3 million to $16.6 mil- 
lion depending on whether Provident were valued at $800 
or $1,000 per common share. (See Exhibit VIII) Added 
to these figures would be the expenses of liquidation and 
expenses of disposing of both marketable and non-market- 
able assets. These expenses could be substantial. In addi- 
tion, the Internal Revenue Service would, of course, re- 
examine the asset values of Provident perhaps giving rise 
to estate and other similar problems. There would be a 
considerable period of time before all assets received on 
liquidation could be worked into liquid form. Liquid assets 
would have to be sold to pay tax on the total received in 
liquidation. In this connection the stock of Crocker Es- 
tate held by Provident poses the most difficult problem, 
which problem will be discussed later in the report. 

Liquidation of Provident would relieve the ‘personal 
holding company’’ problem and would to some extent lay 
to rest the problem of immobility of investment because of 
unrealized gain. It would also allow the reinvestment of 
assets by each shareholder or fiduciary in what they con- 


a 


news Ait eee eS 


A145 
Exhibit 1 Annezed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


sidered their best interest rather than the group as a whole. 
It may be assumed that some differences in investment 
philosophy would continue to exist between fiduciaries and 
beneficiaries of trusts as to the handling of the assets 
distributed. 

Whether or not the shareholders would receive more 
income and/or build the portfolio faster on their own or 
by remaining in Provident depends on a number of im- 
ponderables including their ability and objectives and the 
views of the fiduciaries. (See Exhibits IX, X, XI, XII, 
XIU, XVI) 

Liquidation of Provident would require the shareholders 
to provide for their own investment advice, tax accountants 
and other services now rendered by Provident. However, 
there would be nothing to prevent certain former share- 
holders of Provident in combining into partnerships which 
performed such services or which undertook ventures in 
real estate or other areas. 

A plan of liquidation would have to be flexible enough 
to prevent any delay beyond one year. Any such delay 
would produce disastrous tax results. During the year of 
liquidation, Provident itself would recognize no gain or 
loss taxwise; however, prior to that time gains or losses 
would be Provident’s. 

The marketable securities present little problem. Large 
blocks such as the shares of Crocker-Citizens N ational Bank 
stock, Texas Instruments and Gulf Resources & Chemical 
should probably be sold as blocks in an attempt to get a 
premium above the existing market price. An orderly dis- 
position of the assets is of great importance as a distribu- 
tion in kind and subsequent selling, one stockholder against 

ld prove costly. . 
ae ood ro a could be sold in whole or in part and 
failing that be distributed in the form of participations in 
a partnership or a trust which could in turn operate or 


A146 
Exhibit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental A fidavit 


subsequently sell the property. The real estate property 
could not be spun off in a corporation nor could it be incor- 
porated after liquidation, since this would destroy the capi- 
tal gain nature of the liquidation. The same entity which 
held the real estate or a similar vehicle could be formed 
to hold other non-liquid assets. 

The Crocker Estate stock could be distributed to Provi- 
dent shareholders, either in the form of trust certificates in 
a voting trust or the shares themselves. 

Consideration has been given to a proportionate partial 
liquidation and to a disproportionate liquidation. The 
former would result in a very heavy taxation and loss of 
liquidity. A disproportionate liquidation would shrink 
Provident’s assets making it a smaller company and rela- 
tively more expensive to run and would involve compli- 
cated valuation problems with respect to the non-liquid 
assets, particularly in view of the large number of people 
involved. If it were assured that those shareholders who 
wished to get out of Provident could do so completely, there 
might be some reason to pursue the matter as Provident, 
although smaller, wculd then have the advantage of a uni- 
fied body of shareholders. However, if fiduciaries and 
beneficiaries of trusts and shareholders were of different 


opinions, the conflicts now present in Provident would still 
be present. 


Possibility +3—Provident to merge, 


The merger route would be advantageous as compared 
to liquidation provided that it be accomplished without the 
sacrifice of values inherent in Provident and provided 
further that the end result would be a thoroughly market- 
able security of proper investment quality which could be 
liquidated by the individual stockholders at will. Such a 
merger would in effect allow each stockholder to control 


A147 
Exhibit 1 Annezed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


the timing of the capital gains taxes he will have to pay 
rather than accepting them in one lump at the date of 
liquidation. | 

It must be recognized that any merger candidate would 
take into account the large unrealized capital gains in 
Provident when determining the terms of the merger. (See 
Exhibit XV) . 

It is recognized that when contemplating a merger 
whether or not Provident would end up as the surviving 
corporation, the large minority holding in Crocker Estate 
creates a substantial problem. It has been suggested in 
this connection that as a first step in.a merger program 
Crocker Estate be merged into Provident. 

While it is evident that a merger of Provident and 
Crocker Estate would provide substantial additional re- 
sources to Crocker Estate, it would, by the same token, 
reduce the liquidity of Provident. 

Because of the above and because such a merger would 
result in the introduction of more shareholders in Provi- 
dent thus intensifying the diversity of interest now present, 
we would not recommend such a merger unless it should 
become an agreed condition to an agreement of merger with 
another company, the combination of which would provide 
the quality and liquidity above-mentioned as a prerequisite. 
In fact, because of the already existing diversity of interest 
we doubt, as a practical matter, that any merger between 
Provident and Crocker Estate could be successfully nego- 
tiated under any conditions except the one above outlined. 


3(a) Provident as the surviving corporation to acquire 
one or more other companies looking to the elim- 
ination of its personal holding company status 
and with a view to the subsequent issuance of 


shares to the puolic. 


The successful conclusion of a program such as 4 
in our opinion, would require certain basic elements whic 


A148 
Exhibit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


we have already stated could not be accomplished without 
the existence of a management thoroughly trained in this 
highly competitive area, able to act promptly and deci- 
sively with the complete confidence and unanimous support 
of its directors, and willing to take risks of a nature not 
common to investment companies particularly where fidu- 
ciaries are concerned. The very reasons which led us to 
believe that Provident should not continue as is militate 


also against the successful embarkation by Provident on 
this course. 


3(b) Provident not the surviving corporation merging 


into a large publicly-owned corporation with a 
ready market for its securities. 


It has been suggested that a merger of this nature could 
be effected with a large and well-known investment com- 
pany or with an industrial company with proper quality 
and size. 


Merger with a large investment company 


Such a merger might well be explored but it should be 
recognized that it would involve special problems not in- 
herent in a merger with an industrial corporation. One 
immediate and obvious problem in Provident is the exist- 
ence of the real estate properties and the Crocker Estate 
stock which could not be distributed separately to share- 
holders in connection with a merger for tax reasons. Also, 
it is questionable whether a diversified investment com- 
pany would desire or would be allowed by the Securities 
and Exchange Commission to acquire the Provident real 
estate assets or the Crocker Estate stock. Moreover, the 
terms of any such merger would be subject to the approval 
of the Securities and Exchange Commission including the 
ratio of exchange as related to the relative portfolio values 


A149 
Exhibit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


after considering the tax liabilities built into each port- 
folio’s unrealized gains. In addition, we are informed by 
counsel that a tax ruling would in all probability not be 
obtainable in advance with respect to the non-taxability of 
the exchange. (See Exhibit XIV) 

It has been mentioned that perhaps Provident should 
become a larger investment company with new shares is- 
sued to the public. This course of action for Provident is 
regarded as impractical. The problems inherent in this 
possibility are much the same as if Provident were to seek 
a merger with a larger investment company, i.e. Provident’s 
holding of real estate and the Crocker Estate stock. In 
addition, the large unrealized capital gains would pose a 
problem as to what shares in Provident were actually worth. 


(See Exhibit V) 


Merger with a corporation other than 
an investment company 


It appears to us that this possibility offers the most 
real likelihood of accomplishment as an alternative to 
liquidation. 

As stated above, the merger candidate would necessar- 
ily have a management in which the stockholders of Prov- 
ident could have confidence. The merger candidate should 
be of sufficient quality so that the Provident stockholders, 
including the fiduciaries, would be justified in retaining 
whatever portions of the stock received in exchange as 
might seem desirable in order to postpone or avoid capital 
gains taxes. . 

Also as stated above, the combination of real estate 
holdings and the minority ownership in Crocker Estate 
together with the large portfolio of liquid securities will 
create some obvious problems in locating the most likely 
candidates. In this connection, it should be stated that we 


A150 


Exhibit 1 Annexzed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


have not been authorized to seek candidates, nor have we 
explored merger prospects in any way other than the re- 
view of certain candidates in our office. However, we do 
feel from this review that there may well be one or more 
suitable companies which might become interested in such 
a merger on an acceptable basis. 


Crocker Estate Company 


Provident’s interest in Crocker Estate (38.9%) is the 
most difficult aspect of either merging Provident or liqui- 
dating it. 

To solve the problems of Provident and Crocker Estate 
at the same time in our opinion is neither practical nor 
feasible. An attempt to do so will, in all probability, pre- 
vent any effective action to solve the problems of either. 

If Provident is liquidated there are the problems of 
(1) valuation and (2) the future of Crocker Estate and 
control of it. If Provident is merged, what value would be 
placed on the minority interest in Crocker Estate? No one 
can reasonably predict the answer to this question. 

If Provident were liquidated, its shareholders would 
have a very substantial tax to pay on Crocker Estate shares 
and would have to liquidate other assets. It is quite im- 
portant that Crocker Estate shares not be involved in any 
transaction which would be the equivalent of an arms- 
length sale and purchase. This would put the maximum 
value on the shares and extract the maximum tax. 

Control of Crocker Estate upon liquidation of Provi- 
dent is another major area to be considered. Crocker Es- 
tate at present has basically three groups of shareholders: 
Provident, the eastern branch of the Crocker family, and 
St. Francis Associates and affiliates. If disturbance of the 
present balance of power in Crocker Estate is deemed un- 
desirable, the Crocker Estate shares could be placed in a 
voting trust upon liquidation of Provident. 


A151 
Exhibit 1 Annezed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


Various suggestions have been made for the disposi- 
tion of Provident’s interest in Crocker Estate: (a) dis- 
proportionate liquidation of Crocker Estate, (b) liquida- 
tion of Crocker Estate into undivided interests, interests 
in a trust or partnership, (c) assuming Provident continues 
as it is, payment of dividends to its shareholders in Crocker 
Estate shares and (d) the purchase of additional shares 
of Crocker Estate by Provident thus giving Provident 
clear-cut control of Crocker Estate. 

None of these alternate courses are considered accept- 
able at the present time and for the following reasons: 


(a) Disproportionate liquidation would require a very 
complicated trade out among a number of people and per- 
haps could not be accomplished since any one disaffected 
shareholder could block the whole transaction. 


(b) Liquidation of Crocker Estate into undivided in- 
terests or interests in a trust would also pose a number 
of questions. Crocker Estate has a considerable amount 
of debt and a large amount of valuable real estate, the 
full value of which can probably be realized only by the 
expenditure of large amounts of capital. Once liquidated 
Crocker Estate cannot be reincorporated and thus, for it 
to continue its current activity, some form must be devised 
(probably a partnership) which is empowered to honor 
large amounts of money—again a complicating factor bet- 
ter left until after Provident’s problems have been solved. 


(c) The payment of dividends on Provident shares in 
Crocker Estate shares, assuming Provident stays as is, 
would have two important tax effects (1) the value of the 
shares paid out would be taxed as income and (2) the 
shares would attain tax basis equivalent to the value taxed 
as income. The Crocker Estate shares are not liquid and 
although the cash dividend paid on them is partially tax 
free, other funds would be required to pay the tax. While 


A152 
Exhibit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental Affidavit 


Provident shareholders would get an increase in basis for 
their Crocker Estate stock to the extent it was paid out 
as income less the amount of tax free dividend, other share- 
holders of Crocker Estate would experience a continually 
reducing basis. 


(d) Purchase of an additional interest in Crocker Es- 
tate by Provident would allow Provident to deliver control 
to a merger partner; however, it would reduce /’rovident’s 
liquidity and greatly increase the difficulties in liquidating 
Provident. 


As noted above, the liquidation of Provident would have 
perhaps only one effect on Crocker Estate—that of a shift 
in control. Crocker Estate could still be sold, merged or 
liquidated. The development of the Crocker Estate prop- 
erties and the passing of maximum benefits to the Crocker 
Estate stockholders is a very complex problem and will 
probably take years to work out. Much would depend on 
the direction Crocker Estate wished to pursue and on fu- 
ture developments, such as: the commercial success of the 
Crocker Building, the action taken with respect to the Vis- 
itation property, the Suburban Realty Co. investment and 
the eventual outcome of the Westbay Community Asso- 
ciates project. Phe success, or lack of success, of Crocker 
Estate’s activities will be dependent primarily on real es- 
tate management skills of the highest order and astute 
financial planning. As with Provident, retaining such man- 
agement would require confidence of the shareholders and 
full cooperation of the Board of Directors. 


Summary and Conclusions 


In light of the reasons set forth in the preceding re- 
port, we have reluctantly been forced to the conclusion that 
Provident should not continue as is. We have concluded 
that among all of the alternatives which have come under 


A153 
Exmbit 1 Annexed to de Limur Supplemental A fidavit 


our consideration the one most measurable and the one 
which appears most feasible and acceptable is the liquida- 
tion of Provident. 

However, it is our opinion obtained from a preliminary 
review within our office that a merger into a large operat- 
ing company on a satisfactory basis might be concluded 
and we thus recommend that an effort be made in this di- 
rection before taking any steps to liquidate. 

It is our understanding that for various reasons any 
plan which could be construed as a plan of liquidation 
should not be adopted for some period in the future. It is 
our recommendation that this period be utilized to make 
an aggressive search for a suitable merger candidate. 

In connection with this search we recommend that you 
employ a firm or firms of investment bankers experienced 
in this area, not only to search for suitable candidates on 
your behalf but also to negotiate and analyze on your be- 
half any offers which may result from such a search or 
which may come in from other sources once it is known 
that such a search is under way.

JUDGMENT 


The motion of defendant and counterclaimant Fore- 
most-McKesson, Inc. for partial summary judgment and 
the motion of plaintiff and counterdefendant Provident 
Securities Company for summary judgment having come 
on for hearing before the Honorable Robert H. Schnacke, 
Judge of the United States District Court for the North- 
ern District of California on August 18, 1971, the Court 


having examined the pleadings, the affidavits, admissions, 
interrogatory answers and all exhibits submitted and hav- 


ing read and heard the arguments of counsel, and being 
fully advised herein, 


A155 
Judgment 


It is hereby Onperep, Apyupcep and Decrexp that: 


1. Provident Securities Company has no liability under 
Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for 
the sale of Foremost-McKesson, Inc. convertible subordi- 
nated debentures in 1969. 


2. The motion for partial summary judgment of Fore- 
most-McKesson, Inc. is hereby denied, and the motion for 
summary judgment of Provident Securities Company is 
hereby granted; and 


3. Plaintiff and counterdefendant shall receive its costs 
of suit herein.

BRIEF IN OPPOSITION TO 
PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI 


It is undisputed that when Provident Securities Com- 
pany (hereinafter ‘‘Provident’’) made its single and only 
‘*purchase’’ of securities of Foremost-McKesson, Ine. 
(hereinafter ‘‘Foremost’’) it did not own any other se- 
curity of Foremost.’ Accordingly, under §16(b) of the 


1Throughout this brief we assume arguendo that Provident’s 
acquisition of the Foremost securities was a “purchase” within 
the meaning of § 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. 
As is discussed in Provident’s conditional cross-petition for a writ 
of certiorari (at pp. 10-14) filed on December 17, 1974 (No. 
74-758), we believe that there was no such “purchase” and that 
therefore the transaction is also exempt for that reason, 


2 


Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. § 78p(b); 48 
Stat. 896), Provident was not a statutory ‘‘insider’’ until 
after consummation of the very purchase here in question. 
Section 16(b) provides an express exemption for ‘‘any 
transaction where such beneficial owner was not such both 
at the time of the purchase and sale * * * of the se- 
curity involved” (15 U.S.C. §78p(b); 48 Stat. 896; em- 
phasis added). The Ninth Cireuit held that Provident’s 
acquisition was exempt under that provision ( Appendix 
to Petition, pp. 1lla-29a). 


Foremost errs in its assertions that there are ‘‘nu- 
merous federal court decisions’’ (Petition, p. 9) and ‘‘a 
substantial body of precedent’’ (Petition, p. 14) to the 
contrary. Only two Courts of Appeals other than the 
Ninth Cireuit (the Second Cireuit and the Eighth Cir- 
cuit) have passed upon the question here involved (Stella 
v. Graham-Paige Motors Corporation (2 Cir. 1956) 282 
F.2d 299, 300-301; Emerson Electric Co. v. Reliance Elec- 
tric Company (8 Cir. 1970) 434 F.2d 918, 923-924, affirmed 
on other grounds, Reliance Electric Co. v. Emerson Electric 
Co. (1972) 404 U.S. 418). The Second Cirenit affirmed, 
without analysis, the construction of a district judge. The 
Eighth Circuit, commenting upon the “paucity of judi- 
cial decision on the precise question presented” (434 F.2d 
923), decided to follow the Second Circuit (434 F.2d 924). 
Contrary to Foremost’s contention (Petition, p. 9), there is 
no holding of the First Cireuit on the question. 


Neither the Second Circuit nor the Eighth Circuit an- 
alyzed, as did the Ninth Circuit, the legislative history 
of the language here in question. As we will show, that 
analysis demonstrates that the Ninth Cireuit’s holding is 


3 


in accord with the terms of the statute, its history, 
and its purpose. It is also in accord with this Court’s 
observation that § 16(b) is not aimed at speculation which 
‘‘could not have been based on inside information ob- 
tained from substantial stockholdings that did not yet 
exist’’ (Kern County Land Co. v. Occidental Corp. (1973) 
411 U.S. 582, 597). 


QUESTION PRESENTED 

Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 
is applicable to ‘‘any purchase and sale’’ by a ‘‘bene- 
ficial owner of more than 10 per centum of any class of 
equity security * * * which is registered pursuant to this 
section”’ but exempts ‘‘any transaction where such bene- 
ficial owner was not such both at the time of the purchase 
and sale’ (15 U.S.C. §§ 78p(a), (b); 48 Stat. 896). Fore- 
most’s statement of the question ignores this statutory 
language and also includes reference to irrelevant matters. 


The question presented is: When a person becomes a 
beneficial owner of more than 10% of an issuer’s securi- 
ties as a result of a purchase of those securities, was that 
person a beneficial owner of the securities ‘‘at the time of 
the purchase”’?

STATEMENT OF THE CASE 
A. The facts. 

As Foremost acknowledges (Petition, p. 3), the basic 
facts of this case are undisputed. Those facts, however, 
are not fully nor accurately set forth in Foremost’s brief. 
We therefore present the following statement: 


Provident, now dissolved, was a personal holding com- 
pany which in 1969 decided to liquidate. In order to have 
liquid assets to distribute to its shareholders in the liqui- 
dation, Provident entered into a contract with Foremost 
under which Foremost agreed to purchase approximately 
two thirds of Provident’s assets in exchange for cash 
and Foremost convertible debentures to be issued expressly 
for that purpose. During those negotiations, Foremost 
had complete access to Provident’s books and records.? 


Although Provident wanted to receive only cash and 
no securities, it accepted the Foremost debentures in a 
compromise under which Foremost agreed to accommo- 
date the sale of up to one half of those debentures as 
soon as possible. Provident thereafter received the Fore- 
most debentures pursuant to the single contract under 
which Foremost purchased Provident’s assets. Prior 
to acquisition of the debentures, Provident had no legal 
or beneficial ownership in any security of Foremost. 
As Foremost notes, the debentures were immediately con- 
vertible into common shares comprising more than 10% 
of Foremost’s common stock (Petition, pp. 3-4). Shortly 


2Foremost refers (Petition, pp. 2, 7) to the Ninth Cireuit’s 
speculation that Provident “could well have had” access to inside 
information about Foremost (Appendix to Petition, p. 7a). The 
fact is that it was Foremost that had access to information about 
Provident. 


5 


thereafter, pursuant to the contract between Provident 
and Foremost, Provident sold one half of the debentures 
received.® 


The question whether any actual profit was realized 
and, if so, the amount of such profit was left open in the 
proceedings below and was not decided by either the 
district court or the Court of Appeals. 


B. The proceedings below. 

The decision of the district court: The district court 
granted Provident’s motion for summary judgment on 
the question of nonliability. The court based its decision 
on an examination of “the surrounding circumstances 
and the equities inherent therein’? (Appendix to Petition, 
p. 39a), concluding that the transaction was not subject 
to speculative abuse (Appendix to Petition, pp. 39a-41la). 
The district court did not pass upon any of the other 
grounds advanced by Provident. 


The decision of the Court of Appeals: On appeal, the 
Court of Appeals disagreed with the district court’s 
holding and rejected or did not pass upon other grounds 
advanced by Provident. Those grounds are discussed in 


8For the purposes of the question presented by Foremost’s peti-

with the contention (see Petition, p. 4) that the date of sale was 
October 21, 1969 (see Provident’s conditional cross-petition for a 
writ of certiorari in No, 74-758, at pp. 14-15). We also do not 
agree with Foremost’s assertion that the Form 4 statement filed 
by Provident shows “the sale as of October 21, 1969” (Petition, p.

writing Agreement dated October 21, 1969” (Appendix to Petition, 
p. 44a; emphasis added). The underwriting agreement itself defines 
“the time of purchase” by the underwriters as October 28, 1969.

Provident’s conditional cross-petition for a writ of certio- 
rari (No. 74-758). 

The Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment because 
Provident had not owned any security of Foremost when 
it entered into the contract under which it received the 
Foremost debentures. The court held that therefore Provi- 
dent was not a beneficial owner of any security of Fore- 
most ‘‘at the time of the purchase.’”* 


ARGUMENT 


IL NO OTHER COURT HAS EXAMINED THE PROVISO HERE IN 
QUESTION IN LIGHT OF ITS HISTORY. 


Only two other Courts of Appeals have passed upon the 
question here in issue.® The Second Circuit approved, with- 
out aralvsis, the holding of a district judge that an initial 
acquisition of more than 10° was a statutory purchase 
(Stella v. Graham-Paige Motors Corporation (2 Cir. 1956) 
232 F.2d 299, 300-301, affirming Stella v. Graham-Paige 
Motors Corp. (S.D.N.Y. 1952) 104 F.Supp. 957, 959).® 


‘Foremost emphasizes that this argument was not “urged” by 
Provident (Petition, pp. 6, 7). It was not so urged because Provi- 
dent believed, as it still believes, that there also exist several 
other grounds in support of the judgment. Although not urged, 
the argument in fact was noted in Provident’s brief. In its reply 
brief, Foremost did not respond to that argument nor did it file 
a petition for a rehearing by the Court of Appeals. 

5The First Cireuit decision cited by Foremost (Booth v. Varian 
Associates (1 Cir. 1964) 334 F.2d 1) involved director insiders 
and not beneficial owners of securities (334 F.2d 2, 3). The proviso 
here in question applies only to beneficial owners and it has long 
been recognized that § 16(b) treats ‘directors and officers as one 
eategory of ‘insiders’ and 10% beneficial owners as another” 
(Adler v. Klawans (2 Cir. 1959) 267 F.2d 840, 845). 

®The Second Circuit later restated its views in dictum in New- 
mark v. RKO General, Inc. (2 Cir. 1970) 425 F.2d 348, 356. 


ae eee ee, wy aa en meee 


7 


The district judge in Stella had based his decision solely 
upon the fear that, under any other interpretation, 


‘** * * it would be possible for a person to purchase 
a large block of stock, sell it out until his ownership 
was reduced to less than 10%, and then repeat the 
process, ad infinitum” (104 F.Supp. 959). 


As the Ninth Circuit pointed out, such a result should 
not—and would not—be permitted: 


**Where a shareholder was within a class of persons 
who had access to inside information by reason of 
their relationship to the issuer prior to making his 
initial decision to speculate, the conclusive presump- 
tion should be applied if simultaneously with the 
conclusion of the closing transaction he is the owner 
of 10 percent of the issuer’s stock’’ (Appendix to 
Petition, p. 26a). 


Neither the Second Circuit nor the Eighth Circuit, 
which subsequently followed the Second (Emerson Elec- 
tric Co. v. Reliance Electric Company (8 Cir. 1970) 434 
F.2d 918, 923-924, affirmed on other grounds, Reliance 
Electric Co. v. Emerson Electric Co. (1972) 404 U.S. 418), 
examined the legislative history of the proviso. The two 
commentators cited by Foremost (Petition, p. 12) also 
ignored that history. Every commentator of whom we are 
aware who has examined the legislative history has 
reached conclusions in accord with those of the Ninth 
Cireuit (see Insider Liability for Short-Swing Profits: 
The Substance and Function of the Pragmatic Approach 
(1974) 75 Mich.L.Rev. 592, 602-606, 616-619; Section 16 
(b): An Alternative Approach to the Six-Month Limita- 
tion Period (1973) 20 UCLA L.Rev. 1289, 1312, ftn. 125; 
Note (1957) 9 Stan.L.Rev. 582). 


8 


‘We respectfully submit that, as is discussed in the 
section which follows, the Ninth Circuit’s holding is cor- 
rect. We also respectfully suggest that, if the Second 
Cireuit and Eighth Circuit were to reconsider the ques- 
tion in view of the material analyzed judicially for the 
first time in the opinion below, they might well reach the 
same conclusions as the Ninth Circuit. 


Il. THE OPINION OF THE COURT OF APPEALS IS IN ACCORD 
WITH THE TERMS OF THE STATUTE, ITS HISTORY AND 
ITS PURPOSE. 


Foremost dismisses the Ninth Cireuit’s detailed review 
of the legislative history without discussion (Petition, p. 
15). Instead, it merely refers to a purported analysis 
of the legislative history by the Securities and Exchange 
Commission wherein the Commission asserted that the 
exemptive provision was designed solely to exclude ‘‘other 
than a voluntary purchase or sale’’ (quoted at Petition, 
pp. 15-16, ftn.). As this Court has already pointed out, 
this limited construction is based upon “a fragment 
of legislative history’’ and ‘‘not only strains, but flatly 
contradicts, the words of the statute’? (Reliance Electric 
Co. v. Emerson Electric Co. (1972) 404 U.S. 418, 425, 
427). 


Foremost also argues that 4 16(b) should be **broadly 
interpreted’’ (Petition, pp. 10-11). This Court has can- 
tioned, however, that 4 16(b) does not reach every trans- 
action which might involve the possibility of speculative 
abuse (Reliance Electric Co. v. Emerson Electric Co. 


9 


(1972) 404 U.S. 418, 422; Blau v. Lehman (1962) 368 U.S. 
403, 411). The appropriate inquiry is not simply whether 
a particular ‘‘interpretation’’ might help ‘‘curb insider 
abuses” (sce Petition, pp. 10-11) but also whether that in- 
terpretation is in accord with the terms of the statute 
viewed in light of its purpose and history. In its argu- 
ment that the proviso should be ‘‘broadly interpreted’’ 
(Petition, pp. 10-11), Foremost assumes the answer to 
the interpretive inquiry without any examination of these 
factors. 


A. Section 16(b) applies to beneficial owners who enter into 
short-swing transactions at a time when they are presumed 
to have access to inside information. 


The Ninth Circuit examined the legislative history of 
§ 16(b) in light of its recognized purpose of curbing short- 
swing speculation by corporate insiders (see Appendix to 
Petition, pp. 15a-29a). In the case of a beneficial owner, 
the court concluded that the statute’s conclusive presump- 
tion of intention to speculate applied to a purchaser who, 
at the time he made the decision to purchase, was within 
the class of persons who could reasonably be expected to 
have access to inside information by reason of their rela- 
tionship to the corporation (Appendix to Petition, p. 27a). 
Application of the conclusive presumption to a purchaser 
who had no such relationship would, as the court noted, 
“impose an arbitrary hardship on a good faith investor” 
(Appendix to Petition, p. 27a). These conclusions are in 
accord with the legislative history which demonstrates that 
§ 16(b) was intended to apply to beneficial owners who 
enter into short-swing transactions at a time when they 


may be pressuned to have access to inside information, 


10 


Under the initial draft presented to Congress, it was 
clear that insider status must precede the questioned pur- 
chase. That draft provided: 


“(b) Jt shall be unlawful for any director, officer, 
or owner of securities, owning as of record and/or 
beneficially more than 5 percent of any class of stock 
of any issuer, any security of which is registered on 
a national securities exchange— 


(1) To purchase any such registered security with 
the intention or expectation of selling the same secu- 
rity within 6 months; and any profit made by such 
person on any transaction in such a registered secu- 
rity extending over a period of less than 6 months 
shall inure to and be recoverable by the issuer, irre- 
spective of any intention or expectation on his part 
in entering into such transaction of holding the secu- 
rity purchased for a period exceeding 6 months” 
(Hearings on S.Res. 84, S.Res. 56 and S.Res. 97, Sen- 
ate Comm. on Banking and Currency, 73 Cong. ( 1934) 
(hereinafter ‘‘Senate Hearings”), p. 6430; Hearings 
on H.R. 7852 and H.R. 8720, House Comm. on Inter- 
state and Foreign Commerce, 73 Cong. (1934) (here- 
inafter “House Hearings”), p. 9; (emphasis added) ). 


As Thomas Corcoran, one of the chief draftsmen of the 
statute explained, this section was intended to prevent 


“* * * any short-term speculations in the stock. He [an 
insider] cannot, with his inside information get m 
and out of stock within six months’? (House Hear- 
ings, p. 133; emphasis added). 


Thus, the draft affected those who were already insiders 
and might have utilized inside information gained from 
that relationship in entering into the short-swing trans- 
action. 


ee a ea 


CO  —__——————— LL 


11 


When the draft was discussed in hearings before Senate 
and House Committees, there was no suggestion that it 
should be altered to place more stringent limitations on 
beneficial owners. To the contrary, there was concern 
whether beneficial owners should be included at all and, 
if so, whether the five per cent figure should be raised 
(see Senate Hearings, pp. 6556, 7741-7743; and see dis- 
cussion in Appendix to Petition, pp. 20a-23a). There was 
agreement that directors and officers should be covered 
by the statute (see Senate Hearings, pp. 6556, 7742-7743). 
There was also agreement that the statute should cover 
a sale and repurchase of securities as well as a purchase 
and sale (see Senate Hearings, pp. 6557-6558; and see 
discussion in Appendix to Petition, pp. '7a-18a). 


The draft was thereafter amended to include a sale 
and repurchase and also to raise from 5 to 10 per cent 
the amount of beneficial ownership necessary to bring the 
statute into play. In the course of amendment, the in- 
troductory clause was altered. A declaration of purpose 
and the proviso here in question were added. Congress de- 
clared that 4 16(b) was directed against ‘‘unfair use of 
information which may have been obtained by [an insider] 
by reason of his relationship to the issuer.”” Congress also 
specified that, in the case of a beneficial owner, the rela- 
tionship must exist ‘both at the time of the purchase 
and sale.”’ Plainly, there can be no abuse of inside infor- 
mation ‘‘at the time of the purchase” if no relationship 


then exists. 


Because Congress’ concern was that the draft provi- 
sion relating to beneficial owners might be too stringent, 
there is no basis for concluding that the proviso was 


12 


intended to change the requirement that beneficial owner 
status must precede a questioned purchase. To the con- 
trary, the addition of both the proviso and the declaration 
of purpose makes it clear that Congress intended that 
such requirement apply to beneficial owners. As this Court 
has noted, the proviso excludes transactions which ‘‘could 
not have been based on inside information obtained from 
substantial stockholdings that did not yet exist’’ (Kern 
County Land Co. v. Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 582, 
597). 


Therefore, as the Ninth Circuit concluded, ‘‘at the time 
of the purchase’ means ‘‘before giving effect to,” rather 
than ‘‘as a result of,’’ the contract of purchase. This read- 
ing results in a consistent interpretation of ‘‘at the time 
of” in applying it to a purchase of securities followed by 
a sale of the same securities. The words ‘‘at the time of” 
modify both ‘‘the purchase and sale * * * of the security 
involved.”’ In all cases of a sale, ‘‘at the time of’’ neces- 
sarily means ‘‘before giving effeet to” the contract of sale. 
If interpreted to mean ‘‘as a result of’’ the contract of 
sale, then a single sale of all stock would not be covered 
by the statute. 


As the Ninth Circuit noted (Appendix to Petition, p. 
27a) and Foremost stresses (Petition, pp. 8, 15), this in- 
terpretation may involve an ‘‘inconsistency’’ in applica- 
tion of § 16(b) to a sale which is followed by a repurchase. 
If a shareholder sells to below 10% and then repurchases, 
both the sale and repurchase may well have resulted from 
inside information gained from stockholdings. In order 
to bring that transaction within the statute, it is necessary 
to read ‘‘ac the time of’’ as ‘‘as a result of’’ the contract of 


13 


repurchase. Such ‘‘inconsistency”’ is, as the Ninth Circuit 
pointed out (Appendix to Petition, p. 27a), consistent with 
the statutory purpose. It also involves much less ‘‘incon- 
sistency’’ than reading ‘‘at the time of’’ differently in the 
case of a purchase and sale of the same securities. 


B. There is no merit to Foremost’s other arguments. 

Certainly, one may speculate about various possibilities 
of speculative abuse in different factual contexts. How- 
ever, Congress provided diffcrent remedies for different 
situations and § 16(b) is only one of those remedies. Fore- 
most’s complaint that § 10(b) of the Securities Exchange 
Act (15 U.S.C. § 78j(b), 48 Stat. 891) is not self-operative 
(see Petition, p. 15) is beside the point. As the Ninth 
Circuit noted (Appendix to Petition, pp. 28a-29a), § 10(b) 
was enacted at the same time as §16(b) to provide a 
remedy against ‘‘manipulative or deceptive” practices (15 
U.S.C. § 78j(b), 48 Stat. 891). It is a matter of common 
knowledge that §10(b), and Rule 10b-5 (17 C.F.R. 
§ 240.10b-5) formulated under it, have been used with in- 
creasing effectiveness (see, generally, Loss, Securities Reg- 
ulation (Supp. 2d Ed. 1969) Vol. 6, p. 3559; Note, 1974 
Duke L. Jour. 610). 

Contrary to Foremost’s assertion (Petition, p. 16), no 
anomaly arises from the fact that there were separate 
**deliveries’’ of debentures. All ‘‘deliveries’’ were pursu- 
ant to the same contract, and hence were part of the same 
**purchase.’’ And, it is the statute itself which requires 
that some purchases by beneficial owners be excluded. For 
reasons already discussed, the Ninth Cireuit decided that 
the statute excluded purchases by investors who could not 


14 


be presumed to have access to inside information at the 
time of their purchase. 

Lastly, there is no merit to Foremost’s attempt (see Pe- 
tition, pp. 16-17) to find comfort in certain passages from 
this Court’s opinion in Kern County Land Co. v. Occi- 
dental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 582. There, the Court com- 
mented upon the obvious fact that one becomes a statutory 
insider as a result of acquisition of more than 10% of 
a corporation’s outstanding stock (411 U.S. 584, 595, 598). 
This does not mean that one is a statutory insider ‘‘at the 
time of’’ entry into the contract by which the more than 
10% was acquired.’ Of more significance is this Court’s 
observation in Kern that there could be no access to inside 
information, and thus no liability, arising ‘‘from substan- 
tial stockholdings that did not yet exist” (411 U.S. 597). 


7For example, the opinion notes that “By May 10, 1967, 
Occidental acquired more than 10% of the outstanding shares 
of Old Kern” (411 U.S. 598). It does not conclude that Occi- 
dental was an insider at the time it purchased those shares. 
Rather, 

“It [Occidental] was thus a statutory insider when, on May 
11, it extended its tender offer * * *” (411 U.S. 598; empha- 
sis added).

For the foregoing reasons, we respectfully submit that 
the petition for a writ of certiorari should be denied.

in connection with the purchase or sale of any se- 
curity.”

REPLY BRIEF FOR PETITIONER 


This brief is submitted in reply to Respondent’s Brief 
in Opposition (‘‘Res. Br.’’). Respondent argues that the 
Ninth Circuit’s decision should stand, but it concedes that 
the decision has created a direct conflict with explicit hold- 
ings of the Second and Eighth Circuits on a fundamental 
point of interpretation of Section 16(b). Economic plan- 
ning requires that a holder of more than 10% of a class of 
equity securities knows whether his initial purchase of such 
securities will bring a subsequent short-swing sale within 
Section 16(b) or not. Although the legislative history and 
the stated purpose of the statute place the ‘‘responsibility 


2 


for meticulous observance of the provision upon the shoul- 
ders of the insider,’’ Bershad v. McDonough, 428 F.2d 693, 
696 (7th Cir. 1970), cert. denied, 400 U.S. 992 (1971), until 
the present conflict is resolved the burden on the 10% 
holder of ‘‘meticulous observance’’ becomes unreasonably 
heavy. 


We will forego detailed response to Respondent’s argu- 
ments until such time as briefs on the merits are required, 
and confine ourselves at this time to but a few observations 
on certain of the matters raised in the Brief in Opposition. 


Respondent seems to suggest that certiorari should be 
denied because ‘‘only’’ two other Courts of Appeal have 
ruled upon the question in issue contrary to the ruling of 
the Ninth Cireuit. (Res. Br. p. 6) Respondent also sug- 
gests that those two other Circuits might well reconsider 
their determination in light of the Ninth Circuit decision. 


To take the second point first, it should be noted that 
the Second Cireuit on December 20, 1974, three months 
after the Ninth Circuit decision, albeit without reference 
to it, reaffirmed its adherence to the Stella case in Perine 
v. William Norton & Company, Inc., CCH Fed. Sec. L. 
Rep. 794,922 (Current Volume). The court there said: 
‘*Applying the plain language of the rule as thus inter- 
preted [referring to Stella], Norton became an insider 
when it purchased more than 10% of Designcraft’s stock.’’ 
(Id. at 97,171) The Court of Appeals there additionally 
relied on the identical holding in Newmark v. RKO General, 


3 


Inc., 425 F. 2d 348 (2d Cir.), cert. denied 400 U.S. 854 
(1970).* 


As to Respondent’s reference to ‘‘only’’ two Circuit 
Courts having reached contrary conclusions, no extant de- 
cision supports the Niuth Circuit’s decision, the one Dis- 
trict Court case to have reached the same result having 
been overruled, sub silentio, by the Eighth Circuit. (See 
Petition, p. 13) Moreover, in addition to the direct hold- 
ings of the Second and Eighth Circuits, both the Sixth and 
the Seventh Circuits have reached the same result by impli- 
cation or alternative holding with respect to persons who 
were both 10% shareholders and officers or directors: 
Bershad v. McDonough, 428 F. 2d 693 (7th Cir. 1970), cert. 
denied 400 U.S. 992 (1971); Champion Home Builders Co. 
v. Jeffress, «90 F. 2d 611 (6th Cir. 1974), cert. denied, 42 
U.S.L.W. 3631 (May 14, 1974). At present, this question 
is again before the Seventh Circuit: Allis-Chalmers Manu- 
facturing Company v. Gulf & Western Industries, Inc., 
Docket Nos. 74-1266 and 74-1267, the issue having been de- 
cided in conformity with Stella by the court below, 372 F. 
Supp. 570 (N.D. Ill. 1974). See also Kahansky v. Emerson 
Radio & Phonograph Corp., 184 F. Supp. 90 (S.D.N.Y. 
1960) ; cf. Booth v. Varian Associates, 334 F.2d 1 (1st Cir. 
1964), cert. denied 379 U.S. 961 (1965). 


Moreover, numerous cases on both the Circuit and Dis- 
trict level have held the initial purchases by officers and 
directors subject to Section 16(b), even when such purchase 


* Respondent refers to the Newmark discussion on this point as 
“dictum” (Res. Br., p. 6, n. 6), but on the contrary, such a finding 
was necessary to the court’s determination of liability on the insider. 


4 


was made before the individual became an officer and di- 
rector: Adler v. Klawans, 267 F. 2d 840 (2d Cir. 1959) ;* 
Blau v. Allen, 163 F. Supp. 702 (S.D.N.Y. 1958); Blaw v. 
Hodgkinson, 100 F. Supp. 361 (S.D.N.Y. 1951); Booth v. 
Varian Associates, supra (point assumed without discus- 
sion). A ‘‘not-yet’’ director can hardly be said to have 
more access to inside information than a ‘‘not-yet’’ share- 
holder who is engaged in intensive negotiations prepara- 
tory to acquiring a major position in the issuer’s equity. 


In a number of other situations where the potential for 
speculative abuse existed (and sometimes when it existed 
only at the time the profit was realized from the second 
transaction) the courts have been quick to find that the 
initial transaction was within the statute’s ambit, even 
though a literal reading of the statute might not have sup- 
ported the conclusion. For example, prior to 1964 when 
the statute applied only to transactions in securities of 
‘*listed corporations,’’ a federal court held that the pur- 
chase of an equity security prior to its listing on a national 
securities exchange, when matched with the sale of a secu- 
rity of the same class fellowing such listing and within six 
months of the purchase, created a liability for insider’s 
profits. Perfect Photo Inc. v. Grabb, 205 F. Supp. 569 (E.D. 
Pa. 1962). Similarly, Feder v. Martin Marietta Corpora- 
tion, 406 F. 2d 260 (2d Cir. 1969), cert. denied 396 U.S. 1036 
(1970), held that a purchase of an equity security by a 


* Indeed, Adler v. Klawans, supra, in reaching the above-described 
result, referred to and relied upon the Stella decision, while acknowl- 
edging that it was not directly applicable, to illustrate “that the pur- 
pose of the statute is remedial, rather than penal, and that it must be 
strictly construed in favor of the corporation and against an person 


who makes profit dealing in the corporation stock.” 267 F. 2 
7 rpo d at 


5 


company having a representative on the issuer’s Board of 
Directors could be matched with a sale of such security, 
within six months, even though the representative had 
ceased to be a director of the issuer at the time of the sale. 
SEC Securities Exchange Act Release No. 8574 (April 17, 
1969), issued shortly after and based upon the principles 
propounded in the Feder decision, observed that Section 
16(b) would seem to apply ‘‘where equity securities be- 
come registered, or cease to be registered, between the 
dates of purchases and sales, or sales aud purchases, made 
within a period of six months.’’ All of these decisions 
reflect a recognition of the dominant statutory purpose of 
providing a highly efficient and virtually automatic remedy 
against the possibility of abuse of inside information by 
speculative short-swing trades in equity securities by in- 
siders. 


The basic thrust of Respondent’s Brief in Opposition is 
an attempt to bring this case within the umbrella of Kern 
County Land Co. v. Occidental Petroleum Corp., 411 US. 
582 (1973). Respondent points out that prior to its entry 
into the Purchase Agreement with Foremost, it owned no 
Foremost securities and, repetitiously quoting from Kern, 
urges that §16(b) is not aimed at speculation which ‘‘could 
not have been based on inside information obtained from 
substantial stockholdings that did not yet exist.’’ Jd. at 
597. (Res. Br. pp. 3, 12, 14). This argument betrays a 
desperate striving to inject into the case a defense predi- 
cated on Respondent’s alleged non-possession of inside in- 
formation. 


6 


The statute itself offers as its purpose the prevention 
of unfair use of information ‘‘which may have been ob- 
tained by such beneficial owner’’. (Emphasis added.) This 
stated purpose is, of course, consistent with the history of 
the legislation and with all judicial and administrative 
precedents. 


If all of this had not made it clear that the statutory 
purpose requires that the courts be excused from grappling 
with subjective intent, surely the Ninth Circuit’s opinion 
should have put this underlying issue to rest, at least for 
this case. Not only did the Court below determine that the 
transactions in issue were to be measured by objective 
standards without reference to intent or potential for abuse, 
but it articulated a fall-back position—even if a pragmatic 
inquiry were appropriate, it said, Respondent’s actions may 
have reflected ‘‘exactly the kind of speculative abuse that 
section 16(b) is designed to discourage’’ (8a), because 
‘‘([T]he general cooperation involved in the transaction 
would indicate that Provident conferred intimately with 
the Foremost management and could well have had access 
to confidential corporate information’’ (7a).* 


It is contended that, despite this ‘‘cooperation’’, Provi- 
dent, prior to its purchase of the Debentures, could not 


* The statement is substantiated by the record. Provident ‘ad 
in 1968 employed Dillon, Read & Co. (“Dillon Read”) to analyze its 
financial structure and prospects. (R. 251) Asa result of its recom- 
mendations, Dillon Read was then employed by Provicent to search 
for suitable purchasers and “to negotiate and analyze . . . any offers 
which may result ... .” (Docket Entry #35, Ex. 1, p. 18) It was 
on the basis of the analysis of Foremost’s offer undertaken by Dillon 
Read and on its recommendation that Provident entered into the 
transaction. (See Docket Entry #17, Ex. D) Unlike the Kern 
County situation, neither the purchase nor sale of the Foremost De- 
bentures by Provident was anything but voluntary. 


] 


— 


7 


have acquired inside information ‘‘by reason of [its] rela- 
tionship to the issuer.’’ A similar contention was discussed 
by the Securities and Exchange Commission more than two 
decades ago. In its amicus brief in Stella v. Graham-Paige 
Motors Corp., it said: 


‘*A person who acquires a large block of stock in a 
single transaction normally has access to inside infor- 
mation. He necessarily would deal in the negotiations 
looking toward the purchase, with either the issuer or 
an insider holding a large interest in the issuer. In 
either event he would be in a position to bargain for 
disclosures not available to the public. It is against 
abuse of information so obtained as well as of infor- 
mation obtained after representation in management 
is secured that the section is directed.’’ Brief for the 
SEC as Amicus Curiae, pp. 5-6, Stella v. Graham-Paige 
Motors Corp., 104 F.Supp 957 (S.D.N.Y. 1952). 


More recently, one of the anonymous commentators relied 
upon by Respondent seems to have reached the same con- 
clusion. See, Note, Insider Liability for Short-Swing Prof- 
its, 72 Micu. L. Rev. 592, at 616, nn. 90, 91 (1974). 


Other considerations as well lead to the conclusion that 
this Court’s reference in Kern County to lack of inside 
information ‘‘from substantial stock holdings that had not 
yet existed’’ was offered only in the context of a hostile 
tender offer—a situation which is the very antithesis of a 
cooperative negotiation involving the exchange of infor- 
mation prior to the time of purchase.* Thus, for example, 


*In a recent decision, the Second Circuit commented as to Kern 
County: “We believe that Kern County holds the defensive merger 
situation to be sui generis in terms of §16(b) liability.” American 
Standard, Inc. v. Crane Co., CCH Fed. Sec. L. Rep. 94,924 at 
97,186 (2d Cir., 1974). 


8 


Section 3(a)(11) of the Act (15 U.S.C. §78e(a)(11)) de- 
fines an ‘‘equity security’’ to include any ‘‘stock or similar 
security’’ or ‘‘any security convertible, with or without 
consideration, into such a security, or carrying any war- 
rant or right to subscribe to or purchase such a security 
....? If the draftsmen of the statute had in fact intended 
to exclude, as a class, transactions which ‘‘could not have 
been based on inside information obtained from substantial 
stockholdings that did not yet exist,’’ they would not have 
defined ‘‘equity security’’ so as to include a warrant or a 
right or a convertible debenture. It cannot seriously be 
argued that one who has invested a comparatively small 
sum to purchase warrants or rights (which perhaps years 
later, and only after making a much larger payment, can be 
exchanged for 10% of an issuer’s common stock) has a 
greater opportunity ‘‘by reason of his relationship to the 
issuer’’ to obtain inside information than does a respon- 
sible person who is negotiating in earnest through invest- 
ment bankers to buy upwards of 10% (or for that matter 
75% or more) of the equity of a major publicly-held com- 


pany. 


Indeed, in this case, it was Respondent’s purchase of 
convertible debentures that lead the Ninth Circuit to con- 
clude that ‘‘Provident became a beneficial owner of more 
than 10 percent of a class of Foremost equity securities.”’ 
(3a) When the purchase of convertible debentures gives 
one the right to acquire more than 10% of a class of equity 
securities, such purchase falls within the statute’s reach. 
Chemical Fund, Inc. v. Xerox Corporation, 377 F. 2d 107 
(2d Cir. 1967). This result is of course consistent with the 
definition of ‘‘purchase’’ in Section 3(a)(13) (15 U.S.C. 


9 


§78ce(a)(13)) which includes as a purchase a mere right to 
acquire equity securities pursuant to a contract. In neither 
the case of warrants or convertible debentures nor in the 
case of a contract to buy does the statute permit it to be 
said that a relationship sufficient to permit the abuse of 
inside information does not exist. Yet in all of these 
cases ‘‘substantial stockholdings . . . did not yet exist.’’ 
Obviously it is not the ripening of the equity ownership, 
but the potential for obtaining inside information in con- 
nection therewith, which may in turn result in cashing in 
a profit within six months by means of a matching trans- 
action, with which the statute is concerned. 


Respondent contends that the clause of Section 16(b) 
which exempts a transaction where the 10% beneficial own- 
er ‘‘was not such both at the time of the purchase and sale’’, 
means that the initial purchase of 10% of the stock should 
not be matched with a sale within six months. While the 
legislative history may not afford a clear explanation of 
the proviso, we submit that this clause was designed pri- 
marily to ensure that 10% shareholders who had reduced 
their holdings to less than 10% would not be held liable for 
their subsequent sales: ‘‘[T]he intention of the languag> 
was to exclude the second sale in a case where 10% is pur- 
chased, 5% sold within three months and the remaining 
5% a month later.’”’ E. Seligman, Problems Under the 
Securities Exchange Act, 21 Va. L. Rev. 1, 20 (1934), quoted 
with approval in Reliance Electric Co. v. Emerson Electric 
Co., 404 U.S, 418, 423, n. 3 (1972). In that case this Court 


10 


rejected an interpretation of the statute which would have 
imposed liability on ‘‘all sales within six months by one who 
has gained the position of a 10% owner through voluntary 
purchase, regardless of the amount of his holdings at the 
time of the sale’’ (id. at 426), but said nothing about ex- 
empting that initial purchase. The clause may also be read 
to ensure, in the context of a ‘‘purchase’’ transaction anal- 
ogous to the ‘‘sale’’ transaction involved in Emerson, that 
one who purchases 6% of the corporation’s stock and then 
another 6%, would not have the first purchase matched 
against a sale of 8% within six months. 


To reiterate a point made in our petition, if there is 
ambiguity in the language of the proviso, there can be no 
doubt that the statute’s expressed purpose of ‘‘ preventing 
the unfair use of [inside] information’’ is best carried out 
by the interpretation which includes the initial purchase 
by a 10% holder with Section 16(b) : 


‘¢. ,. There is no surer guide in the interpretation of 
a statute than its purpose when that is sufficiently dis- 
closed; nor any surer mark of oversolicitude for the 
letter than to wince at carrying out that purpose be- 
cause the words used do not formally quite match with 
it.’’ Federal Deposit Ins. Corp. v. Tremaine, 133 F. 
2d 827, 830 (2d Cir. 1943) (L. Hand, C.J.). 


Conclusion 


The Ninth Cirecuit’s decision creates a clear conflict 
among the Circuits and a fundamental uncertainty in the 
administration of a statute with respect to which predict- 
ability was a principal legislative goal. The decision is in 


11 


conflict with the stated legislative purpose of preventing 
the unfair use of information which may have been ob- 
tained by a 10% owner of equity securities. We respect- 
fully submit that for the foregoing reasons, the petition for 
certiorari should be granted. 


Respectfully submitted,

Jurisdiction 


This Court’s jurisdiction is invoked under 28 U.S.C. 
§1254(1). The judgment of the Court of Appeals for the 
Ninth Circuit was entered on September 19, 1974 (A2) and 
the petition for certiorari was filed within ninety days of 
such date. The petition was granted on February 18, 1975. 


Statutes and Rules Involved 


48 Stat. 896, 15 U.S.C. §§78c, 78p are set forth in ihe 
attached Appendix at page App-1. 17 C.F.R. §§240.16a-3, 
240.16a-4 and 240.16b-2 are set forth at page App-4. Calli- 
fornia Corporations Code, §§4607, 4618, 4800, and 4801 are 
set forth at page App-7. 


Questions Presented 


1. When a corporate holder of 10% of the equity secu- 
rities of an issuer who ‘‘could well have had access to 
confidential corporate information’”’ sells such equity secu- 
rities at a profit within six months of their purchase, is 
such holder liable for such profit under Section 16(b) of 
the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 where the only pur- 
chase within the six-month period is the one by means of 
which it became a 10% holder, or must there be an inde- 
pendent purchase thereafter in order for liability to attach? 


2. In determining whether a **purchase”’ in terms of 
Section 16 has occurred, does a transaction which would 


be considered ‘‘orthodox”’ if cash had been exchanged for 


se +5 sé 
curities become ‘‘unorthodox”’ for purposes of measuring 


— - ee a ed 


Ee ee ee eee ee 


3 


the potential for abuse if payment of the purchase price 
is instead made by exchanging other property, to wit, cor- 
porate assets, for securities? 


3. If the transaction in the case at bar was unorthodox, 
did it nevertheless involve the potential for speculative 
abuse where the prospective purchaser had acted volun- 
tarily, had ‘‘conferred intimately’’ with the issuer’s man- 
agement and ‘‘could well have had access to confidential 
corporate information’’ prior to the purchase and sale? 


4. Is Provident exempt from Section 16(b) liability on 
grounds that it was a ‘‘liquidating agent’’, when the un- 
contested facts demonstrate that it was not a court super- 
vised fiduciary and was acting for itself in both buying and 
selling the securities? 


Statement of the Case 


A. Proceedings Below 


Provident filed its complaint (A3) for a declaratory 
judgment on March 3, 1970, seeking a determination: (1) 
that it had not violated Section 16(b) as a result of certain 
transactions in Foremost 0% Convertible Subordinated De- 
bentures (the ‘‘Debentures’’) described in the complaint; 
and (2) that it was not liable to Foremost for any Section 
16(b) profits as a result thereof. Foremost’s answer and 
counterclaim (A8) seeking recovery of the Section 16(b) 
profit was filed on May 28, 1970. 


On August 14, 1970, while discovery was progressing 
in the present action, Provident filed in the California 
Superior Court, City and County of San Francisco, a 


— 


4 


Report and Petition with respect to its Winding Up and 
Dissolution (A32). In that Petition, Provident described 
this litigation, and asked that $312,500 be set aside in 
a liquidating trust ‘‘to cover any award of damages to 
Foremost from the Section 16(b) claim’’ (A32-33). Provi- 
dent stated that ‘‘such sum represents the amount that was 
received from the sale of the Debentures in excess of their 
face amount.’’ By order filed August 31, 1970, the state 
court provided for a liquidating trust, and after considering 
a submission by Foremost as to the Section 16(b) claim, 
but ‘‘without deciding the merits,’’ required that $804,000 
be set aside for such claim (A62). 


By notice of motion filed October 27, 1970, Foremost 
moved for summary judgment on the issue of liability 
(R84). Provident filed its cross-motion (R179) on June 
14, 1971, and both motions came on for argument before 
Judge Schnacke on August 18, 1971. The court’s opinion 
denying Foremost’s motion and granting Provident’s mo- 
tion was filed on September 15, 1971 (30a, A1). 


Foremost appealed from that decision and the matter 
was argued and submitted to the Ninth Circuit on Novem- 
ber 14, 1973. The decision of the Ninth Circuit affirming 
the judgment below, but on wholly different grounds, was 
filed on September 19, 1974 (1a, A2). Foremost’s petition 
for certiorari was granted on February 18, 1975. 


B. The Statement of Facts 


The basic facts are undisputed. 


On September 25, 1969, Provident entered into an agree- 
ment to sell its assets to Foremost for $54,000,000, consist- 


5) 


ing of $4,250,000 in cash and $49,750,000 face amount of 
Debentures. The closing under this agreement took place 
on October 15, 1969, at which time Foremosrt delivered to 
Provident at least $40,000,000 of the Debentures, which 
Debentures were immediately convertible into more than 
10% of Foremost’s Common Stock. On October 21, 1969, 
while Provident still held all of such Debentures, it entered 
into an Underwriting Agreement providing for the sale by 
it of $25,000,000 worth of the Debentures. The total price 
paid to Provident by the Underwriters under this Agree- 
ment was more than $350,000 in excess of the face amount 
of such Debentures. These key facts involve a purchase 
and sale of equity securities within a six-month period at a 
profit by a statutory ‘‘insider’’. We submit that these 
circumstances require the insider, under Section 16(b) of 
the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, to account to the 
issuer for the profit realized. 


The following recitation of facts is but an elaboration 
on the foregoing: 


1. The Purchase Transaction 


In late 1968, Provident, a holding company, tentatively 
decided to liquidate and employed Dillon, Read & Co. 
(**Dillon, Read’’) to analyze its current financial structure 
in great detail (A137). A memorandum dated November 
6, 1968, was prepared and \pdated on January 24, 1969 
(A137). In these memoranda the complexities of Provi- 
dent’s assets and operations were analyzed and the need 
for detailed knowledge and expert judgment in evaluation 
were set forth. For example, Dillon, Read noted that the 


6 


development of the Crocker Estate properties ‘‘is a very 
complex problem and will probably take years to work out. 
*** The success, or lack of success * * * will be dependent 
primarily on reai estate management skills of the highest 
order and astute financial planning’’ (A152). As recom- 
mended by these studies, Provident employed Dillon, Read 
as investment bankers to search for suitable purchasers 
and ‘‘to negotiate and analyze * * * any offers which may 
result * * *’’ (A153). 


As a result of this search, Foremost and Provident 
entered into negotiations and on September 25, 1969, a 
Purchase Agreement (A35) was signed providing for the 
sale to Foremost of approximately two-thirds of the assets 
of Provident (including real estate and certain securities 
for which there was no readily available market) for a total 
purchase price of $54,000,000. The $54,000,000 was to be 
paid $4,250,000 in cash and $49,750,000 in Debentures, which 
class of securities was created solely for the purpose of this 
transaction. The Debentures contained an absolute and an 
immediate conversion privilege (R650). 


Provident negotiated to include in the Purchase Agree- 
ment provisions that would permit it (or its shareholders) 
to sell $25,000,000 principal amount of the Debentures in a 
public offering at any time over a period of many years, 
commencing promptly after the date of closing (October 15, 
1969) of the Purchase Agreement (A25-26). To this end, 
because the Securities Act of 1933 permits only an issuer of 
securities to file a registration statement with respect to 
its securities, the Purchase Agreement contained Fore-

On September 25, 1969, a hearing was held in San Fran- 
cisco by the Department of Corporations of the State of 
California in connection with the appiication of Foremost 
for a Permit to issue the above-described Debentures in

(A37). At that hearing, a partner of Dillon, Read, Provi-

a result of which ‘‘you come up with a valuation of 
$54,000,000. And that is the valuation on the assets to be 
purchased by Foremost McKesson * * *’’ (A42). When 
questioned as to whether the transaction was fair, just and 
equitable to the shareholders of Provident, he added: 


‘*We think it’s fair because we think that based 
on our expericnce and a review of the assets of this 
Company [Provident] we are getting a fair price for 
these assets’’ (A 46). 


The Permit to offer, sell and issue the Debentures ‘‘for the 
consideration, uses and purposes, and in the manner set 


forth in said application’’ was issued to Foremost on Sep-

2. Interim Events 


On October 13, 1969, the Board of Directors of Provi- 
dent adopted a resolution to the effect that after Provident 
transferred the assets to Foremost in exchange for the 
Debentures, Provident would distribute all of the Deben- 
tures to its shareholders at an undetermined future time 
‘“‘upon dates established by’’ the officers of Provident (A79, 
A120). This resolution did not fix any date for the con- 
templated distribution and it was never implemented in the 
manner expressed therein, —$#25,000,000 principal amount 
of the Debentures were instead sold directly by Provident 
in a public offering. 


According to the papers submitted below by Provident 
(A80) it had realized early in October that the®e were sev- 
eral difficulties in having its shareholders make the public 
offering of the Debentures. In particular, it was impos- 
sible to obtain consents from the minor shareholders and 
one other shareholder who was in the Brazilian jungles. 
Consequently, Provident ignored the Board resolution and, 
at an informal meeting of its shareholders on October 13, 
1969, obtained the consent of two-thirds of its preferred 
stockholders and a majority of the common shareholders 
to make the sale directly, without prior distribution to 
the shareholders (A80-81). This sale, in obvious nega- 
tion of the October 13 resolution, was subsequently ratified 
hy a resolution of Provident’s Board of Directors adopted 
at a December 9, 1969, meeting (R70). 


The agenda for the October 13 shareholders’ meeting 
(A126) included as Item 3 the ‘‘Section 16(b) Problem’’. 
The President of Provident, Mr. Charles de Limur, in his
