C. The Decisions Below 


1. The Opinion of the District Court 


District Judge Schnacke’s opinion, granting Provident’s 
motion for summary judgment, and denying Foremost’s 
motion, did not analyze the facts in terms of the require- 
ments of the statute—that is, in terms of whether there 
was: (1) a purchase and sale, (2) of any equity security 
of the issuer, (3) within any period of less than six months, 
(4) by a beneficial owner of more than 10% of any class 
of any equity security. He did not find any material issues 
of fact which would bar Foremost from summary judgment. 
Nor did he accept the contentions of Provident that for 
various asserted legal reasons it was exempt from Section 
16(b). Instead, the court held that it would ‘perpetrate 
** * an inequity” to permit recovery by Foremost (41a). 


The court did find that the Purchase Agreement was 
executed on September 25, 1969 ( 32a) and closed on Octo- 
ber 15, 1969 (35a) and that the Debentures were delivered 
to Provident as called for by that Agreement (35a). It 
made no suggestion—nor was it argued by Provident—that 
the Debentures were not ‘equity securities’’ within the 
meaning of Section 16(b), or that Provident’s ownership 
of more than $40,000,000 of said Debentures was less than 
ten percent of a class of equity securities. The court ac- 
knowledged that the sale was made by Provident (36a), 
and that the Underwriting Agreement, by which the sale 
was made, was executed on October 21, 1969 (36a). This 
was prior to Provident’s distribution of the other Deben- 
tures to its shareholders (36a), so that its percentage own- 
ership was thus greater than 10% on that date. The court 


viet vatmannie ie rates ian ht NO sleds Re NT eT EE eT SN ee 


et i. etal? 


=. 7 


atin nad: 


pews ~~ ~~ 


7 
: 


13 


explicitly acknowledged that Provident had realized a prof- 
it on the transactions (41a), although it characterized it as 
‘*small’’ and ‘‘almost miniseule’’ in comparison to the 
overall transaction involving $54,000,000. 


The court apparently conceded that ‘‘a starkly literal 
reading of Section 16(b) * * * would make Provident, by 
virtue of its short-lived position as holder of the convertible 
debentures of Foremost, accountable to it as provided in 
16(b) for the relatively small profit resulting from the 
underwriting * * *’’ (38a). However, the court refused 
to accept such a literal reading, and referred to language 
in three cases (none of which involved analogous factual 
situations) which indicated that in certain circumstances, 
the court should determine whether a ‘‘ potential for abuse’’ 
was involved and whether the imposition of liability would 
further the purposes of the statute (38a-40a). Without 
actually analyzing the issue of the possibility of abuse 
on the facts involved or whether the purposes of Section 
16(b) would, in fact, be furthered by a decision in favor 
of Provident, the court simply held: 


‘*To allow Foremost under these circumstances to re- 
cover the small profit of Provident (almost miniscule 
in terms of the total amounts involved) simply by a 
mindlessly literal application of Section 16(b) would 
be to perpetrate rather than correct an inequity’’ (41a). 


2. The Decision of the Court of Appeals 


On appeal, the Ninth Circuit declined to follow the 
approach of the District Court but nevertheless affirmed 
the District Court on other grounds—grounds not even 
urged by Provident. The Court of Appeals analyzed the 


14 


ease in terms of the statute, finding that at least by the 
time of the closing on October 15, 1969, Provident had be- 
come by purchase a beneficial owner of more than 10% of 
a class of Foremost’s equity securities (3a). Furthermore, 
the court held that when six days later, on October 21, 
Provident executed the Underwriting Agreement, its sale of 
the Debentures was complete (10a). In addition, although 
the question of damages was not before it, the court explic- 
itly acknowledged the fact that the sale was in an amount 
of $366,666.66 in excess of the face amount of the Deben- 
tures (3a). Moreover, the court held that the transaction, 
involving the transfer of Provident’s assets for Foremost 
securities and resulting in Provident becoming a more than 
10% holder, was not ‘‘unorthodox’’ and further adopted 
Foremost’s position that in such circumstances the question 
of whether there was a potential for speculative abuse was 
not even applicable (4a-6a). However, the court went on 
to hold that if the Foremost-Provident transaction were to 
be considered unorthodox, in terms of this Court’s decision 
in Kern County Land Co. v. Occidental Petroleum Corp., 
411 U.S. 582, 595 (1973) (hereafter ‘‘Kern County’’), nev- 
ertheless ‘‘it involved the potential for speculative abuse 
of inside information and therefore is subject to section 
16(b) serutiny’’ (6a-8a). In reaching that conclusion, the 
court noted that Provident, as a holder of 10 percent of the 
equity securities, could reasonably be presumed to have had 
access to inside information and further distinguished this 
case on its facts from one such as Kern County which in- 
volved a hostile tender offer, saying: 


“To the contrary, the general cooperation involved 
in the transaction would indicate that Provident con- 
ferred intimately with the Foremost management and 


15 


could well have had access to confidential corporate 
information.’’ (7a) 


The court also agreed with Foremost that the Provident 
purchase and sale were voluntary and that indeed Provident 
had entered into the transaction when it was aware of the 
Section 16(b) problem and ‘‘in spite of the possibility that 
it might be held liable for the profits’’ (7a-8a). 


Despite all of this, the Court of Appeals nevertheless 
concluded that Section 16(b) did not apply because Provi- 
dent was not a 10% owner prior to its purchase of the De- 
bentures. This issue was not mentioned by the District 
Court, not urged by Provident, and not dealt with by either 
party during oral argument before the Ninth Circuit. The 
key statutory language provides: 


‘‘This subsection shall not be construed to cover any 
transaction where such beneficial owner was not such 
both at the time of the purchase and sale, or the sale 
and purchase, of the security involved * * *.’’ 


In construing this language to require that before the stat- 
ute can apply a prior beneficial ownership of more than 
10% of a class of equity securities is required, and in hold- 
ing that the purchase by which one becomes a more than 
10% holder of stock is not itself a Section 16(b) ‘‘pur- 
chase’’, the court ignored many of the considerations here- 
inafter discussed. It did, however, acknowledge that it 
was placing itself in direct conflict with the position adopted 
in two other circuits, the Second and Eighth (12a-13a). 
(In fact, it was taking a stance also at odds with that of 
other circuits as to the analogous issue of the Section 16(b) 
liability of officers and directors.) The court based its con- 
clusion primarily on its construction of certain language 


16 


in the Kern County case (14a-15a) and on that portion of 
the legislative history of Section 16(b) which it viewed as 
supportive of its position (15a-25a). 


The Court of Appeals conceded that in order to reach 
its conclusion, it was necessary to read the phrase ‘‘at the 
time of’’ in Section 16(b) to mean ‘‘prior to’’ in reference 
to the purchase half of a purchase and sale transaction, but 
to mean ‘‘simultaneously with’’ in reference to the purchase 
half of a sale and purchase (26a-27a). The court further 
noted that its construction of the statutory language would 
not prevent all abuses of inside information and specifically 
would not provide a remedy in a situation—the very situa- 
tion at bar—where a person might have access to inside in- 
formation at the time he makes the purchase that makes 
him a 10% shareholder; nevertheless, the court felt that 
other remedies under the Securities Exchange Act were 
sufficient to solve those problems (28a-29a). 


Summary of Argument 


1. Effectuation of the purposes of Section 16(b) re- 
quires that the initial purchase of more than 10% of the 
issuer’s equity security be included within the statutory 
prohibition, so that there will be automatic divestment of 
insider profit on any sale within 6 months of such purchase. 
This is the construction of the statutory language favored 
by the overwhelming weight of judicial authority and 
espoused by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Any 
other interpretation would render an existing exemptive 
rule under the statute meaningless. Such construction in- 
volves neither a tortured construction of language nor in- 


' 


17 


consistency with the legislative history. On the contrary, 
the construction of the four key words adopted by the 
Ninth Circuit requires that they mean one thing in the case 
of one type of transaction and another thing in the case of 
another type. Nothing in either the legislative history of 
the statute or in this Court’s decision in Kern County sug- 
gests that the initial purchase of more than 10% of a class 
of equity securities through cooperative negotiations be- 
tween the potential purchaser and the issuer, in which the 
potential purchaser could well have access to inside in- 
formation prior to the ripening of its equity ownership, 
should be treated as anything but a ‘‘purchase’’ under 
Section 16(b). 


2. The traditional elements of Section 16(b) liability 
are present here. Thus, the voluntary purchase of Fore- 
most equity securities in exchange for selected assets of 
Provident was a purchase of more than 10% of a class of 
such securities. A voluntary sale of certain of such secu- 
rities at a profit was made by Provident, the beneficial 
holder of such securities, within six months of the date of 
purchase. 


3. There are no grounds for exempting Provident’s 
purchase and sale of the Foremost Debentures from the 
application of Section 16(b). This Court’s decision in 
Kern County is not dispositive because the transaction 
by which Provident became a 10% holder—involving the 
exchange of assets for securities—was not unorthodox and 
was voluntary on Provident’s part. Moreover, even if 
the transaction were to be considered unorthodox, there 
was, as the Ninth Circuit found, a potential for speculative 
abuse in the transaction. 


18 


4. Provident was not a liquidating agent within the 
meaning of Rule 16a-4. It was at all relevant times acting 
for itself in the purchase and sale of securities: ¢.g., it was 
not a third party authorized by law to administer the 
estates or assets of other persons—but rather was a com- 
petent person having full control over its status and the 
disposition of its assets. Both the purchase and sale were 
made by Provident, thus its holding of the equity securities 


did not devolve upon it by operation of law as required for 
exemption under the Rule. 


ARGUMENT 
I 


The purposes of Section 16(b) are frustrated by the 
decision below exempting the initial purchase of 10% 
of the issuer’s stock from the prohibitions of the statute. 


A. The Prophylactic Purposes of Section 16(b) 


Prior to the enactment of Section 16(b), Congress had 
uncovered many instances where those in control of large 
corporations had used inside information or had manip- 
ulated the affairs of their corporations to profit from 
short-term speculative trading in their corporations’ se- 
curities (see e.g. S. Rep. No. 1455, 73rd Cong., 2d Sess. 55- 
68 (1934)). In enacting Section 16(b), Congress removed 
the incentive for engaging in such practices by providing 
that any profits realized by any officer, director or more 
than 10% beneficial owner of the equity securities of cer- 
tain corporations (originally the securities of corporations 
listed on a stock exchange and now more broadly applica- 
ble) from a purchase and sale or sale and purchase within 


19 


six months would be recoverable automatically by or on be- 
half of the corporation irrespective of whether the insider 
had in fact used inside information or engaged in manip- 
ulative activity. The courts have recognized the intent 
of Congress to curb insider abuses and have broadly in- 
terpreted Section 16(b) to effectuate that intent. 


As the Second Circuit stated in Feder v. Martin Marv- 
etta Corp., 406 F.2d 260, 262 (2d Cir. 1969), cert. denied, 
396 U.S. 1036 (1970): 


‘‘The judicial tendency * * * has been to interpret 
Section 16(b) in ways that are most consistent with 
the legislative purpose, even departing where neces- 
sary from the literal statutory language.’’ 


This is fully consistent with decisions of this Court giv- 
ing primary emphasis to the congressional purpose under- 
lying a statute, even ‘‘sacrificing, if necessary, the literal 
meaning in order that the purpose may not fail.’’ Ozawa 
v. United States, 260 U.S. 178, 194 (1922). 


In its recent decision in Reliance Electric Co. v. Emer- 
son Electric Co., 404 U.S. 418 (1972), this Court confirmed 
the earlier recognition by the Second and Ninth Circuit 
Courts of Appeal ‘‘that the only method Congress deemed 
effective to curb the evils of insider trading was a flat 
rule taking the profits out of a class of transactions in 
which the possibility of abuse was believed to be intolerably 
great.’’ 404 U.S. at 422. It quoted with approval the state- 
ment of the Seventh Circuit: 

‘¢ ‘Tn order to achieve its goals, Congress chose a 


relatively arbitrary rule capable of easy administra- 
tion. The objective standard of Section 16(b) imposes 


20 


strict liability upon substantially all transactions oc- 
curring within the statutory time period, regardless of 
the intent of the insider or the existence of actual 
speculation. This approach maximized the ability of 
the rule to eradicate speculative abuses by reducing 
difficulties in proof. Such arbitrary and sweeping cov- 
erage was deemed necessary to insure the optimum 
prophylactic effect.’ Bershad v. McDonough, 428 F. 
2d 693, 696 [(7th Cir. 1970), cert. denied, 400 U.S. 992 
(1971)].”’ Id. 


Mr. Justice Stewart’s majority opinion affirms that in 
respect of Section 16 ‘‘the congressional design’’ was one 
‘‘of predicating liability upon an ‘objective measure of 
proof’.’’ 404 U.S. at 425. He recognized the need in re- 
spect of the statute to ‘‘preserve(s) its mechanical quality”’ 
and the inappropriateness of ‘‘a judicial search for the 
will-o-the-wisp of an investor’s ‘intent’ in each litigated 
ease.’’ Id. In footnote 4, the majority adds that in no re- 
spect is liability predicated upon ‘‘considerations of intent, 
lack of motive, or improper conduct ‘that are irrelevant in 
§16(b) suits’.’’ 404 U.S. at 424, citing Blau v. Oppenheim, 
250 F.Supp. 881 (S.D.N.Y. 1966). Moreover, and most sig- 
nificantly, ‘‘where alternative constructions of the terms of 
§16(b) are possible, those terms are to be given the con- 
struction that best serves the congressional purpose of 


curbing short-swing speculation by corporate insiders.’’ 
Id. 


B. The Clear Weight of Authority Has Held the 
Initial Purchase of 10% of the Issuer’s Stock 
Subject to the Restrictions of Section 16(b). 


. Transactions of the type effected by Provident in the 
instant case present the potential for the speculative and 
manipulative abuses which Section 16(b) was designed to 


21 


prevent. The fact that Provident was not a more than 
10% beneficial owner prior to its purchase of the Fore- 
most Debentures but became such a statutory insider si- 
multaneously with such purchase does not take this trans- 
action out of the category of insider trading which is ¢a- 
pable of abuse. Effectuation of the statute’s prophylactic 
purposes accordingly requires that Section 16(b) liability 
be imposed on the profit made on this transaction. 


The issue was first raised and exhaustively discussed 
in Stella v. Graham-Paige Motors Corp., 104 F.Supp. 957 
(S.D.N.Y. 1952). That case involved a purehase which 
brought the owner of 614% of the issuer’s stock to the 
status of beneficial owner of 21% of the shares. Faced 
with the arguable ambiguity of the phrase ‘‘at the time 
of’’, the court construed it to mean ‘‘simultaneously with”’ 
rather than ‘‘prior to’’. On appeal, the Second Cireuit 
approved District Judge Kaufman’s construction. 232 F. 
2d 299 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 352 U.S. 831 (1956). The 
SEC filed an amicus brief in the District Court urging 
the construction ultimately affirmed by the Second Circuit, 
having distilled from the legislative history the conclusion 
‘“that the Congress intended to include such purchases 
[i.e., those by which one becomes a more than 10% holder] 
within the scope of the Act.’’ (Brief for SEC as Amicus 
Curiae at 6-7, Stella v. Graham-Paige Motors Corp.) 


Among other commentators, Professor Loss has stated 
that ‘it is difficult to quarrel with the [Second Cireuit’s] 
preference for the construction which would serve to ef- 
fectuate the legislative purpose and still leave some mean- 


22 


ing for the statutory language when there is an ambiguity 
*** > 92 L. Loss, Securities Recuntation 1060 (2d ed. 
1961). Likewise, Messrs. Cook and Feldman (then SEC 
Chairman and Special Counsel, respectively) in Insider 
Trading under the Securities Exchange Act, 66 Harv. L. 
Rev. 612, 631-32 (1953), state that to construe the phrase 
‘*both at the time of the purchase and sale’’ so as ‘‘to ex- 
empt a transaction unless ten percent were held both 
before and after would destroy the effectiveness of this 
section * * °°”, 


The Stella interpretation has on several occasions been 
reaffirmed by the Second Circuit, recent examples includ- 
ing Newmark v. RKO General, Inc., 425 F. 2d 348 (2d Cir.), 
cert. denied, 400 U.S. 854 (1970), and Perine v. William 
Norton €& Co., Inc., 509 F.2d 114 (2d Cir. 1974). The Stella 
interpretation was also explicitly adopted by the Eighth 
Circuit in Emerson Electric Co. v. Reliance Electric Co., 
434 F. 2d 918 (8th Cir. 1970), aff’d on other grounds, 404 
U.S. 418 (1972), the court stating that this construction 
was consistent with Congress’ purpose in enacting the stat- 
ute and overruling by implication the only court (coinci- 
dentally located within the Eighth Circuit), until the Ninth 
Cireuit’s decision in this case, to reach a contrary conclu- 
sion: Arkansas Louisiana Gas Co. v. W. R. Stevens In- 
vestment Co., 141 F.Supp. 841, 847 (W.D. Ark. 1956). The 
Emerson case came before this Court on another issue; 
however, in an amicus brief, the SEC urged the interpreta- 
tion here urged by petitioner. 


Moreover, in addition to the direct holdings of the Sec- 
ond and Eighth Circuits, both the Sixth and the Seventh 


23 


Circuits have reached the same result by implication or 
alternative holding with respect to persons who were both 
10% shareholders and officers or directors: Bershad v. 
McDonough, 428 F. 2d 693 (7th Cir. 1970), cert. denied, 
400 U.S. 992 (1971); Champion Home Builders Co. v. Jef- 
fress, 490 F. 2d 611 (6th Cir.), cert. denied, 416 U.S. 986 
(1974). At present, this question is again before the Sev- 
enth Circuit: Allis-Chalmers Manufacturing Co. v. Gulf 
& Western Industries, Inc., Docket Nos. 74-1266 and 74- 
1267, the issue having been decided in conformity with 
Stella by the court below, 372 F. Supp. 570 (N.D. Tl. 1974). 
See also Simon v. Sunasco, Inc. [1969-1970 Transfer Bind- 
er] CCH Fed. Sec. L. Rep. 192,547 (S.D.N.Y. 1970) ; Kahan- 
sky v. Emerson Radio & Phonograph Corp., 184 F. Supp. 
90 (S.D.N.Y. 1960). 


Moreover, numerous cases on both the Circuit and Dis- 
trict level have held the initial purchases by officers and 
directors subject to Section 16(b), even when such purchase 
was made before the individual became an officer or di- 
rector: Adler v. Klawans, 267 F. 2d 840 (2d Cir. 1959) ;* 
Blau v. Allen, 163 F. Supp. 702 (S.D.N.Y. 1958) ; Blau v. 
Hodgkinson, 100 F. Supp. 361 (S.D.N.Y. 1951); Booth v. 
Varian Associates, 334 F.2d 1 (1st Cir. 1964), cert. denied, 
379 U.S. 961 (1965) (point assumed without discussion ). 
A “‘not-yet’’ director can hardly be said to have more ac- 
cess to inside information than a ‘‘not-yet’’ shareholder 


* Indeed, Adler v. Klawans, supra, in reaching the above-described 
result, referred to and relied upon the Stella decision, while acknowl- 
edging that it was not directly applicable, to illustrate “that the pur- 
pose of the statute is remedial, rather than penal, and that it must be 
strictly construed in favor of the corporation and against any person 
who makes profit dealing in the corporation stock.” 267 F. 2d at 
846-47.

who is engaged in intensive negotiations preparatory to 
acqu ring a major position in the issuer’s equity. 


C. Rule 16b-2 Is Without Purpose if the 
Ninth Circuit’s View Is Correct. 

The SEC’s understanding of the meaning of the stat- 
ute is reflected not only by its amicus briefs in the Stella 
and the Emerson cases, but by its promulgation in 1935 of 
what is now Rule 16b-2 as amended (17 C.F.R. §240.16b-2), 
exempting certain underwriting transactions from Section 
16(b). Unless a person who acquired 10% of the stock 
by virtue of an underwriting agreement becomes subject 
to the statute thereby, the exemption would have been un- 
necessary. Thus, unlike the view of the legislative history 
it espoused in the Emerson case, the SEC’s interpretation 
of the meaning of ‘‘at the time of purchase”’ is fully con- 
sistent with its actions taken in implementation of the 
purposes of Section 16(b). 


The adoption of Rule 16b-2 was preceded by an ar- 
ticle by Eustace Seligman entitled Problems under the 
Securities Exchange Act, 21 Va. L. Rev. 1 (1934), which 
discussed the instant problem of statutory construction, 
concluding that the initial purchase making one a 10% 
shareholder should be a purchase for 16(b) purposes and 
that any other construction ‘‘would seem to be contrary 
to the purpose of the Act.’’ Jd. at 20. Mr. Seligman, how- 
ever, went on to note that such a construction would create 
a bar to stock financing and urged that ‘‘there is a press- 
ing need for regulations by the Commission exempting 
financing both in the case of 10% owners and directors.”’ 
Id, at 21. In its amicus brief in Stella, the SEC itself stated 
that this Rule ‘‘would not have been necessary * * * un- 


25 


less section 16(b) is given the liberal construction we have 
suggested.’’ (Brief, p. 7). 


So much conduct of so many has for so long been pred- 
icated on the almost universally accepted view that the 
transaction by which one becomes a 10% beneficial owner 
is subject to the statute, that nothing short of an unassail- 
able, completely compelling justification should at this late 
date be required in order to cast aside such a substantial 
body of precedent. 


D. The Language of the Statute, Interpreted in 
Light of the Statutory Purpose, Requires That 
the Initial Purchase of 10% of the Issuer’s 
Stock Be Subjected to Section 16(b). 


The Court of Appeals based its decision primarily on 
the proviso in Section 16(b) which states that the prohibi- 
tion of that section does not ‘‘cover any transaction where 
such beneficial owner was not such at the time of the pur- 
chase and sale, or the sale and purchase, of the security 
involved * * *.’’ In essence, the Ninth Circuit concluded 
that the language of the statute, the legislative history’ 
and a statement of this Court in Kern County supported 
the view that because a person buying 10% of the issuer’s 
stock allegedly could not have based his decision on inside 
information, then such purchase was not intended to be 
included within Section 16(b). We respectfully submit 
that both the premise and the conclusion are wrong, and 


* We note that the Court of Appeals was without the benefit of 
briefing from either party on the legislative history, Provident having 
determined not to urge this issue on appeal. 


26 


that the language of the statute, its legislative history, and 
the analysis of this Court in Kern County all lead to a 
conclusion opposite to that of the Ninth Circuit. 


When a purchase-sale transaction is being considered, 
the Ninth Circuit reads ‘‘at the time of the purchase’’ to 
mean ‘‘prior to’’ rather than ‘‘simultaneously with.’’ Yet 
we submit that to say that when or at the time that the pur- 
chase took place Provident owned 10% of the stock in- 
volves no straining of the English language. To read ‘‘at 
the time of’’ as meaning ‘‘when’’ or ‘‘simultaneously with’’ 
is consistent with the way the statute must be read if a 
sale-repurchase transaction is under consideration, as the 
Ninth Cireuit conceded (26a-27a). Foremost’s position 
thus has the additional virtue of consistency and does not 
require a tortured construction. 


If there is, however, any ambiguity in the language of 
the statute, its purpose of ‘‘preventing the unfair use of 
[inside] information’’ is best carried out by the interpre- 
tation here urged: 


‘*There is no surer guide in the interpretation of 
a statute than its purpose when that is sufficiently dis- 
closed; nor any surer mark of over solicitude for the 
letter than to wince at carrying out that purpose be- 
cause the words used do not formally quite match with 
it.”’ Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Tremaine, 
133 F. 2d 827, 830 (2d Cir. 1943) (L. Hand, C.J.). 


We are of course mindful of this Court’s observation 
in Emerson Electric that with respect to the specific lan- 
guage of the proviso, ‘‘the legislative history affords no 
explanation of the purpose of the proviso’’ (404 U.S. at 


27 


424); we do submit, however, that the purpose of Section 
16 as a whole is carried out only by the interpretation here 
urged. Thus the statute is designed to prevent the unfair 
use of information ‘‘obtained by such beneficial owner * * * 
by reason of his relationship to the issuer.’’ Such infor- 
mation can be obtained prior to the time when one becomes, 
and in connection with his becoming, a 10% beneficial own- 
er, and still be information obtained ‘‘by reason of his 
relationship to the issuer.’’ As the SEC stated in its 
amicus brief in Stella: 


‘A person who acquires a large block of stock in a 
single transaction normally has access to inside infor- 
mation. He necessarily would deal in the negotiations 
looking toward the purchase, with either the issuer or 
an insider holding a large interest in the issuer. In 
either event he would be in a position to bargain for 
disclosures not available to the public. It is against 
abuse of information so obtained as well as of infor- 
mation obtained after representation in management 
is secured that the section is directed.’’ Brief for SEC 
as Amicus Curiae at 5-6, Stella v. Graham-Paige Mo- 
tors Corp., 104 F.Supp. 957 (S.D.N.Y. 1952). 


The same observation is certainly pertinent here where the 
Ninth Circuit specifically noted: 


‘(T]he general cooperation involved in the transac- 
tion would indicate that Provident conferred intimately 
with the Foremost management and could well have 
had access to confidential corporate information.’’ (7a) 


There were frequent references in the hearings leading 
to the adoption of the Act to promoters and market manip- 
ulators who were granted interests in large blocks of stock 
prior to a market rise in the shares and who distributed 


28 


these shares during the ensuing rise. Such references were 
discussed in the portion of the Senate Report dealing with 
Section 16(b). S. Rep. No. 1455, 73rd Cong., 2d Sess. 55-68 
(1934). If, under the circumstances discussed in the hear- 
ings, the initial purchase is excluded from the calculation 
of the profits which inure to the corporation, the section 
would be largely ineffective to prevent one of the prime 


evils uncovered in the congressional investigation. See 
S. Rep. No. 1455, supra. 


Other instances of abuse in contravention of the statu- 
tory purpose could occur if the Ninth Circuit’s interpreta- 
tion were adopted. A person could purchase a large block 
of stock in anticipation of engaging in practices upon be- 
coming an insider which would raise the market price and 
enable him to sell at a profit. Or, a person could, soon 
after, and very possibly because of, his purchase of 10% 
of the corporation’s stock, come upon inside information 
which he could immediately utilize in its sale. The point 
is placed in even clearer focus if one postulates the 
purchase by a holder of 9% of an issuer’s equity of an 
additional 50% of the issuer, followed by a sale within 6 
months of some or all of such holdings. Under the Ninth 
Cireuit’s opinion, such a series of events would not give 
rise to any Section 16(b) liability because no purchase 
was ever made by a 10% holder. In each of these cases, 
the Ninth Circuit’s interpretation would leave a large 
loophole in the application of Section 16(b). 


It is no answer to suggest, as the Ninth Circuit does 
(28a-29a), that Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange 
Act, 15 U.S.C. §78j(b), may in many cases provide an alter- 


29 


native remedy, especially when the principal burden of the 
Ninth Cireuit’s argument rests on its view of the alleged 
legislative history. Section 10(b) is by its very terms not 
self-operative. It only proscribes conduct ‘‘in contraven- 
tion of such rules and regulations as the Commission may 
prescribe.’’ Rule 10b-5, 17 C.F.R. §240.10b-5, was first pro- 
mulgated in May of 1942, some eight years after Sections 
16 and 10(b) were enacted. Moreover, as this Court af- 
firmed .u Limerson, when it spoke with favor about the 
Congressional design of predicating liability upon an ob- 
jective measure of proof, Section 16(b) does not depend 
upon proof of intent or of injury to the plaintiff, factors 
which obviously make Section 10(b) more difficult of en- 
forcement than Section 16(b). 


We submit that the legislative history relied upon by 
the Ninth Circuit is totally inapposite. The language which 
forms the core of the Ninth Circuit’s analysis suggested a 
limitation of the applicability of the statute to pre-existing 
beneficial owners, but it appeared only in a bill (S. 2693, 
73rd Cong., 2d Sess. (1934)) which never became law." 
The bill which provided the actual basis for the present 
section (H.R. 8720, 73rd Cong., 2d Sess. (1934)) eliminated 
the limiting language of S. 2693. We submit that the 
elimination of this limiting language and the substitution 
in the bill of new language—language which ultimately 
became the law—all without explicit Congressional com- 
ment, hardly supports the Ninth Circuit’s conclusion that 
the limitation included in the old draft should be read into 
the new bill. 


* S. 2693 was not the only proposed bill which fell by the wayside. 
See H.R. 7852, H.R. 8720, S. 3420 and H.R. 9323, 73rd Cong., 2d 
Sess. (1934). Why the language of S. 2693 should be given such 
great weight escapes us. 


30 


A further factor which suggests that the Stella inter- 
pretation was indeed the one contemplated by Congress is 
the presence in Section 16, as enacted, of subsection (d) ex- 
empting: 


‘‘any purchase and sale, or sale and purchase, * * * of 
an equity security not then or theretofore held by him 
in an investment account, by a dealer in the ordinary 
course of his business and incident to the establish- 
ment or maintenance by him of a primary or secondary 
market * * * for such security’’. 15 U.S.C. §78p(d). 
(emphasis added). 


This provision might well have been prompted by concerns 
such as those expressed in the Congressional hearings that 
Section 16(b): 


‘** * * might prevent arbitrage transactions, because it 
is very common, in arbitrage, for a man to buy one se- 
curity and at the same time sell against it an equiva- 
lent security. While that process of the arbitrage is 
going on he might conceivably accumulate more than 
5 percent of this security, and he would be the bene- 
ficial owner of that 5 percent. He would, of course, 
have offsetting contracts or obligations against it, but 
they are not reflected in the definition, which imposes 
penalties upon a stockholder owning 5 percent or more 
of a registered security.’’ Hearings on S. Res. 84, 
S. Res. 56 and S. Res. 97 before the Senate Committee 
on Banking and Currency, 73rd Cong., 2d Sess., pt. 16 
at 7567 (1934) (hereinafter ‘‘1934 Hearings’’). (State- 
ment of Roland L. Redmond, Attorney for the New 
York Stock Exchange on H.R. 8720). [At that stage, 
the draft bill reached down to 5% holders. ] 


Such problems—and the problems relating to underwrit- 
ings solved by Rule 16b-2, 17 C.F.R. §240.16b-2, referred 
to above (p. 24)—would not have arisen if the interpre- 


31 


tation adopted by the Ninth Circuit were indeed the inter- 
pretation contemplated by Congress. 


To return to the discussion of the proviso in the Emer- 
son case, we note that this Court there quoted with ap- 
parent approval the statement of Eustace Seligman, Esq. 
(in the very article in which he urged the adoption of what 
came to be Rule 16b-2) that: 


‘‘(T]he intention of the language was to exclude the 
second sale in a case where 10% is purchased, 5% sold 
within three months and the remaining 5% a month 
later.’’ Seligman, Problems Under the Securities Ex- 
change Act, 21 Va. L. Rev. 1, 20 (1934), quoted at 404 
U.S. 423 n.3 (1972). 


In Emerson this Court rejected an interpretation of the 
statute which would have imposed liability on ‘‘all sales 
within six months by one who has gained the position of 
a 10% owner through voluntary purchase, regardless of 
the amount of his holdings at the time of the sale’’ (id. at 
426), but said nothing about exempting the initial pur- 
chase. The interpretation urged by Foremost here is con- 
sistent with that adopted by the Court in Emerson: we 
suggest that the language ensures, in the context of a ‘‘pur- 
chase’’ transaction analogous to the ‘‘sale’’ transaction 
involved in Emerson (and in Mr. Seligman’s example) that 
one who purchases 7% of the corporation’s stock (for pur- 
poses of illustration, 7,000 shares) and then another 6%, 
would not have his profits measured by matching 8% of 
the shares against a sale of 8% (i.e., 8,000 shares) within 
6 months of the date of both purchases. Both in this 
hypothetical illustration and in the case at bar, the purchase 
by which one becomes a 10% holder should be subject to the 
statute and in our hypothetical the purchaser should be 


32 


required to disgorge his profits arising only from a match- 
ing of 6,000 of the shares sold against 6,000 of the shares 
purchased. See L. Loss, op. cit., at p. 1060. 


In its amicus brief in Emerson the SEC analyzed the 
legislative history and concluded that the purpose of the 
proviso was to exclude from the statute’s coverage those 
who became 10% shareholders ‘‘involuntarily’’. Brief for 
SEC as Amicus Curiae at 34, Reliance Electric Co. v. Emer- 
son Electric Co., 404 U.S. 418 (1972). This Court re- 
jected such view of the legislative history on grounds that 
it contradicted the SEC’s own reporting requirements and 
the plain language of the statute. 404 U.S. at 425-27." 
No such problems derive from the interpretation suggested 
here. The statute (Section 16(a)) and the SEC require the 
reporting of the transaction by which one reaches the 
plateau of holding 10% of the stock. Moreover, as pointed 
out above, the language of Sections 16(b) and 16(d) of the 
statute and the SEC’s promulgation in 1935 of Rule 16b-2 
suggest a contemporaneous view identical with that urged 
by petitioner. 


Finally, the Ninth Cireuit sought to bolster its conclu- 
sions by what we submit is an overly broad interpretation 
of a comment of this Court in the Kern County case relating 
to a tender offeror’s calculations that it might be able to 


resell stock at a profit. Such matters, said Mr. Justice 
White: 


‘‘do not represent the kind of speculative abuse at 
which the statute is aimed, for they could not have been 


* We note that in the instant case the Ninth Circuit specifically 
found Provident’s transactions “voluntary” (7a-8a ). 


33 


based on inside information obtained from substantial 
stockholdings that did not yet exist.’’ 411 U.S. at 597. 


From this, the Ninth Cireuit concluded that this Court 
‘‘must have intended for section 16(b) to apply only after 
that person becomes a statutory insider.’’ 


There are several considerations which lead to the con- 
clusion that the quoted statement was offered only in the 
context of a hostile tender offer—a situation which is the 
very antithesis of that presented here, involving coopera- 
tive negotiation and exchange of information between 
issuer and purchaser prior to the time of purchase. In 
a recent decision, the Second Circuit commented as to 
Kern County: ‘*‘We believe that Kern County holds 
the defensive merger situation to be sui generis in 
terms of §16(b) liability.’’ American Standard, Inc. v. 
Crane Co., [Current] CCH Fed. Sec. L. Rep. 794,924 (2d 
Cir. 1974). The Ninth Circuit would read the qaoted lan- 
guage from Kern County far more expansively. Yet at 
the same time that the Ninth Cireuit was exonerating 
Provident, it was also concluding that Provident’s actions 
may have reflected ‘‘exactly the kind of speculative abuse 
that section 16(b) is designed to discourage’’ (8a) because 
of the cooperative negotiations that preceded such pur- 
chase. 


While the Ninth Circuit emphasized the fact that prior 
to September 25, Provident owned no Foremost securities, 
the framework of the statute—as well as the legislative 
history discussed above—demonstrates that it is the poten- 
tial for obtaining inside information, not the ripening of 
equity ownership, which is the important factor. Thus, for 
example, Section 3(a)(13) of the 1934 Act, 15 U.S.C. §78¢ 


34 


(a) (13), defines ‘‘purchase’’ as including ‘‘any contract to 
buy, purchase or otherwise acquire’’, and Section 3(a) (14), 
15 U.S.C. §78e(a)(14), defines ‘‘sale’’ to include ‘‘any 
contract to sell or otherwise dispose of.’’ Moreover, Sec- 
tion 3(a)(11) of the Act, 15 U.S.C. §78e(a)(11), defines an 
‘tequity security’’ to include any ‘‘stock or similar secu- 
rity’’ or ‘‘any security convertible, with or without con- 
sideration, into such a security, or carrying any warrant 
or right to subscribe to or purchase such a security * * *.’’ 
If the draftsmen of the statute had in fact intended to 
exclude, as a class, transactions which ‘‘could not have been 
based on inside information obtained from substantial 
stockholdings that did not yet exist,’’ they would not have 
defined purchase and sale to include contracts to buy and 
sell and they would not have defined ‘‘equity security’’ so 
as to include a warrant or a right or a convertible deben- 
ture. 


Taking the second definitional considerations first, it 
cannot seriously be argued that one who has invested a com- 
paratively small sum to purchase warrants or rights (which 
perhaps years later, and only after making a much larger 
payment, can be exchanged for 10%, or as the Ninth Cir- 
cuit would have it, 10% first and then an incremental 
purchase, of an issuer’s common stock) has a greater 
opportunity ‘‘by reason of his relationship to the issuer’’ 
to obtain inside information than does a responsible person 
who is negotiating in earnest through investment bankers 
to buy upwards of 10% (or for that matter 75% or more) 
of the equity of a major publicly-held company. 


Indeed, in this case, it was Provident’s purchase of 
convertible debentures that lead the Ninth Circuit to con- 


35 


clude that ‘‘Provident became a beneficial owner of more 
than 10 percent of a class of Foremost equity securities.’’ 
(3a) When the purchase of convertible debentures gives 
one the right to acquire more than 10% of a class of equity 
securities, such purchase falls within the statute’s reach. 
Chemical Fund, Inc. v. Xerox Corp., 377 F. 2d 107 (2d 
Cir. 1967). This result is of course consistent with the 
“ee of ‘‘purchase’’ in Section 3(a)(13). In neither 

of warrants or convertible debentures nor in the 


the: 
case of a contract to buy does the statute permit it to be 
said that a relationship sufficient to permit the abuse of 
inside information does not exist. Yet in each of these 
eases ‘‘substantial stockholdings * * * did not yet exist.’’ 


In passing, it should not escape notice that a second 
delivery of Debentures convertible into 236,46442 common 
shares of Foremost took place on October 20, 1969 (3a), 
after Provident became a statutory insider and before the 
October 21 sale. We do not urge that this second delivery 
be matched against the next day’s sale, but only point out 
the anomaly of a construction that might arguably permit 
liability to flow only from this second delivery and not from 
the first. No one could seriously contend that the two «e- 
liveries under one contract involve different potentials for 
misuse of inside information. Nor should the result de- 
pend upon whether the second delivery stemmed from a 
separate contract. If the ‘‘closing’’ transaction, the sale, 
gives rise to a realizable profit, then it is hard to understand 
why, unless the statutory language clearly compelled it, 
the purchase by which one becomes a 10% holder should 
be distinguished from a purchase one day or one week later. 


36 


In conclusion, we submit, the language of Kern County 
relied upon by the Ninth Circuit was not directed to the 
issue present in this case. In fact, we submit that rather 
than supporting the decision of the Ninth Circuit with re- 
spect to the applicability of the statute to the initial pur- 
chase, the Kern County case suggests the opposite result. 
Such is the clear import of the following passages: 


‘*Unquestionably, one or more statutory purchases oc- 
curs when one company, seeking to gain control of an. 
other, acquires more than 10% of the stock of the latter 
through a tender offer made to its shareholders.’’ 411 
U.S. 582, 584. 
. > > 

‘In the present case, it is undisputed that Occidental 
became a ‘beneficial owner’ within the terms of §16(b) 
when, pursuant to its tender offer, it ‘purchased’ more 


than 10% of the outstanding shares of Old Kern.”’ 
Id. at 595 


‘““By May 10, 1967, Occidental had acquired more than 
10% of the outstanding shares of Old Kern. It was 
thus a statutory insider when, on May 11, it extended 


its tender offer to include another 500,000 shares.’’ 
Id. at 598 


We note that in Allis-Chalmers Manufacturing Co. v. Gulf 
& Western Industries, Inc., 372 F. Supp. 570 (N.D. Il. 
1974), appeal docketed, Nos. 74-1266 and 74-1267 (7th Cir.), 
the court stated that Kern County supported its finding that 


defendant’s initial purchase of 10% of the issuer’s stock 
was subject to Section 16(b) restrictions. 


37 


The other elements of Section 16 liability were cor- 
rectly found to exist by the Ninth Circuit. 


The sole ground for the Ninth Cireuit’s decision in favor 
of Provident in this case was its novel view of whether the 
initial purchase was subject to Section 16(b). It found that 
‘the other’’ (or as we contend, ‘‘all the’’) basic elements 
of Section 16(b) liability—(1) a purchase and sale, (2) of 
any equity security of the issuer, (3) within any period of 
less than six months, (4) by a beneficial owner of more than 
10% of any class of any security—were satisfied in aecord- 
ance with long-standing precedent. 


A. Provident’s Purchase of the Debentures Made It 
the Beneficial Owner of More Than 10% of a 
Class of Equity Securities of Foremost. 


1. Provident Purchased the Debentures 
on September 25, 1969. 


As the Ninth Circuit held: 


‘*Provident exchanged its assets for Foremost stock. 
The only distinction between this transaction and the 
usual cash-for-stock sale is the nature of the considera- 
tion. * * * We see no meaningful distinction between 
consideration in the form of cash and consideration in 
the form of a corporate asset.’’ (6a) 


It has been held in several cases that a sale of assets in 
exchange for securities is a ‘‘purchase’’ of those securities 
within the meaning of Section 16(b). Stella v. Graham- 
Paige Motors Corp., 132 F. Supp. 100, 102-03 (S.D.N.Y. 
1955), aff’d im part and rev’d in part, 232 F. 2d 299 (2d 


38 


Cir.), cert. denied, 352 U.S. 831 (1956) ; Marquette Cement 
Manufacturing Co. v. Andreas, 239 F. Supp. 962, 965-66 
(S.D.N.Y. 1965). 


The Ninth Circuit further apparently held that the pur- 
chase took place on September 25, the date of the Purchase 
Agreement, as it found that ‘‘[t]he rights and obligations 
of the parties were fixed when the purchase agreement was 
executed’? (5a). Such a holding is in accord with Section 
3(a)(13) of the 1934 Act, 15 U.S.C. §78e(a) (13), which de- 
fines ‘‘purchase’’ as including ‘‘any contract to buy, pur- 
chase or otherwise acquire.’’ See Blau v. Ogsbury, 210 F. 
2d 426 (2d Cir. 1954), where it was held, in line with other 
cited Second Circuit cases, that an optionee purchased stock 
at the time when he mailed a notice to the corporation of his 
election to purchase rather than at the time he made pay- 
ment for the stock. What was important for the court was 
that at the earlier date the insider’s obligation was, for all 
practical purposes, fixed. Similarly, here, there were no 
unusual conditions upon Provident’s obligations under the 
Purchase Agreement (see paragraph 7 of the Agreement 
in particular) (A35, 17).* 


2. Provident Acquired More Than 10% of 
a Class of Equity Securities of Foremost. 


There is also no question—and Provident raised none 
below—that by its purchase of the Debentures Provident 
acquired an equity security of Foremost. The common 


* In fact, in the instant case, it makes no difference whether Sep- 
tember 25, 1969, the date of the Purchase Agreement, or October 15, 
1969, the date on which delivery of the Debentures was made, is con- 
sidered the date of purchase because, as discussed below, the Ninth 
Circuit found the sale to have taken place on October 21, 1969, well 
within six months of either date.
