stock of Foremost is clearly an ‘‘equity security.’’ More- 
over, Section 3(a)(10) of the 1934 Act, 15 U.S.C. 
§78¢(a) (10), defines the term ‘‘security’’ as specifically in- 
cluding debentures, and Section 3(a)(11), 15 U.S.C. §78e 
(a)(11), defines the term ‘‘equity security’’ to include any 
security convertible into stock of the issuer. The Deben- 
tures are an equity security within the Section 3(a)(11) 
detinition because they are convertible into shares of com- 
mon stock. 


Looking at September 25, the date of the Purchase 
Agreement, Foremost’s outstanding common stock, inelud- 
ing the shares issuable to Provident upon a hypothetical 
conversion of the Debentures, comprised about 12,700,000 
shares. By the Purchase Agreement, Provident had con- 
tracted to purchase Debentures convertible into 1,600,000 
shares, more than 10%. On the other hand, if October 15 
is considered the purchase date of the $40,000,000 principal 
amount of Debentures delivered then, Foremost’s outstand- 
ing common stock, upon conversion of the Debentures on 
that date, would have consisted of about 12,400,000 shares 
and Provident would have held about 1,300,000 of such 
shares, again more than 10%. (It is not necessary to even 
consider in this respect the effect of the delivery into escrow 
on October 15 of $2,500,000 principal amount of Debentures, 
convertible into 81,53914 shares.) The later delivery of 
additional Debentures on October 20 merely increased 
Provident’s percentage holdings, and did not alter its posi- 
tion as a more than 10% owner. 


40 


3. By Virtue of Its Purchase of Debentures, Provident 
Became the Beneficial Owner of the Debentures. 


Provident contended in the court below that it did not 
become the beneficial owner of the securities by virtue of 
the September 25 Purchase Agreement because it allegedly 
acquired the Debentures as agent and trustee for its share- 
holders by virtue of its adoption of a Plan of Dissolution 
on September 26. The Ninth Circuit rejected this argument 
without discussion, simply stating that Provident ‘‘ became 
a beneficial owner’’ of the securities by virtue of the total 
transaction (3a). 


The argument that Provident was not a beneficial owner 
after September 26, 1969, flies in the face of the Forms 3 
and 4 filed by Provident with the SEC on October 31, 1969 
(A53, A55) which specifically state that Provident was the 
‘‘beneficial owner of more than 10% of the Company’s 6% 
Convertible Subordinated Debentures due June 13, 1994.’* 


According to one of the draftsmen of the Exchange Act, 
Mr. Thomas Corcoran, the phrase ‘‘ beneficial ownership’’ 
is ‘‘the broadest term you can have.’’ 1934 Hearings, pt. 15, 
at 6556. According to SEC Securities Exchange Act Re- 
lease No. 7793 (January 19, 1966) (2 CCH Fed. See. L. Rep. 
126,032) one of the basic concomitants of ‘‘beneficial owner- 
ship’’ is ‘‘the ability to exercise a controlling influence over 
the purchase, sale or voting of * * * securities.’’ All of 
these Provident clearly had. 


_* “Tf a record owner—or any person who might be deemed a bene- 
ficial owner but does not think he is—wants to protect himself, he may 
file a report and disavow any implication that the filing is an admission 
of beneficial ownership.” 2 L. Loss, Securities REGULATION 1100 
(2d ed. 1961). This Provident did not do. 


41 


The rule in general is that ‘‘a corporation obviously 
beneficially owns any securities it holds of another com- 
pany. Such securities are an asset of the corporation.’’ 
Feldman & Teberg, Beneficial Ownership under Section 16 
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, 17 W. Res. L. Rev. 
1054, 1080 (1966). It could be argued that in every situa- 
tion in which a corporation owns stock that stock is ‘‘bene- 
ficially owned’’ by the shareholders as well. Whether such 
an argument has any merit or not, it has never been upheld 
in order to exonerate a corporation, which has all the indicia 
of ownership including the power to sell and the right to 
receive dividends or interest, from its Section 16 respon- 


sibilities. 


Thus, examination of the Underwriting Agreement (A 
135) signed on October 21, 1969, shows that under para- 
graph 5(b)(A), Provident’s counsel was required to, and 
on October 28, 1969, in fact did, furnish to the underwriters 


its opinion that: 


«* * * the Selling Debentureholder (Provident) has 
valid marketable title to the Debentures and has the 
legal right and power to enter into this agreement and 
to sell, transfer and deliver the Debentures to the 
Underwriters. * * *’’ (A135, 75(b)(A)) 


Under paragraph 9(a)(i) of the Underwriting Agreement, 
Provident made a warranty to the same effect and also rep- 
resented that it owned and held on October 21 and would 
own or hold on October 28, the Debentures ‘‘free and clear 
of all liens, claims, encumbrances and equities * * *’’ (A135, 
19(a)(i)).* In its letter of October 15, 1969, to the SEC, 


*In paragraph 9(a)(ii) Provident further warranted that in 
furnishi inberteation ~ Reena for use in the Registration State- 
ment or Prospectus, it did not make an untrue statement of a “material 
fact” and aa ast “omit to state a material fact,” and in paragraph 
9(b) Provident agreed to indemnify Foremost and the underwriters 
for any such misstatement or omission (A135, f]9(a) (ii), 9(b)). 


42 


Provident referred to itself as the ‘‘selling stockholder’’ to 
be named in the Prospectus (A127). The payment by the 
underwriters of the purchase price (including interest) of 
the Debentures was made to Provident at the closing, not to 
its shareholders and not to it in any agency or other fiduci- 
ary capacity (A32). In such circumstances, Provident can 
hardly deny that it was the beneficial owner of the Deben- 
tures. 


Even if Provident’s argument that it was a ‘‘trustee’’ 
or a ‘‘fiduciary’’ were accepted, it would be of no help; 
at most, it would mean that both Provident and its share- 
holders were ‘‘beneficial owners.’’ See Feldman & Teberg, 
Beneficial Ownership under Section 16 of the Securities 
Exchange Act of 1934,17 W. Res. L. Rev. 1054, 1074 (1966). 
But it is not necessary to reach that point here for Provi- 
dent was not a ‘‘trustee’’, ‘‘agent’’ or ‘‘fiduciary”’ for its 
shareholders during liquidation to any greater extent than 
an on-going corporation ever is. It is clear under Cali- 
fornia law that the Board of Directors of a corporation 
in voluntary liquidation maintains its status as a Board of 
Directors, and the Board members do not become trustees 
for the shareholders. See Calif. Corp. Code §4800, 4801; 
Hartman v. Hollingsworth, 255 C.A.2d 579, 63 Cal. Rptr. 


563 (1967); Chase v. Super-Cold Corp., 163 C.A.2d 83, 328 
P.2d 812, 814 (1958). 


Provident argued below that all its transactions in the 
Debentures ‘‘were for its shareholders and for its share- 
holders’ benefit.’’ To the extent that this statement is in- 
tended to be anything more than a truism regarding the 
relationship between a corporation and its shareholders, it 
is, as demonstrated above, without substance. 


43 


B. Provident Sold the Debentures Within 
Six Months of the Date of Purchase. 


1. The Sale Took Place on October 21. 


The Ninth Circuit held that the sale of the Debentures 
took place on October 21. On that date, 


«<* * * when Provident executed the underwriting 
agreement, it was bound and the price was fixed. * * * 
As to Provident, the sale was at that date complete, 
subject only to the usual conditions precedent to 
closing.’’ (10a) 


Many considerations support this conclusion, including 
Provident’s own Form 4, which indicates a date of sale 
of October 21, 1969. Moreover, Section 3(a)(14) of the 
1934 Act, 15 U.S.C. §78e(a) (14), defines ‘‘sale’’ to include 
‘‘any contract to sell or otherwise dispose of * * * unless 
the context requires otherwise.’’ It is essential in the 
context of Section 16(b) that a contract of sale be con- 
sidered a ‘‘sale’’. Otherwise, an insider could easily 
avoid the proscriptions of Section 16(b) by entering into 
a contract to sell stock within the six-month period, thereby 
fixing his profit, but provide that the closing take place after 
the six-month period. In order to prevent such simple 
evasion of Section 16(b), the date of the sale must, as the 
statutory definition recognizes, be considered to be the date 
of the contract of sale. At that point, the rights of the 
seller and purchaser become fixed and any profits received 
by the insider at the closing may be said to have been 
‘‘realized’’ under the terms of the contract of sale. This 
was the position reached by the District Court in Stella v. 
Graham-Paige Motors Corp., 132 F. Supp. 100, 105-06 


44 


(S.D.N.Y. 1955), aff’d in part and rev’d in part, 232 F. 2d 
299 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 352 U.S. 831 (1956) (this 
holding was not disturbed on appeal). The District Court 
there rejected the argument that the sale took place at the 
closing held after the six-month period rather than at the 
time of the contract of sale which was within the statutory 
period. 


As the Ninth Circuit recognized, the existence of routine 
conditions of closing cannot alter the result. The statutory 
scheme would be destroyed if liability could be avoided by 
the mere addition of a condition which common experience 
indicates will be met with the mere passage of time. In 
Stella v. Graham-Paige Motors Corp., supra, defendant 
argued that the sale did not take place until stock to fulfill 
the contract of sale had been released from a voting trust. 
The District Court rejected this contention: 


‘*T cannot see that Graham-Paige’s inability to acquire 
a particular block of 155,000 shares to fulfill its com- 
mitments would have any effect upon those commit- 
ments as ‘sales’ within the meaning of the statute. 
For example, a contract for the sale of stock which 
the seller expected to fill by delivering stock which 
was subject to a pledge at the time of the making of 
the contract would result in a ‘sale’ as of that time 
rather than as of the date that the seller succeeded 
in redeeming it from the pledge.’’ 132 F. Supp. at 106. 


Provident on October 21, 1969, bound itself to sell the 
Debentures and to take a short-swing profit, within six 
months after their purchase. It was at this time that, after 
receiving the Debentures, Provident insulated itself from 
the continuing ordinary risks of the market by entering into 
an agreement which set the sale price of the Debentures at 


45 


1014% of their aggregate principal amount, plus interest. 
The conditions of Provident's obligations under the Under- 
writing Agreement—that the Registration Statement be ef- 
fective, that no stop order be issued, that Foremost’s coun- 
sel submit a written opinion to Provident (A135, 6)— 
were ready to fall into place and Provident could not pre- 
vent their occurrence. As is always predetermined when 
an underwriting agreement is signed, the SEC had been 
alerted to niake the registration statement effective, and 
indeed it was made effective later on the same day, October 
21. It was thus on October 21 that Provident exercised its 
speculative judgment and insulated itself from further 
market risks and thus it was at this point that the ‘‘sale’’ 
took place for purposes of Section 16(b). Blau v. Ogsbury, 
210 F. 2d 426, 427 (2d Cir. 1954). 


2. Provident Was the Beneficial Owner of 10% of the 
Equity Securities of Foremost at the Time of Sale. 


Provident further argued below that by the time of the 
sale, it had divested itself of beneficial ownership of the 
requisite amount of Debentures. One branch of this argu- 
ment depends upon fixing a sale date of October 28, and 
arguing that Provident’s distribution of $22,227,000 prin- 
cipal amount of Debentures on October 24 reduced its 
holding to less than 10%. However, this contention is of 
no avail if, as the Ninth Circuit correctly held, the sale date 
is held to be October 21. This contention is also in conflict 
with Provident’s Form 4 which stated that it was a 10% 
owner at the time of sale, and that the $22,227,000 of De- 
bentures were distributed as a liquidating dividend on 
October 24, 1969, three days after the sale (A55). 


46 


The second branch of the argument—not discussed by 
the Ninth Cireuit—depends upon an assertion that the dis- 
tribution of the dividend took place in some metaphysical 
fashion at the time of a resolution of the Provident Board 
of Directors on October 13, 1969, prior to the Underwriting 
Agreement of October 21, 1969. (See p. 8 supra). All that 
this resolution—subsequently repudiated—provided was 
that after payments had been made with respect to the 
Preferred Stock, the officers were to distribute the Deben- 
tures ‘‘as received’’ to shareholders of record upon dates 
to be then established by the officers ‘‘as expeditiously as 
possible’? (A118). There is no authority which supports 
Provident’s contention that its shareholders had ‘‘vested 
rights’’ in the Debentures at that point. 


First, because the resolution did not fix a record or 
payment date but only stated that the Debentures were 
to be distributed ‘‘as received’’ upon dates to be fixed by 
the officers, there was never established as of any fixed 
time an enforceable debtor-creditor relationship between 
the corporation and its shareholders. Second, Provident 
obviously did not itself treat the resolution as creating a 
debtor-creditor relationship because it deviated from the 
terms of the resolution and never carried it out. It never 
distributed the Debentures—described specifically and sig- 
nificantly in the resolution as ‘‘assets of the Corporation’’ 
and directed to be distributed to the shareholders ‘‘pro 
rata’’ and ‘‘as received’’—in the manner contemplated 
by the resolution. Instead, it sold $25,000,000 worth of 
them. Third, the authorities relied upon by Provident 
below which speak of shareholders’ ‘‘vested rights’’ in 
dividends all dealt with dividends of a going corporation, 
not liquidating dividends as were here involved. Unlike 


47 


this liquidating dividend, all of those non-liquidating divi- 
dends had been declared to be payable on a fixed future 
date. In D. Kent, Corporate Divipenps (1941), the distine- 
tion is made at any early point: 


‘‘Quite different considerations apply to payments 
which purport to be liquidations and payments which 
purport to be made from profits. It is the latter type 
of payment which is peculiarly the province of cor- 
porate dividend law * * *’’ Jd. at 23 (footnote omitted). 


This distinction is illustrated in the California Corpora- 
tions Code with the contrast between Section 5000 et seq. 
dealing with Distributions in Liquidation, and Section 1500 
et seq. dealing with Dividends. It is clear that declaration 
of distributions in liquidation under the former sections 
(even had the resolution fixed a date for payment and a 
record date, neither of which it did) cannot create a debt 
or a vested right against the corporation. Under Section 
5000, distribution of the corporation’s assets cannot be 
made until it has been determined ‘‘that all the known 
debts and liabilities * * * have been paid or adequately 
provided for * * *’’; and then distribution must be made 
among the shareowners ‘‘according to their respective 
rights and preferences.’’ The Plan of Liquidation adopted 
by Provident on September 26, 1969 (A102) provided that 
the liquidation preference in respect to the Preferred Stock 
must have been paid in cash before any other distributions 
of assets of the corporation were to be made to the common 
stockholders, and, in addition, explicitly provided that 
funds would have to be reasonably retained to meet claims 
against Provident or its assets (A104). The dividend reso- 
lution of October 13 itself stated that distribution of the 


48 


corporate assets (including the Debentures) was dependent 
upon ‘‘full and final payment with respect to the Preferred 
stock’? having been made prior to such distribution (A 
120). In no sense can the mere Board resolution of Octo- 
ber 13, which was never carried out, and which was subject 
to numerous contingencies and legal requirements, be held 
to have divested Provident of the beneficial ownership of 
the Foremost Debentures as of October 13. 


C. The Transction Resulted in Profit to Provident. 


The Purchase Agreement called for the exchange of 
$54,000,000 worth of Provident’s assets for $54,000,000 
principal amount of Debentures. Promptly after their 
delivery to Provident, $25,000,000 principal amount of the 
Debentures were sold in a public offering, and Provident 
received $25,366,666.66. Suffice it to point out for present 
purposes that in the California state proceedings in con- 
nection with its winding up, Provident admitted that, with- 
out reference to interest received on the Debentures, it 
received $312,500 ‘‘from the sale of the Debentures in 
excess of their face amount.’’ The California court has set 
aside $804,000 ‘‘for Foremost’s Section 16(b) claim’’ 
(A62). Although the parties excluded the question of com- 
putation of profit from the summary judgment motions, the 
Ninth Circuit noted that Provident had received $366,666.66 
‘in excess of the principal amount of the debenture * * *”’ 
(9a). Foremost expects, at the appropriate time, to show 
that the realizable profit was much greater than $312,500 or 
$366,666.66. However that may turn out, there can be no 
question that Provident obtained a profit on these trans- 
actions, and that this case should be remanded for hearing 


49 


to determine the precise amount of such profit. Contrary 
to the intimation of the District Court below, that the profit 
may arguably have been relatively small in comparison 
with the over-all transaction is certainly no ground for 
refusing to find liability. In Stemberg v. Sharpe, 95 F. 
Supp. 32, 34 (S.D.N.Y. 1950), aff’d per curiam, 190 F. 2d 
82 (2d Cir. 1951), for example, the total recovery, out of 
which attorneys’ fees of the stockholder-plaintiff were paid, 
was only $168.75. 


There is no ground for refusing to carry out the 
statutory mandate of imposing liability on Provident. 

The Ninth Circuit rejected Provident’s contention below 
that the adoption of a ‘‘ pragmatic approach’’ by this Court 
in Kern County served to exonerate it from Section 16 lia- 
bility. The Ninth Cireuit decision was on two grounds: 
(1) the transaction was not of an unorthodox type which 
would give rise to a pragmatic test; (2) even if the trans- 
action were to be considered unorthodox, it involved ‘‘the 
potential for speculative abuse of inside information.”’ 


A. The Transaction Was Not Unorthodox. 


As we have demonstrated above, the transaction in- 
volved the transfer of assets for stock (convertible deben- 
tures). Such transactions have long been held to constitute 
‘“‘purchases’’ of the stock. See e.g., Stella v. Graham-Paige 
Motors Corp., 132 F. Supp. 100, 102-03 (S.D.N.Y. 1955), 
aff’d in part and rev’d in part, 232 F. 2d 299 (2d Cir.), 
cert, denied, 352 U.S. 831 (1956). The Ninth Circuit saw 


50 


no meaningful distinction based on the form of considera- 
tion involved, and saw no reason to treat the Provident- 
Foremost transaction as anything other than orthodox 
(6a, 5a). 


As the Ninth Circuit further pointed out, the rights and 
obligations of the parties, including the price, were fixed 
by the execution of the Purchase Agreement and the trans- 
action was not a record-keeping maneuver, but ‘‘was an 
actual transfer of stock for assets’’ (5a). Nor did the 
transaction involve the reclassification or conversion of one 
type of security into another, or an involuntary purchase 
or sale, two further types of unorthodox transaction which 
have been discussed by the courts. See e.g., Blau v. Max 
Factor & Co., 342 F. 2d 304, 306 n.3 (9th Cir.), cert. denied, 
382 U.S. 892 (1965) and Ferraiolo v. Newman, 259 F. 2d 
342, 346 (6th Cir. 1958), cert. denied, 359 U.S. 927 (1959). 


With respect to the question of voluntariness, the Ninth 
Circuit stated: 


‘*There is no evidence in this case to suggest that 
Provident was forced to enter into any of the trans- 
actions. There is evidence, however, to show that 
Provident’s management was aware of the section 
16(b) problem and entered the transaction in spite of 
the possibility that it might be held liable for the 
profits. Provident has not suggested that it would 
have suffered any detriment had it not completed the 
transactions when it did.’’ (7a-8a) 


This finding is compelled by the record. Provident at- 
tempted to base an argument below on the assertion that it 
would have preferred to have received cash rather than 


51 


Debentures. That hardly means that its receipt of the 
latter was not voluntary. Indeed, if one is to assume that 
a cash deal would have been pegged at the face amount of 
the Debentures, Provident’s argument is to the effect that 
Debentures which were quickly to be sold at 1014%4% of 
face value had to be thrust upon it against its corporate 
will. And no claim was made that the sale on October 21 
was anything but Provident’s free choice. Foremost did 
not in any way insist upon, or even encourage, the sale 
of the Debentures, much less insist upon such sale within 
six months. If Provident had chosen to retain the De- 
bentures (and Provident had five years within which to 
call upon Foremost for a registration statement (A135)), 
Foremost could not have forced it to sell nor to execute 
the Underwriting Agreement, and, as noted by the Ninth 
Cirenit, at the time that Provident did enter into the con- 
tract to sell, it and its shareholders were fully aware of 
the ‘‘Section 16(b) Problem’’ which its President had out- 
lined at the October 13 informal shareholders’ meeting 
(A80, A126). 


B. The Transaction Involved the Potential 
for Speculative Abuse. 

-The Ninth Circuit went further though. Hypotheti- 
cally assuming that the transaction was unorthodox, it 
discussed whether there was a potential for speculative 
abuse—in particular, whether the officer-director or 10% 
shareholder could reasonably be expected to have had 
access to inside infermation? 


In this connection, the Court first noted that the statute 
itself presumés access to inside information on the part of 


52 


a 10% beneficial owner (7a). See e.g., Newmark v. R.K.O. 
General, Inc., 425 F. 2d 348, 356 (2d Cir.), cert. denied, 400 
U.S. 854 (1970), citing 2 L. Loss, Securities Recu.ation 
1060-61 (2d ed. 1961). The Court then considered the Kern 
County case as holding that such presumption can be rebut- 
ted where, as in a contested tender offer situation, the 
hostility of management precludes any real possibility of 
access to inside information on the part of the defeated 


offeror.* However, the Court found, no such situation 
existed here: 


‘** * * Provident has not demonstrated that the Fore- 
most management was hostile. To the contrary, the 
general cooperation involved in the transaction would 
indicate that Provident conferred intimately with the 
Foremost management and could well have had access 
to confidential corporate information.’’ (7a) 


The Court went on to illustrate the type of abuse which 
could occur in this type of transaction: 


‘For example, assume Provident learned that Fore- 
most had decided not to declare a dividend in order 
to maintain the capital it would need to develop the 
real estate just acquired from Provident. On the basis 
of this information, Provident might have reasoned 
that the market value of Foremost stock would rise 
in response to the news of the acquisition and then 
fall in response to the news of the decision not to de- 
clare a dividend. Provident might have concluded that 
it should sell its stock just after the acquisition news, 
but just before the dividend news, became public. Such 
trading is exactly the kind of speculative abuse that 
section 16(b) is designed to discourage.’’ (8a) 


* Cf. Makofsky v. Ultra Dynamics Corp., [Current] CCH Fed. 
Sec.L.Rep. 94,832 (S.D.N.Y. 1974), where the en” for specu- 


lative abuse was found to exist when the defeated offeror had placed 
representatives on the Board of Directors. 


53 


Indeed there can be no doubt, based simply on the ex- 
hibits submitted by Provident below, that it possessed 
knowledge far superior to that of either Foremost or the 
average Foremost security holder regarding the value of 
the real estate properties and unmarketable securities 
transferred to Foremost by Provident. The non-public 
nature of the information regarding the value of the assets 
is borne out by the provisions of the Purchase Agreement 
(A35): for example, in paragraph 5(a) of the Purchase 
Agreement, the confidentiality of the information regard- 
ing the business and properties of Provident was specif- 
ically provided for, in case the Purchase Agreement was 
not consummated (A35, 5(a)). In paragraph 5(d), Provi- 
dent agreed to furnish Foremost, after the closing, ‘‘in- 
formation, evidence, testimony and other assistance’’ re- 
garding assets and properties acquired by Foremost in 
case of any disputes with third parties involving those 
properties (A35, 5(d)). 


Specifically, what was sold to Foremost included real 
estate assets of Provident and 38.9% of the stock of an 
entity entitled Crocker Real Estate Company which in turn 
owned real estate and securities. The assets also included 
certain securities which were not otherwise readily mar- 
ketable. The value of these securities, the equity interest 
in the real estate assets, and the stock of Crocker was no 
less than approximately $26,000,000 (A25), obviously a 
significant amount; however, the nature and value of all 
these assets were best known by Provident. In analyzing. 
Provident’s net worth prior to the Purchase Agreement, 
Provident’s investment bankers, Dillon Read, had com- 
mented that the value of the real estate properties ‘‘is a 
very complex problem and probably will take years to work 
out’’ (A152). 


54 


More importantly, Dillon Read had been instructed to 
seek out a suitable purchaser for Provident’s assets and 
‘‘to negotiate and analyze * * * any offers.’’ Provident thus 
is charged with all of the knowledge about Foremost that 
resulted from Dillon Read’s negotiation and analysis as 
well as with what Provident learned from its direct nego- 
tiations with Foremost. But it is charged even more specif- 
ically with knowledge of what it sold to Foremost. 


Moreover, the Purchase Agreement gave Provident con- 
trol over how long it would hold the Foremost Debentures— 
in other words, it gave Provident the power or potential to 
speculate with the inside information it possessed regard- 
ing the value of the properties delivered to Foremost or by 
virtue of any other inside information it might have ob- 
tained about Foremost in the course of, or after, becoming 
a 10% beneficial owner. There was no requirement that 
the Debentures be sold at any particular time. On the other 
hand, under paragraph 5(k) (i) of the Purchase Agreement, 
Foremost was required by Provident to use its best efforts 
to cause a Registration Statement covering up to $25,000,000 
of the Debentures to be filed, to effect registration ‘‘as 
expeditiously as practicable’’ and to qualify the Indenture. 
Indeed, under subparagraphs (ii) and (iii) of paragraph 
5(k), Foremost, upon request, was required to use its best 
efforts to register the Debentures for two consecutive 
thirty-month periods after the closing date (A135, 75(k)). 
Thus, the Purchase Agreement contemplated possible sales 
of the Debentures for up to five years after the closing date 


of the Purchase Agreement. It was Provident’s choice to 
sell almost immediately. 


The fact that this transaction involved such potential 
for abuse demonstrates not only that the ‘‘hostile tender 


ah) 


offeror’’ rule of Kern County should not apply, but also 
that the rule adopted by the Ninth Circuit below exempting 
the initial purchase from Section 16 coverage unnecessarily 
frustrates the statutory purpose of preventing the unfair 
use of inside information. 


IV 


Provident was not a “liquidating agent” within the 
meaning of Rule 16a-4. 

Provident has asserted throughout this litigation that 
even if it were otherwise subject to Section i6(b), the De- 
bentures purchased and sold by it were exempt from the 
prohibitions of Section 16(b) by virtue of Rule 16a-4 (17 
C.F.R. §240.16a-4), which by its terms provides exemption 
for securities ‘‘held’’ by executors, administrators, guard- 
ians or committees for an incompetent, receivers, trustees in 
bankruptcy, assignees for the benefit of creditors, conserva- 
tors, ‘‘liquidating agents, and other similar persons duly 
authorized by law to administer the estate or assets of 
other persons,’’ the exemption being limited to the twelve- 
month period following such persons’ ‘‘appointment and 
qualification.’’ Both the District Court and the Ninth Cir- 
cuit chose to ignore this argument. 


It is clear that the burden of proving an exemption from 
Section 16 is on the person who claims it. Rheem Manu- 
facturing Co. v. Rheem, 295 F. 2d 473, 475 (9th Cir. 1961). 
On the face of the Rule itself, Provident does not qualify: 
it was not a third party ‘‘authorized by law to administer 
the estate or assets of other persons’’; it was not under 
court supervision until at least August 1970 (A56-69). 
Moreover, it never received any ‘‘appointment’’ nor took 
any steps constituting ‘‘qualification’’ as a fiduciary; cer- 


56 


tainly it was never appointed or qualified by a court. And, 
as explained below, the exemptive Rule is also limited to 
securities ‘‘held’’ by fiduciaries, that is, those that devolve 
upon the fiduciary. It does not apply where, as Provident 
urged here, the so-called ‘‘fiduciary’’ both bought and sold 
the securities during the period when it allegedly had 
fiduciary status. 


It has been said that the limited exemption furnished by 
Rule 16a-4 is justified by ‘‘the limited life of the estate, the 
supervision of the court and the publicity from periodic 
filing of accounts. * * *’’ Cook & Feldman, Insider Trading 
under the Securities Exchange Act, 66 Harv. L. Rev. 385, 
391 (1953). Obviously such rationale cannot apply to volun- 
tary dissolution procedures under California law, in which 
the putative ‘‘liquidating agent’’ is self-appointed and sub- 
ject only to self-imposed qualifications, if any, and where 
no court supervision is required, no time limit is prescribed 
(although Provident’s shareholders did, presumably with 
an eye to personal tax considerations, voluntarily impose a 
one-year deadline on the dissolution (A145)) and no peri- 
odic filing of accounts is required. 


Provident placed great importance below on the adop- 
tion of the Plan of Dissolution on September 26, 1969 (A 
102-107). However, the Plan itself repeatedly describes the 
assets and properties to be sold as ‘‘assets of Provident’’ 


or ‘‘its assets,’’? not Provident’s shareholders’ assets (A* 


102-107). In addition, Provident represented to the SEC 
by letter of October 15, 1969 that it was the selling share- 
holder of the Foremost securities under registration (A 
127), and on October 28 Provident’s counsel opined to the 
underwriters that Provident had title to the Foremost De- 
bentures and the right and power to contract to sell them 


57 


and to transfer and deliver them (A135, 75(b)(A)). None 
of these recitals made any reference to any fiduciary status. 
The same is true with respect to the Forms 3 and 4 dated 
October 31 filed by Provident (A53, A55).* 


Moreover, the Plan could have been revoked by a 
majority vote of the shareholders prior to distribution. 
Calif. Corp. Code §4606.*°* The power of revocation is 
very important because it gave Provident power to struc- 
ture the transaction to its own ends; Rule 16a-4 was not 
designed to exempt arrangements by which a party could 
declare itself a ‘‘liquidating agent,’’ engage in securities 
transactions, and then cause the liquidating agent status to 
be revoked. 


Further, there is nothing in the California law which 
suggests that, simply by adopting a plan of dissolution, 
Provident became an agent or similar person, administering 
‘*the estate or assets of other persons.’’ Indeed, (5000 of 
the California Corporations Code provides that after the 
debts and liabilities of the corporation have been paid or 
provided for, ‘‘the directors shall distribute all the remain- 
ing corporate assets among the shareholders. * * *’’ (em- 


* In these forms Provident referred to itself as the beneficial owner 
of the Debentures, stated that its ownership was “direct,” and stated 
nothi ing an alleged status as “agent” or “trustee,” although 
the SEC forms invite the disclosure of anything else “deemed rele- 
vant” by the person filing. (Instruction 11 to Form 3, Instruction 12 
to Form 4, 2 CCH Fed. Sec. L. Rep. 133,701 and 33,721 respective- 
ly.) Indeed, if Provident were truly “exempt” or had considered 
itself so, it need not have filed these reports at all or at least it could 
have availed itself of the specific right afforded by SEC Rule 16a-3 to 
disclaim beneficial ownership by an express statement to that effect. 


** There is indeed a second method of revocation: §4607 of the 
California Corporations Code which provides that certain persons, 
including the corporation itself or holders of 5 per cent or more of its 
outstanding shares, may petition the court for judicial supervision of 
winding up; and §4618 of the Code which provides that with respect 
to dissolutions so supervised the court can revoke the election to wind 
up and dissolve. 


58 


phasis added). Clearly, then, until the time of distribution, 
the assets are the corporation’s, not the shareholders’. 
Moreover, under California law, adoption of the Plan of 
Dissolution did not alter Provident’s responsibilities, or 
those of its officers and directors.* 


Provident contended below that it both purchased and 
sold the Debentures as a ‘‘liquidating agent.’’ The Rule, 
however, only exempts securities which are ‘‘held’’ by the 
fiduciary, i.e., which devolved upon him from the insider’s 
estate. As Loss states: 


‘‘The primary purpose of the rule, in other words, is 
to permit liquidation without filing reports and without 
liability under §16(b) even though the insider (or late 
insider) happened to buy within less than six months 
before the fiduciary’s sale.’”’ 2 L. Loss, Secuniries 
Reoeunation 1111 (2d ed. 1961). 


Thus, the exemption does not apply to a purchase and sale 


by the fiduciary (or a purchase by the fiduciary after an 
insider’s sale).** 


The Rule was not designed, we submit, to allow able 
and competent parties having full control over their status 


* Section 4800 of the California yey i pe Code provides that 
the Board of Directors will continue to function as a Board and shall 
have full powers to wind up and settle the corporation’s affairs. Sec- 
tion 4801 provides that after commencement of dissolution proceed- 
ings the directors are to act “in the name and on behalf of the co 
ration” with to numerous matters. See Chase v. Super 
Corp., 163 C.A.2d 83, 328 P.2d 812 (1958) in which it was specifi- 
cally held that the duty of care of the officers and directors after the 
vote for dissolution remains that of officers and directors, and that 
they do not have a trustee’s duties or liabilities. 


**See also Rule 16a-4(b) which provides that after the one~year 
pererng aed pany Sections 16(a) and 16(b) will apply only if the 
estate i is a 10 per cent owner; i.¢., the estate of a deceased 
director would not be required to file. This, Loss states, “indicates 
that the Commission views the fiduciary as standing in the insider's 
shoes during that year [of exemption].” Op. cit. at p. 1111. There- 
fore, securities purchased by the fiduciary (in contrast to those pur- 
chased by the insider) do not fall within the exemption. 


59 


and the disposition of their assets, to structure their affiairs 
so their transactions will fall within it. It exempts only 
those securities ‘‘held’’ in the estate of the decedent or 
among the assets of a corporation to which the fiduciary 
succeeds: therefore, had Provident attempted to structure 
the transaction so that it would purchase and receive the 
securities in the status of an exempt person and would 
also sell those securities within six months thereafter, the 
attempt would have failed, both on grounds of the language 
of the Rule and on grounds of policy. In fact, no such 
attempt was made at the time of the transaction; rather 
the argument was first advanced in the courts below as an 
ex post facto rationalization of a completed transaction. 


Conclusion 


Provident became a 10% beneficial owner of Fore- 
most equity securities by a voluntary purchase, volun- 
tarily sold such securities within a six-month period, 
realizing a profit, and thus is liable under Section 16 
(b). In these circumstances, the judgment below must 
be reversed, and the case remanded with directions to 
the District Court to grant summary judgment to Fore- 
most on the issue of liability and to set the case down 
for hearing as to the amount of damages.

§4607. Judicial supervision of winding up: Petition and 
notice: Provision in order to protect rights of purchasers 
of homes. If a corporation is in the process of voluntary 
winding up, the superior court of the county in which the 
principal office of the corporation is located, upon the peti- 
tion of (a) the corporation, or (b) the holders of 5 percent 
or more of the numbers of its outstanding shares, or of (c) 
three or more creditors, or of (d) three or more persons 
who have purchased homes from a construction corporation, 
and upon such notice to the corporation and to other per- 
sons interested in the corporation as shareholders or cred- 
itors as the court may order, may make orders and adjudge 
as to any and all matters concerning the winding up of the 
affaires of the corporation. 


§4618. Same: Revocation of election to wind up. The 
jurisdiction of the court includes the revocation of the 
election to wind up and dissolve by the shareholders, and 
the making of orders for the withdrawal and termination 
of proceedings to wind up and dissolve, subject to condi- 
tions for the protection of shareholders and creditors. 


§4800 Directors to act as board in voluntary proceed- 
ings: Election of officers: Acts authorized by majority of 
directors as binding. When voluntary proceedings for 
winding up or dissolution of a corporation have been com- 
menced, the board of directors shall continue to act as a 


App-8 


board and shall have full powers to wind up and settle its 
affairs. If the directors have not theretofore elected officers 
of the corporation pursuant to Section 821, the directors 
shall elect them and such assistants as the directors deem 
proper. Any act authorized or approved by a majority of 
the directors acting as a board is valid and binding as 
though authorized and consented to by all of the directors. 


§4801. Same: Powers and duties of directors. The 
powers and duties of the directors after commencement of 
such proceedings include but are not limited to, the follow- 
ing acts in the name and on behalf of the corporation: 


(a) To elect officers and to employ agents and attor- 
neys to liquidate or wind up its affairs. 


(b) To continue the conduct of the business insofar 
as necessary for the disposal or winding up thereof. 


(c) To carry out contracts and collect, pay, com- 
promise, and settle debts and claims for or against the 
corporation. 


(d) To defend suits brought against the corpora- 
tion. 


(e) To sue, in the name of the corporation, for all 
sums due or owing to the corporation or to recover 
any of its property. 


(f) To collect any amounts remaining unpaid on 


subscriptions to shares or any overpayments or unlaw- 
ful distributions. 


(g) To sell at public or private sale, exchange, con- 
vey or otherwise dispose of, all or any part of the as- 


App-9 


sets of the corporation upon such terms and conditions 
and for such considerations as such board deems rea- 
sonable or expedient, and to execute bills of sale and 
deeds of conveyance in the name of the corporation. 
If sale or exchange of all or substantially all of the as- 
sets of a corporation for profit is made for a con- 
sideration consisting in whole or in part of shares, obli- 
gations, or securities of another corporation domestic 
or foreign, or any consideration other than money, 
it shall be approved or ratified by the vote or written 
consent of holders of shares entitled to exercise a 
majority of the voting power of the corporation, either 
before or after the action of the directors. 


(h) In general, to make contracts and to do any 
and all things in the name of the corporation which 
may be proper or convenient for the purposes of wind- 
ing up, settling, and liquidating the affairs of the 
corporation.

QUESTIONS PRESENTED 
Foremost’s statement of the questions presented ignores 
the statutory language and is based upon irrelevant mat- 
ters. The questions presented are: 


1. When a person becomes a beneficial owner of more 
than 10% of an issuer’s securities as a result of a pur- 
chase of those securities, was that person a beneficial 
owner of the securities “at the time of the purchase”?! _ 


2. Does the potential for speculative abuse test enunci- 
ated in this Court’s opinion in Kern County Land Co. v. 
Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 582 exempt a transac- 
tion in which a dissolving corporation received convertible 
debentures in exchange for its assets, in which the recipi- 
ent of the debentures had no access to inside informa- 
tion about the issuer and was not likely to have such 
access by virtue of ownership of the debentures, in which 
the debentures were received solely at the insistence of 
their issuer and the recipient wished only cash to dis- 
tribute in liquidating dividends, and in which the deben- 
tures created no rights other than a debtor-creditor 
relationship and were never converted into common stock? 


3. When, under an underwriting agreement, the owner 
of debentures retains possession and the incidents of own- 
ership and cannot benefit from a rising market and is not 
insulated from a falling one, is the date of the sale of the 
debentures the date on which the underwriting agreement 


‘In discussion of this first question, we assume arguendo that 
Provident “purchased” a type of “securities” within the meaning 
of § 16(b). As is diseussed in the portion of the Argument relating 
to the second question presented (infra, pp. 32-48), we believe 
that there was no such “purchase” and that the transaction is 
exempt under this Court’s ruling in Kern County Land Co. v. 
Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 582. 


~*~ 


3 


was executed or the actual date of transfer of the deben- 
tures and relinquishment of the incidents of ownership? 


4. Under a plan of complete corporate liquidation pur- 
suant to state law, may a corporate legal owner of deben- 
tures become a liquidating agent or other similar person 
authorized to administer the assets of its shareholders so 
as to render any sale of the assets exempt from § 16(b) 
under Securities and Exchange Commission Rule 16a-4 
(17 C.F.R. § 240.16a-4) ? 


5. Under a plan of complete corporate liquidation pur- 
suant to state law, may the corporate legal owner of 
debentures be divested of beneficial ownership and its 
shareholders vested with such beneficial ownership so that 
§ 16(b) will apply to transactions by those beneficial own- 
ers and not by the legal owner? 


STATEMENT OF THE CASE 

A. The facts. 

As Foremost acknowledges (Foremost Br., pp. 3-4), the 
basic facts of this case are undisputed. Those facts, how- 
ever, are not fully set forth in Foremost’s brief. We there- 
fore present the following statement: 


1. Background. 

Provident, now dissolved, was a personal holding com- 
pany incorporated under the laws of California for the 
purpose of managing various assets for the benefit of its 
shareholders (Jt.Appx., p. A73?). At no time were any of

the officers or directors of Provident either officers or

in late 1968, Provident tentatively decided to liquidate 
and to distribute its assets, or the proceeds from a sale 
thereof, pro rata to its shareholders (Jt.Appx., p. A74). 
After investigation of various proposals, Provident de- 
cided to pursue negotiations on a proposal under which 
Foremost would purchase most of Provident’s assets (Jt. 
Appx., p. AT4). Negotiations followed between Provi- 
dent and Foremost regarding the form of the trans- 
action and the nature of the consideration to be paid (Jt. 
Appx., pp. A74-A76). During all negotiations, Foremost 
had full access to Provident’s books and records; Fore- 
most also had access to evaluations of Provident’s financial 
strueture and its assets, both of which were prepared by 
Dillon, Read & Co. (Jt. Appx., pp. A137-A138). In addition, 
Foremost made a complete appraisal of all of Provident’s 
assets, including its marketable and unmarketable securi- 
ties and its real estate (Jt.Appx., pp. A138-A139). 


To facilitate liquidation and dissolution, Provident 
sought to sell its assets for cash; it did not wish to 
receive Foremost securities in any form (Jt.Appx., p. 
A74). Foremost, however, insisted that the major portion 
of the purchase price should be in Foremost convertible 
subordinated debentures to be issued expressly for that 
purpose (Jt.Appx., pp. A74-A75). Although Prov- 
ident argued that Foremost should sell securities itself if 
it wanted to use them to finance the purchase of Provi-

Meanwhile, on September 3, 1969, the Board of Directors 
of Provident determined that it would recommend disso-

On September 8, 1969, Foremost submitted to the Cali-

“The purpose of the plan of exchange is to facili-

will vote upon a voluntary liquidation of the Com-

mentioned Debentures for distribution to its share- 
holders. The Exchange Agreement provides for regis- 
tration of the Debentures under the Securities Act of 
1933” (Jt.Appx., pp. A90-A91). 


At a hearing on the application, representatives of both 
parties expressed the opinion that the transaction was 
fair, just and equitable to their respective interests (Jt. 
Appx., pp. A46, A48).

B. The proceedings below. 

The decision of the district court: The district court 
granted Provident’s motion for summary judgment on the 
question of nonliability. The court based its decision on an 
examination of “the overall character of the transaction 
and its ultimate effect” (Pet.Appx., p. 39a; 331 F.Supp. 
791), concluding that the transaction was not subject to 
speculative abuse (Pet.Appx., pp. 39a-4la; 331 F.Supp. 


eee a a. ..a.Qg ee 


10 


(91-792). The district court did not pass upon any of the 
other grounds advanced by Provident. 


The decision of the Court of Appeals: On appeal, the 
Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment because Provident 
had not owned any security of Foremost when it entered 
into the contract under which it received the Foremost 
debentures. The court held that therefore Provident was 
not a beneficial owner of any security of Foremost “at the 
time of the purchase” (Pet. Appx., pp. lla-29a; 506 F.2d 
607-615). 

The question whether any actual profit was realized 
and, if so, the amount of such profit was left open in the 
proceedings below and was not decided by either the dis- 


trict court or the Court of Appeals.4 


SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT 

1. Section 16(b) expressly provides that it is designed 
to prevent “the unfair use of information which may have 
heen obtained by [an insider] by reason of his relationship” 
to the corporation. Insofar as it applies to a beneficial owner 
of more than 10 per cent of the corporation's securities, that 
relationship must exist “both at the time of the purchase 
and sale, or the sale and purchase, of the security involved.” 


Stockholders were included within §16(b) because an 


4We do not agree with Foremost’s argumentative characteriza- 
tions of the opinions below (see Foremost Br., pp. 12-16). 
For example, the district court did not “concede” that “a starkly 
literal reading of Section 16(b)” would render Provident liable 
(ibid., p. 13). The portion of the opinion quoted is a paraphrase 
of a Foremost argument which the district court rejected (see 
Pet.Appx., p. 38a; 331 F.Supp. 791). Most of Foremost’s argu- 
mentative characterizations are not, however, relevant to the 
questions before this Court. To the extent that they are relevant, 
we comment upon them in the Argument which follows, 


ll 


owner of a large quantity of stock may have access to inside 
information. But one who has become an owner of more 
than 10 per cent of a corporation's securities by virtue of 
a purchase of those securities could not have made his pur- 
chase based upon inside information obtained from a rela- 
tionship with the corporation which did not yet exist. 
Henee, such a purchase is not subject to § 16(b) because it 
could not have been part of a short-swing transaction 
undertaken with the access to inside information which is 


presumed under the statute. 


2. The transaction was not an orthodox cash purchase 
of securities by Provident and involved no potential for 
speculative abuse under the test laid out by this Court in 
Kern County Land Co. v. Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 
582, 597. The Foremost debentures acquired by Provident, 
although convertible into common stock, were never con- 
verted by Provident and they gave Provident no rights in 
Foremost other than as a creditor. In negotiations between 
the parties, Foremost had aecess to information about 
Provident but, as a debenture holder, Provident had no 
inside information about Foremost and no right to obtain 


such information. 


3. Before the sale, Provident had distributed approxi- 
mately one half of the debentures and the remaining de- 
bentures were convertible into less than 10 per cent of 
Foremost’s common stock. Consequently, Provident was 


not, at the time of the sale, an insider subject to § 16(hb). 


4. The transaction was exempt from § 16(b). Provident 
was a liquidating agent within the exemption set forth in 
Rule 16a-4. In any event, Provident had no beneficial own- 
ership of the debentures at the time of the purchase and 


sale. 


12 


ARGUMENT 


I. THE COURT OF APPEALS CORRECTLY DETERMINED 
THAT § 16(b) WAS INAPPLICABLE TO THE TRANSACTION 
BECAUSE PROVIDENT HAD NO OWNERSHIP OR OTHER 
INTEREST IN FOREMOST AT THE TIME OF THE AC- 
QUISITION OF THE FOREMOST DEBENTURES. 


A. The express terms of § 16(b), the statute's purpose and its 
history demonstrate that §16(b) applies to beneficial 
owners of securities who are, by virtue of their relation- 
ship to the issuer, in a position to abuse inside information 
both at the time of the purchase and of the sale. 


l. Under the terms of the statute, a beneficial owner must be such 
both at the time of the purchase and of the sale. 


Section 16(b) is a rule of limited application which does 
“not reach every transaction in which an investor actually 
relies on inside information” (Reliance Electric Co. v. 
Emerson Electric Co. (1972) 404 U.S. 418, 422). As Fore- 
most acknowledges, § 16(b) was directed against “those in 
control of large corporations {who} had used inside infor- 
mation or had manipulated the affairs of their corporations 
to profit from short-term speculative trading in their cor- 
porations’ securities” (Foremost Br., p. 18; emphasis 
added). The beneficial owners of more than 10°. of the 
securities of a corporation were included in § 16(b)_ be- 
cause Congress determined that, by ownership of a large 
number of shares, an individual could obtain aecess to 
inside information and could utilize that information to 
engage in speculative short-swing transactions. Mr. [’e- 
cora, counsel for the Senate Committee conducting hear- 
ings on the proposed Exchange Act, observed: 

“The theory was that the ownership of 5 pereent of 
the stock [the amount then specified in the proposed 
legislation! would practically constitute him an in- 
sider, and by virtue of that position he could acquire 


13 


confidential information which he might use for his 
own enrichment by trading in the open market, against 
the interests of the general body of the stockholders. 
That is the main purpose sought to be served” (Hear- 
ings on S.Res. 84, S.Res. 56 and S.Res. 97, Senate 
Comm. on Banking and Curreney, 73rd Cong. (1934) 
(hereinafter “Senate Hearings”), p. 7741; emphasis 
added). 


Henee, there can be no presumption of access to inside 
information until after such time as one has become an 
owner of more than 10° of an issuer's securities. Even 
the Second Cireuit—which has held contrary to the opinion 
below—has conceded that: 

“The statutory reference to a ten percent beneficial 
owner rests on the presumption that an owner of this 
quantity of securities has access to inside informa- 
tion. * * * [T]his preswmption would not justify the 
conclusion that one who purchases a quantity of shares 
which makes him a ten percent beneficial owner has 
done so on the basis of inside information * * * ” 
(Newmark v. RKO General, Inc. (2 Cir. 1970) 425 
F.2d 348, 356). 


It is for precisely this reason, we submit, that § 16(b) 
is not applicable to the instant transaction. This Court, 
in rejecting the argument that preacquisition calculations 
by one later becoming a 10° beneficial owner should be 
considered in relation to the possibility of speculative 
abuse, noted that such caleulations 

“* * * do not represent the kind of speculative abuse 
at which the statute is aimed, for they could not have 
heen based on inside information obtained from sub- 
stantial stockholdings that did not yet exist” (Kern 


ee SS... 


14 


County Land Co. v. Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 
982, 597). 


Similarly, a person making a decision to purchase stock 
which will make him an owner of more than 10% of a 
corporation's outstanding stock could not have made that 
decision “based on inside information obtained from sub- 
stantial stockholdings that did not yet exist.” Accordingly, 
) 16(b) is not applicable to short-swing transactions by 


that person until after he becomes a statutory insider. 


Section 16(b) expressly specifies that it is designed to 
prevent “the unfair use of information which may have 
been obtained by [an insider] by reason of his relationship 
to the issuer.” It is, by its terms, directed against short- 
swing transactions—a “purchase and sale” or “sale and 
purchase” within six months. It requires, in the case 
of a beneficial owner, that the relationship with the issuer 
exist at both ends of the short-swing transaction—“both 
at the time of the purchase and sale, or the sale and pur- 
chase, of the security involved.” Obviously, no information 
could possibly be obtained by reason of a relationship 
to the issuer until the relationship actually exists. It 
cannot, therefore, be presumed that an outsider whose 
purchase makes him a more than 10° owner has made 
that purchase on the basis of inside information. Hence. 
the necessary relationship from which aecess to inside in- 
formation can be presumed does not exist at one end of 
the short-swing transaction and it should not be subject 
to § 16(b). 


Furthermore, the phrase “at the time of” modifies both 
“purchase” and “sale.” Insofar as a sale is concerned, it 


cannot be disputed that the term “at the time of” means 


15 


before giving effect to the sale. Thus a sale by a more 
than 10° shareholder is subject to the Act because that 
shareholder is presumed to have access to inside informa- 
tion by virtue of a relationship to the corporation. By the 
same token, the required 10°¢ status must be achieved be- 
fore, rather than as a result of, a given purchase. The 
relationship of insider therefore must antedate both the 


purchase and the sale in order for liability to attach. 


foremost uses the phrases “at the time of the pur- 
chase,” “when the purchase occurs,” and “simultaneously 
with the purchase” interchangeably (see Foremost Br., 
pp. 26-27; and see Allis-Chalmers Br., p. 12). How- 
ever, to prevail, Foremost must attribute the meaning 
“as a result of the purchase” to all those phrases. One 
of the commentators relied upon by Foremost (fore- 
most Br., pp. 24, 31), in discussing whether a pur- 
chaser of more than 10° of the shares of a corporation 
is a beneficial owner “at the time of the purchase,” pointed 
up the difficulty with Foremost’s semantic argument. He 
noted that the words “at the time of the purchase” must 
mean either “before the purchase or after giving effect to 
the purchase” (Seligman, Problems under the Securities 
Exchange Act (1934) 21 Va.L.Rev. 1, 20). In the case 
of the second step of a short-swing transaction, the sale 
(or the “resale”), 
“* * * the words ‘at the time’ must mean immediately 
before the resale, for if they mean after giving effect 
to the resale, then the effect of the quoted language 
would be to render Section 16(b) practically ineffee- 
tive since it could be avoided by a single sale of all 
the stock owned. Accordingly, if the words ‘at the 
time’ are to be given the meaning of immediately be- 
fore in the case of the resale, the same meaning 


16 


would seem necessary in the case of the purchase. 
From this it would follow that the transaction under 
discussion comes within the exception contained in 
the quoted language” (ibid.). 


Although that commentator went on to reject such a 
reading of “at the time of” when applied to a purchase, 
he did so without any examination of the statutory pur- 
pose and history. He engaged, as does Foremost (Fore- 
most Br., pp. 20-21), in the simplistic syllogism: (1) that 
speculative abuse might be possible in some transactions, 
(2) that the proposed interpretation could prevent that 
asserted abuse and (3) that, therefore, the proposed in- 
terpretation should be adopted. Such an argument is no 
answer to the interpretative inquiry before this Court. 
Although there have been declarations that § 16(b) should 
be broadly interpreted to effectuate its purpose (see, e.g., 
Foremost Br., pp. 20-22), the courts heretofore have 
clearly pointed out that it may not be expanded to deal 
with supposed speculative abuses which are beyond its 
intended scope. Indeed, this Court has already considered 
—and rejected—precisely the same syllogism presented 
by Foremost. It has expressly refused to extend § 16(b) 
“to include all persons realizing ‘short swing’ profits who 
either act on the basis of ‘inside’ information or have the 
possibility of ‘inside’ information” (Blau v. Lehman 
(1962) 368 U.S. 403, 411).

2. No court other than the court below has examined the proviso 
here in question in light of its purpose and history.

Courts of Appeals have passed upon the question here in

holding of a district judge that an initial acquisition of

vu. Graham-Paige Motors Corporation (2 Cir, 1956) 232

judge in Stella did not directly address the question 
whether a purchase by an outsider of more than 10% 
should be within the statute. Rather, he based his deci- 
sion solely upon the fear that, unless “at the time of” 
were interpreted to mean “as a result of,” then certain 
sales and repurchases would be exempt from § 16(b) cov- 
erage. Ile declared that, if “at the time of” the repur- 
chase meant “before giving effect to” such repurchase, 
“* * * it would he possible for a person to purchase 
a large block of stock, sell it out until his ownership 
was reduced to less than 10%, an’ then repeat the 
process, ad infinitum” (104 F.Supp. 959).

follow. A sale by a more than 10° holder to less than 
10% and a repurchase by him would be subject to § 16(b) 
because such a shareholder 

“* * * was within a class of persons who had access 


to inside information by reason of their relationship

to the issuer prior to making his initial decision to 
speculate * * *” (Pet.Appx., p. 26a; 506 F.2d 614).

F.2d 348, 355-356; Perine v. Wiliam Norton & Company, 
Ine. (2 Cir, 1974) 509 F.2d 114, 118) and a district court 
in the Seventh Cireuit, again without analysis, followed

3. The purpose and the legislative history of §16(b) support the 
conclusion that it applies to beneficial owners of securities who 
are, by virtue of their ownership, in a position to abuse inside 
information at the time of the purchase. 


Section 16(b) was designed to deal with short-swing 
transactions by corporate insiders. Stockholders were in- 
cluded within that class of insiders because ownership of 
a large quantity of stock could result in access to inside 
information, It was against this background that Congress 
specified that the statute would not be applicable to more 
than 10% beneficial owners unless they were such “both 


at the time of the purchase and sale.” 


In addition to the considerations already mentioned, the 
legislative history also supports the conclusion that § 16(b) 
was directed at short-swing transactions by beneficial 
owners when those owners entered into the short-swing 
transaction in a position to utilize inside information. 
Both Foremost (Foremost Br., p. 29) and amicus Allis- 
Chalmers (Allis-Chalmers Br., p. 15) concede that the 


initial draft of what is now § 16(b)—Senate Bill 2693 and 
House Bill 7852—made it clear that insider status must 
precede the questioned purchase.* Thomas Corcoran, one 
of the chief draftsinen of the statute, explained that the 
purpose of the section was to prevent 
“* * * ony short-term speculations in the stock. He [an 
insider] cannot, with his inside information get in and 
out of stock within six months” (House Hearings p. 
133; emphasis added). 


Foremost (Foremost Br., p. 29) and amicus Allis-Chal- 
mers (Allis-Chahners Br., pp. 15-16) point out that the 
initial bills were amended and Foremost protests that the 
“weight” to be given to them “escapes” it (Foremost Br., 
p. 29, ftn.). That “weight”, however, is clear. The initial 
bills were the subject of most of the hearings held by 
hoth the Senate and House Committees and almost all 
comments in the legislative history were directed at them.

B. Foremost’s arguments are founded upon misconceptions of 
the statute’s purpose and history. 


Foremost refers to §16(d) of th Exchange Act as 
asserted “contemporaneous” evidence in support of its 
interpretation, erroneously contending that the problems 
which were the concern of that section “would not have 
arisen if the interpretation adopted by the Ninth Cireuit 
were indeed the interpretation contemplated by Congress” 
(Foremost Br., pp. 30-31, 32; and see Allis-Chalmers Br., 


26 


pp. 14-15). This argument misconstrues § 16(d) and ignores 
its clearly stated purpose. In the first place, what is now 
§16(d) was not enacted until 1964 (Public Law 88-467 
(1964) 78 Stat. 579) and therefore carihot be deemed con- 
temporaneous evidence of anything with respect to § 16(b). 
In the second place, § 16(d) was a part of the amendments 
which extended coverage of the Exchange Act to over- 
the-counter securities. Section 16(d) was ineluded in the 
law not because of any concern about beneficial owners 
but rather to deal with “transactions of a broker-dealer 
who is making a market in a security while represented 
on the issuer’s board of directors” (S.Rept. No. 379 (1963) 
88th Cong., Ist Sess., p. 22). The legislative history makes 
it clear that Congress believed that such broker-dealer- 
directors served a legitimate market function with respect 
to over-the-counter securities. The intent of § 16(d) was 
to avoid unnecessarily penalizing such directors: 
“If section 16(b) were applied to market-making 
transactions by such broker-dealer-directors, they 
would be compelled, as a practical matter, to cease 
their market-making activities or resign their diree- 
torships. To avoid requiring them to choose between 
the two alternatives, S. 1642 would add a new sub- 
section (d) to section 16 to exempt over-the-counter 
transactions in securities by dealers in the ordinary 
course of business and incident to the establishment 
or maintenance of primary or secondary market for 
such securities, provided the securities have not been 
held in the dealer's investment account” (S.Rept. No. 
379 (1963) SSth Cong., Ist Sess., pp. 22-23: see also 
Congressional Record (1964) 88th Cong., 2nd Sess., 
pp. 17921, 17926-17929, 18181, 18182-18183), 


27 


Lastly, even if all the above were not true, § 16(d) 
would nonetheless be necessary to exempt certain trans- 
actions by beneficial owners under the Ninth Cireuit’s 
interpretation of §16(b) as well as under Foremost’s 
interpretation, A dealer trading to maintain a market in 
a security could acquire more than 10% beneficial 
ownership by virtue of one or more purchases and then 
could make additional purchases. In the absence of § 16(d), 
such purchases would be subject to § 16(b).

with our assessment of the ‘wholesome purpose’ of the Act” 
(404 U.S. 424). 


Foremost’s attempted distinction of Kern County Land 
Co. v. Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 US. 582 is equally 
unavailing. In that case, this Court commented upon the 
obvious fact that one becomes a statutory insider as a 
result of acquisition of more than 10° of a corporation’s 
outstanding stock (411 U.S. 584, 595, 598). Although Fore- 
most places great reliance on statements to this effect 
(Foremost Br., p. 36; and see Allis-Chalmers Br., p. 8), 
those statements plainly do not deal with the question 
whether one is a statutory insider “at the time of” entry 
into the contract by which the stock was acquired. 


The opinion did not pass directly upon this question. 
Ifowever, it did, as noted above (pp. 13-14), reject the 
argument that preacquisition calculations by those about 
to become 10% beneficial owners should be considered in 
determining the possibility of speculative abuse. Such 
ealeulations, this Court said, 

“* * * do not represent the kind of speculative 
abuse at which the statute is aimed, for they could 
not have been based on inside information obtained 


from substantial stockholdings that did not vet exist” 
(411 U.S. 597). 


Foremost suggests that this Court did not mean what 
it said, erroneously asserting that “it is the potential for 
obtaining inside information, not the ripening of equity 
ownership, which is the important factor” (Foremost Br., 
p. 33). This assertion is based upon Foremost’s contention 
that the statute contemplates a relationship “suflicient to 
permit the abuse of inside information” in the absence of 


30 


an ownership of “substantial stockholdings” (Foremost 
Br., pp. 33-35). That contention ignores the rationale 
which underlies § 16(b) and demonstrates a complete mis- 
understanding of the statute. Ownership of “substantial 
stockholdings” exists, under the statute, as a result of a 
“purchase” of more than 10% of a class of “equity se- 
curity” as defined therein. If one is not a beneficial owner 
of such an equity security, then there can be no presumed 
access to inside information and no liability under § 16(b). 
Whether or not the presumption of access to information is 
reasonable or should be made in a given situation is an 
entirely different matter.'’* The point, for purposes of 
Foremost’s argument, is that the statute defines the owner- 
ship of stockholdings from which the presumption of access 
to inside information arises and that ownership necessarily 
precedes the presumed access. If such access in fact did 
exist without substantial stockholdings, then the Act pro- 
vides other remedies. 


Certainly, one may engage in conjecture about various 
possibilities of speculative abuse in different factual con- 
texts.'* However, $16(b) is a rule of limited application

Lastly, Foremost’s “passing” comment on a supposed 
“anomaly” (see Foremost Br., p. 35) is based upon its 
continuing failure to recognize that a presumpiion of 
access to information by a beneficial owner is founded 
upon the ownership of securities and that liability under 
§16(b) is dependent upon that ownership. Various “delli- 
veries” under one contract are without significance because 
it is the ownership, not the possession, of securities which 
gives rise to the presumption. It is the statute itself 
which requires that some purchases by beneficial owners 
be“excluded. And, for the reasons discussed above, the 
statute excludes purchases by outsiders who do not have 
more than 10% ownership, and thus cannot be presumed

to have access to inside information, “at the time of the 
purchase.” 


II. THE TRANSACTION WAS NOT SUBJECT TO 
SPECULATIVE ABUSE.'® 


In ruling that the transaction was not exempt under 
this Court’s holding in Kern County Land Co. v. Occi- 
dental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 582, the Ninth Cireuit held 
(1) that the transaction was “orthodox” and therefore 
not subject to the Kern County ruling and (2) that, in 
any event, it was subject to §16(b) (Pet.Appx., pp. 4a- 
8a: 506 F.2d 604-606). Both of these conclusions were in 


error. 


As in Kern County, Provident had no prior association 
with Foremost and owned no Foremost securities before 
the transaction here in question. As a result of the trans- 
action, Provident acquired debentures, not stock, and 
it did not have nor was it likely to have access to informa- 
tion by virtue of that acquisition. Therefore, the transac- 
tion was not of the type at which the statute is aimed and 
it did not present the opportunity for speculative abuse 
with which Congress was concerned. Not only would ap- 


plication of § 16(b)’s conclusive presumption be contrary

to this Court’s opinion in Kern County, but it would also

A. The exchange of assets for debentures was an “unortho- 
dox’”’ transaction. 


In Kern County Land Co. v. Uccidental Corp. (1973) 
411 U.S. 582, this Court ruled that “a ‘pragmatic’ ap- 
proach to §16(b) will best serve the statutory goals” 
(411 U.S. 594, ftn. 26) and it held that the section should 
be applied “only when its application would serve its goals” 
(411 U.S. 595). The Ninth Cireuit, however, erroneously 
held that the transaction here in question was an “ortho- 
dox” purchase and that therefore there was no need to 
determine if application of 4 16(b) to it would serve the 
statutory purpose (Pet.Appx., pp. 5a-6a; 506 F.2d 604-605). 
In so holding, the Ninth Cireuit ignored the facts of this 
ease which demonstrate that the transaction was not “or- 
thodox” and not one to which the statute should be auto- 
matically applied. 

Provident did not, as in a traditional cash-for-stock 
transaction, enter the market seeking to purchase stock. 
Provident did not want Foremost’s, or anyone else’s, stock ; 
it wanted only cash to distribute to its shareholders in 
the liquidation already under way (Jt.Appx., pp. A74- 
A75). Nor did Provident pay cash for the Foremost de- 
bentures. Rather, it was Foremost which sought to 
purchase Provident’s assets and it made payment in cash 
and in debentures “created solely for the purpose of this 
transaction” (Foremost Br., p. 6; and see Jt.Appx., Pp. 
A775). 

Provident never received any Foremost stock but rather 


received debentures which, although convertible into

34 


common stock, were never so converted by Provident. As 
has been observed, debentures are not ordinarily considered 
to be stock (Chemical Fund, Inc. v. Xerox Corporation (2 
Cir. 1967) 377 F.2d 107, 110-111). A convertible debenture 
is an “equity security” under the Exchange Act 
“* * * only because of its convertible nature, since an 
‘equity security’ is defined [in section 3(a)(11))} as 
‘any stock or similar security; or any security con- 
vertible * * * into such a security * * * or any such 
warrant or right * * * ’” (377 F.2d 110). 


Because a holding of debentures creates only a debtor- 


creditor relationship, 

“* * * there is no reason whatever to believe that any 
holder of any Convertible Debentures would, by rea- 
son of such holding, normally have any standing or 
position with the officers, directors or large stock- 
holders of a company so that such holder of Deben- 
tures would be the recipient of any inside informa- 
tion” (377 F.2d 111). 


Thus, the transaction was not an exchange of cash for 
stock and was not one which would ordinarily involve any 
receipt of inside information. We therefore submit that it 
was not a “traditional cash-for-stock” transaction which is 
“clearly within the purview of §16(b)” (Kern County 
Land Co. v. Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 582, 593). 


In addition, this Court, in Kern County, noted that 
“unorthodox” transactions would include “exchanges pur- 
suant to mergers and other corporate reorganizations” 
(411 U.S. 593, ftn. 24). Similarly, Professor Loss has 


noted that “unorthodox” transactions may include “the 


acquisition of securities of one company in exchange for 


35 


the assets of another” (Loss, Securities Regulation (Supp. 
2d Ed. 1969) Vol. V, p. 3029).'* 


Ignoring the siguilicant facts discussed above, the Ninth 
Cireuit concluded that the transaction was “essentially a 
cash-for-stock transaction” because it could see “no mean- 
ingful distinction between consideration in the forin of cash 
and consideration in the form of a corporate asset” (Pet. 
Appx., pp. 5a, Ga; 506 F.2d G04, 605: emphasis added; and 
see Foremost Br., pp. 49-50). The meaningful distinetion 
hetween an orthodox and unorthodox transaction plainly 
exists in this case. When cesh is utilized to purchase stock, 
it is reasonable to conclude that a party wished to acquire 
that stock and that therefore the transaction may involve 
an inherent possibility of speculation. 

Provident, however, did not make a eash purchase, did 
not seek to acquire stock, and did not aequire stock. It re- 
ceived Foremost debentures as part of the consideration 


for its assets and it did se only at Foremost’s insistence. 


'6The court below placed reliance (Pet.Appx., p. 5a; 506 F.2d 
605) on Professor Loss’ statement that: 

“Conversions and merger-like transactions aside, the volun- 
tary exchange of securities, either for assets or for other 
securities, at least of a different issuer, is ordinarily as much 
a ‘purchase’ or ‘sale’ as if the consideration had been cash” 
(Loss, Securities Regulation (2d Ed. 1969) Vol. IT, p. 1072). 

However, Provident did not exchange its securities for assets 
or other securities; rather, Foremost purchased Provident’s assets 
in exchange for cash and debentures. Professor Loss does not 
consider any transaction in which debentures, rather than stock, 
were received, Furthermore, he does not state that even trans- 
actions involving stock are necessarily orthodox, noting only 
that they will “ordinarily” be so considered and also expressly 
exempting “merger-like transactions.” In addition, it should 
be noted that the primary ease cited by Loss (Loss, Securities
