the transaction to see if it would “lend itself to manipulation” 
(Blau v. Lehman (2 Cir. 1960) 286 F.2d 786, 792). 


36 


The undisputed facts demonstrate that Provident had no 
wish to acquire the debentures and, most importantly, 
that Provident never converted the debentures into stock 
which might arguably have given it access to inside in- 
formation. The possibility of speculation was not inherent 
in the transaction. Therefore, the transaction should be 
examined to determine whether there existed any potential 
for speculative abuse. 


Foremost’s attempted defense of the Ninth Circuit’s 
holding on this question involves two separate points: 
(1) that the facts of the transaction were not exactly the 
same as certain other unorthodox transactions in other 
cases and (2) that the transaction was “voluntary” (Fore- 
most Br., pp. 50-51). As to the first point, the trans- 
action is indeed unique and, insofar as we are aware, 
unlike that in any other reported case. There is, how- 
ever, no suggestion in any case that the pragmatic ap- 
proach endorsed in Kern County should be limited to the 
specific fact situations in already reported cases. Indeed, 
there is no logical reason why there should be such a 
limitation. As to the second point, Foremost’s emphasis 
on “voluntariness” is misplaced. The stock option trans- 
action in Kern County was wholly voluntary (411 U.S. 
582-600). Moreover, no “determinative consequences” arise 
from the fact that a transaction was voluntary (Blau v. 
Lamb (2 Cir. 1966) 363 F.2d 507, 520, ftn. 16). 


Finally, it should be noted that the Ninth Circuit’s 
holding on the “orthodox” transaction question would en- 
graft upon the statute an ill-defined and unnecessary re- 
quirement of determining whether a particular noncash 
transaction is “essentially” a cash transaction. This would 


37 


spawn a series of decisions which would attempt to define 
this nebulous concept. The instant transaction unquestion- 
ably did not involve any cash payment by Provident and 
Provident acquired debentures, not stock, of Foremost. 
Therefore, the transaction should be examined for a po- 
tential for speculative abuse because 
“* * * the question is not in any event primarily a 
semantic one, but must be resolved in the light of 
the legislative purpose—to curb short swing specu- 
lation by insiders” (Ferraiolo v. Newman (6 Cir. 
1958) 259 F.2d 342, 344). 


B. The transaction involved no potential for speculative 
abuse. 


1. Provident did not have, and was not likely to have, access to 
inside information or any control or influence over Foremost. 


As this Court has noted, the purpose of § 16(b) is 
*“* = * to curb short-swing trading by insiders whose 
position gives them access to information not avail- 
able to the investing public and the ability to influ- 
ence corporate policy” (Kern County Land Co. v. 
Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 582, 592, ftn. 23). 


In order to implement the statutory purpose, this Court 
has endorsed those decisions which inquire “whether the 
particular type of transaction involved is one that gives 
rise to speculative abuse” (Reliance Electric Co. v. Emer- 
son Elvctric Co. (1972) 404 U.S. 418, 424, ftn. 4). 


The undisputed facts demonstrate that Provident did not 
have, and that there was no likelihood that it could have 
had, any inside information about Foremost or any influ- 
ence over Foremost’s affairs. Prior to the acquisition of 


the Foremost debentures, Provident had no ownership or 


38 


other interest in Foremost (Jt.Appx., pp. A73-A74). 
Therefore, Provident could not be found liable on the 
basis of hypothetical speculative calculations prior to the 
acquisition because any such calculations “could not have 
been based on inside information obtained from substan- 
tial stockholdings that did not yet exist” (Kern County 
Land Co. v. Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 U.S. 582, 597). 


Foremost makes a misleadingly broad reference to “co- 
operative negotiation and exchange of information be- 
tween issuer and purchaser prior to the time of purchase” 
(Foremost Br., p. 33). Assuming the negotiations which 
led to Foremost’s purchase of Provident’s assets to be a 
relevant consideration, nonetheless it is undisputed that 
they involved only an evaluation of Provident’s assets 
which were to be transferred to Foremost. During that 
time, it was Foremost that had complete access to all of 
Provident’s books and records and to complete evaluations 
of Provident’s financial structure and its assets (Jt. Appx., 
pp. A137-A139). But Provident had no right to, and it 
did not in fact have anv access to, Foremost’s books and 
records or any other inside information about Foremost. 


The situation was not altered after the consummation 
of Foremost’s purchase of Provident’s assets. As a result 
of the sale of its assets, Provident acquired Foremost 
debentures. not stock. The debentures, although converti- 


ble into common stock. were never converted by Provi- 
dent. The dehentures themselves did not give Provident 
any voting rights in the affairs of the corporation or any 
other incidents of corporate ownership which might argu- 
ably have provided influencc over Foremost’s affairs or 


39 


afforded the debenture holder access to inside informa- 
tion.'? 


The debentures did no more than evidence a debtor- 
creditor relationship. The Indenture, under which the de- 
bentures were issued and which governs the relationship 
between Foremost and the debenture holders, gives no 
rights to the debenture holders other than rights as cred- 
itors. There is nothing in the Indenture which would make 
inapplicable the general rule that “a debenture is usually 
only an obligation to pay” (Fletcher, Cyclopedia of the 
Law of Private Corporations (1959 Ed.) Vol. 19, § 9162, 
p. 374; and see § 9089, pp. 291-293). Under the terms of 
the Indenture, a debenture holder could not possibly ob- 
tain any access to inside information. Thus, Provident 
had no inside information and was not even in a position 
to have obtained such information “had it wanted to” 
(ef. Allis-Chalmers Mfg. Co. v. Gulf & Western Indus., 
Inc. (N.D.M1L. 1974) 372 F.Supp. 570, 579; appeal pend- 
ing).?*

considered an “equity security” under the Act only be- 
cause of its convertible nature, an “equity seeurity” 


being defined as “any stock or similar security; or any

To the contrary, the Act is not concerned with persons

2. The court below erred in its conjecture that there was a potential 
for speculative abuse. 


The Ninth Cireuit’s erroneous decision on the question 
of the potential for speculative abuse was influenced by 
its consideration of two factors: 

“(1) Could [Provident] reasonably be expected to 
have had access to inside information? And (2) did 
[Provident] initiate the transaction voluntarily?” 
(Pet. Appx., pp. Ga-Ta; 506 F.2d 605). 


The Ninth Cireuit correctly noted that the presumption 
of access to inside information could be rebutted (Pet. 
Appx., p. Ta: 506 F.2d 605). However, it erroneously 
held that Provident had not rebutted that presumption 
simply because Provident had “not demonstrated that the 
Foremost management was hostile” (ibid.; see Foremost 
Br., p. 52), thus making management “hostility” a pre- 
requisite to a Kern County defense. In Kern County, 


| 


43 


however, this Court examined the facts to ascertain 
whether 
“* * * Occidental cither had or was likely to have ac- 
cess to inside information, by reason of its ownership 
of more than 10% of the outstanding shares of Old 
Kern, so as to afford it an opportunity to reap specu- 
lative, short-swing profits * * *” (411 U.S. 596). 


From the fact—among others—that Old Kern’s manage- 
ment was hostile, this Court inferred that the likelihood 
of possession of inside information which would enable 
speculation was remote (411 U.S. 598). Plainly, if the 
presumption of aecess to inside information ean be re- 
butted by such an inference, it can also be rebutted by 
other facts. As discussed above, the record is clear that 
Provident’s brief ownership of the debentures did not 
give, nor was it likely to give, any access to inside infor- 
mation. 


The Ninth Circuit also erroneously asserted that Provi- 
dent, being aware that Foremost might need capital be- 
cause of its purchase of Provident'’s assets, “might have 
had” access to information that Foremost had decided 
not to declare a dividend (Pet.Appx., p. Sa: 506 F.2d 
606; and see Foremost Br., p. 52). By the same token, it 
is possible that Occidental “might have had” access to 
such information about Kern and, indeed, it is perhaps 
possible to engage in conjecture ahout the existence of 
such information in every transaction. But this Court has 
made it clear that the inquiry must be directed to the 
transaction which actually occurred. In Kern County, 
Occidental was an owner of stock and, unlike a debenture 
holder, had voting rights and, under California law, a 


44 


right to access to information not available to the general 
public, including a right to inspect the share register, the 
books of account, and the minutes of shareholders’, board 
of directors’ and executive committee meetings (Cal. 
Corp.Code § 3003). Moreover, Occidental was permitted 
access to Old Kern’s general ledger, consolidated financial 
statements, consolidated journal entries, details of cash 
receipts from oil operations, supporting trial balances, and 
other records (411 U.S. 587, ftn. 12). From these facts, it 
would certainly be possible to theorize that Occidental 
“might have had” access to information which could have 
enabled it to speculate. The controlling consideration, 
however, was that Oecidental did not have and was not 
likely to have access to such information. Again, the rec- 
ord is clear that Provident did not have access to any 
information at all, and was not in a position to obtain it,

only in the sense that, at Foremost’s insistence, it agreed 
to accommodate Foremost’s financing, But Provident 
wished to reeeive only cash and had no desire whatever 
to receive the debentures. Indeed, as the district court 
noted, 
“In all its essential details the form of the trans- 
action was insisted upon if not dictated by Foremost, 
often contrary to the plans and wishes of Provident. 
If the matter had been handled as Provident wished, 


this case could never have arisen” (Pet.Appx., pp. 
40a-tla; 331 F.Supp. 792). 


Moreover, we note again that the “voluntary” nature of 
the transaction is not controlling. In Kern County, in- 
voluntariness was again a fact—among others—involved 
in the stock conversion transaction. However, the subse- 
quent stock option was a wholly voluntary transaction 
and this Court coneluded that there existed no potential 
for speculative abuse in that transaction (411 U.S. 601- 
604+). The voluntary nature of a transaction is simply 
not determinative (Blau v. Lamb (2 Cir. 1966) 363 F.2d 
007, 520). 


C. The application of § 16(b)'s conclusive presumption to the 


facts of this case would raise serious constitutional 
questions. 


Application of § 16(b)’s conclusive presumption to the 
facts of this case would not only be contrary to this 
Court’s opinion in Kern County Land Co. v. Occidental 


Corp. (1973) 411 U.S, 582, but it would also raise serious 


46 


questions under the due process clause of the Fifth 
Amendment. Section 16(b) was enacted following exten- 
sive hearings in which evidence was received concerning 
speculation in stock by a class of insiders. As specified 
in {16(b)’s introductory clause, the section was enacted 
“flor the purpose of preventing the unfair use of 
information which may have been obtained by [a stat- 
utory insider] * * * by reason of his relationship to 
the issuer” (15 U.S.C. § 78p(b), 48 Stat. 896). 
The class of insiders consisted of “directors, officers, and 
principal stockholders of a corporation” (S.Rept. 792 
(1934) 73rd Cong., 2d Sess., p. 9). As this Court has 
noted, these “[i]nsiders could exploit information not gen- 
erally available to others to secure quick profits” (Aern 
County Land Co. v. Occidental Corp. (1973) 411 US. 
582, 592). Accordingly, 
“* * * the only method Congress deemed effective 
to curb the evils of insider trading was a flat rule 
taking the profits out of a class of transactions in 
which the possibility of abuse was believed to be in- 
tolerably great” (Reliance Electric Co, v. Emerson 
Electric Co. (1972) 404 U.S. 418, 422). 

Section 16(b)’s flat rule and its conclusive presumption 
of access to inside information have been previously held 
constitutional when applied to that class of insiders at 
which Congress aimed the statute—ofticers, directors and 
stockholders (Gratz v. Claughton (2 Cir. 1951) IS7 F.2d 
46. 49-50: Park & Tilford v. Schulte (2 Cir, 1947) 160 
F.2d 984, 988: Smolowe v. Di lendo Corporation (2 Cir. 


1943) 136 F.2d 231, 239). Those holdings were all based 


on the fact that 4 16(b) was enacted “upon a considered 


47 


finding, supported by ample evidence, of the abuses of 
inside speculation” (Smolowe v. Delendo Corporation (2 
Cir. 1943) 186 F.2d 231, 239). However, as noted, that 
finding, and the evidence relating to it, concerned insiders 


who were officers, directors and stockholders. 


As discussed above, although § 16(b) was clearly aimed 
at such insiders, the holders of convertible debentures 
were made potentially subject to it as a result of the defi- 
nition of “equity security” as “any stock or similar seeur- 
ity; or any security convertible * * * into such a security” 
(15 U.S.C. § 78e(a)}(11)). Significantly, there is no finding 
and no evidence anywhere in the lengthy hearings which 
preceded the enactment of §16(b), that owners of de- 
bentures would have access to inside information or that 
transactions by them are inherently subject to speculative 
abuse. The Second Circuit has taken express note of the 
nonexistence of any such finding and of evidence pertain- 
ing to the holders of debentures (Chemical Fund, Ine. v. 
Xerox Corporation (2 Cir. 1967) 377 F.2d 107, 110) and it 
has declared that 

“e * * there is no reason whatever to believe that 
any holder of any Convertible Debentures would, by 
reason of such holding, normally * * * be the recipi- 
ent of any inside information” (377 F.2d 111). 


A flat rule may be justified when there exists evidence 
of abuse inherent in a certain class of transactions. In- 
deed, this was the justifieation advanced for §16(b). In 
a brief supporting the validity of §16(b), Thomas Coreo- 
ran, one of the principal authors of the Act, made refer- 


ence to the evidence regarding abuses in transactions “by 


48 


officers, directurs and principal stockholders” and observed 


that this Court 
«“* * * has upheld the power of the legislature to reg- 
ulate or prohibit even acts which are in themselves 
innocent, where control over them is necessary to the 
effective control of abuses” (House Hearings, p. 937; 
emphasis added). 


There is, however, no evidence and no reason to believe 
that holders of convertible debentures would have access 
to inside information and there is therefore no showing 
of any necessity of applying §16(b) to transactions by 
them. In the absence of such a showing, we submit that 
application of the flat rule contained in § 16(b) would be 
contrary to the principle that: 
“Statutes creating permanent irrebuttable presump- 
tions have long been disfavored under the Due Proc- 


ess Clauses of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amend- 
ments” (Vlandis v. Kline (1973) 412 U.S. 441, 446). 


This is particularly so when there exist “other reasonable 
and practicable means of establishing the pertinent facts” 
(412 U.S. 451). Reasonable and practical means ef seek- 
ine redress for actual abuse already exist in general rem- 
edies for fraud, stockholders’ derivative actions, and other 
provisions of the Exehange Aet, including § 10(b) and 
Rule 10b-5. Henee, in the absence of some evidence of 
wrone-doing, the application of §16(b) to Provident’s 
brief holding of the Foremost debentures, when Provident 
was never an officer, director or stockholder of Foremost, 
would raise serious questions under the due process clause 


of the Fifth Amendment.

Ill. PROVIDENT’S SALE OF THE DEBENTURES OCCURRED 
WHEN IT WAS NOT AN OWNER, DIRECTLY OR INDIR- 


ECTLY, OF 10% OR MORE OF FOREMOST’S COMMON 
STOCK. 


The underwriting agreement through which one half of 
the Foremost debentures were sold by Provident was 
signed on October 21, 1969 (Jt.Appx., p. AS2). It ex- 
pressly provided that October 28 was to be the “time of 
purchase” by the underwriters from Provident and that 
Provident would deliver the debentures and receive pay- 
ment at that time (Underwriting Agt., p. 1-2, following 
Jt.Appx., p. 134). Pursuant to that agreement, posses- 
sion and the incidents of ownership were in fact trans- 
ferred on October 28 (.Jt.Appx., p. AS82). Previously, on 
October 24, Provident had distributed to its shareholders 
the other one half of the Foremost debentures held by it 
(Jt.Appx., p. AS2Z) so that, as the Ninth Cireuit correctly 
noted, 
“* * * if the sale was not completed until October 28, 
the date of the closing and a date subsequent to the 
distribution of debentures to the shareholders, then 
Provident was not a beneficial owner of 10 percent at 
the time of sale, and Foremost cannot recover the 
profit” (Pet. Appx., p. 9a; 506 F.2d 606). 

The question, then, is whether the sale by Provident was 

completed on October 21 or on October 28. 


The Act itself broadly defines “sale” to “include any 
contract to sell or otherwise dispose of” (15 U.S.C. 4 78e 
(a)(14)) but it ineludes no reference to the date of the 
sale. Accordingly, it is necessary to construe the language 


of the .\ct in the context of a particular transaction. In 


doing so, the terms “purchase” and “sale” must be con- 


50 


strued “in a manner which will effectuate the purpose 
of the specific section of the Act in which they are used” 
(Bershad v. McDonough (7 Cir. 1970) 428 F.2d 693, 696). 


In determining the date of sale, courts have considered 
not only the date of a firm commitment to sell but also 
the date of the actual exchange, whether the rights of 
ownership are retained, and the date of the relinquishment 
of the incidents of ownership (Champion Home Builders 
Co. v. Jeffress (6 Cir. 1974) 490 F.2d 611, 616). In the 
instant ease, Provident had ownership until October 28 
and the actual exchange of debentures and the incidents 
of ownership took place on that date (Jt.Appx., p. A82). 
October 28 therefore is the date upon which the sale 


would ordinarily be deemed completed. 


Both the court below and Foremost recognize that the 
date of the sale by Provident should be the date upon 
which the sale was completed (Pet.Appx., pp. 9a-lla; 506 
F.2d 606-607; Foremost Br., p. 43). Foremost places great 
reliance on the Form 4 statement filed by Provident, 
erroneously asserting that the statement shows “the sale 
as of October 21, 1969" (Foremost Br., p. 11; and see 
ibid., p. 43). That form did not even purport to specify 
the date of the sale; it reported only a sale “pursuant to 
an Underwriting Agreement dated October 21, 1969” 
(Form 4 (following Jt. Appx., p. A54): emphasis added). 
As noted, the underwriting agreement itself defines Octo- 
ber 28, 1969, as “the time of purchase” by the underwriters 
from Provident (i.e., the sale by Provident) and provided 
that Provident would deliver the debentures and receive 


payment at that time (Underwriting Agt. (following Jt. 


Appx., p. A134), pp. 1-2, par. 2). 


ol 


The argument that the sale to the underwriters was 
complete on October 21 is also based upon the mistaken 
conclusion that Provident was “irrevocably bound” to sell 
and that it insulated itself against all market risks between 
October 21 and October 28 (Pet.Appx., pp. 10a-lla; 506 F. 
2d 607). This conclusion by the court below is based upon 
an erroneous reading of the underwriting agreement. The 
court referred to paragraph 7 which permitted termination 
by the underwriters under certain conditions only until such 
time as the registration statement became effective. Be- 
cause the statement became effective on October 21, the 
court mistakenly concluded that the agreement was not 
subject to termination by the underwriters after that date 
(Pet.Appx., p. Ila; 506 F.2d 607). In reaching that con- 
clusion, the court totally overlooked the faet that, under 
paragraph 5(h), the agreement was subject to the addi- 
tional express condition 

“That, between the time of execution of this agree- 
ment [October 21] and the time of purchase [October 
28], there shall oceur no material and unfavorable 
change, financial or otherwise (other than as referred 
to in the Registration Statement and the Prospectus), 
in the condition of the Company | Foremost] and its 
consolidated subsidiaries as a whole * * *” (Under- 
writing Agt. (following Jt.Appx., p. A134), p. 7, par. 
d(h)). 


The situation is therefore analogous to the stock option 
contract in Kern County Land Co. v. Occidental Corp. 
(1905) 411 U.S. 582, 601-602. The question there was 
Whether the sale oecurred on the date of the option agree- 
ment or the later date of its exercise. The later date was 


chosen because the option was not “an instrument with 


52 


potential for speculative abuse” (411 U.S. 602). This was 
so because Occidental had “no choice but to sell if Ten- 
neco exercised the option” but Occidental gained no ad- 
vantage “if the stock declined and Tenneco chose not to 
exercise its option” (ibid.). 

Provident likewise could not have obtained speculative 
advantage through the underwriting agreement. Under it, 
Provident could not share in a rising market and, be- 
cause the agreement was terminable under adverse condi- 
tions, it was not insulated from a falling one. There is 
therefore no reason to depart from the ordinary defini- 
tion of the word “sale.” Possession and ownership rights 
were not transferred until October 28 and that, accord- 


ingly, was the date upon which the sale was completed. 


IV. THE TRANSACTION WAS EXEMPT FROM §16(b) BE- 
CAUSE PROVIDENT ACTED AT ALL PERTINENT TIMES 
ON BEHALF OF ITS SHAREHOLDERS.*! 


A. Provident was a liquidating agent authorized by Cali- 
fornia law to administer the assets of its shareholders. 


Section 16(b) does not cover “uny transaction or trans- 
actions which the [Securities and Exchange] Commission 
by rules and regulations may exempt as not comprehended 
within the purpose of this subsection” (15 U.S.C. § 78p 


21There is no basis for Foremost’s assertions that the courts 
below did not “accept” or that they “rejected” the arguments 
presented under this heading (see Foremost Br., pp. 12, 40). 
Having found the transaction exempt on other grounds, they did 
not pass upon these arguments. 


oo 


(b)). One of the exemptions formulated by the Commis- 
sion provides: 

“(a) During the period of 12 months following 
their appointinent and qualification, securities held by 
the following persons shall be exempt from sections 
16(a) and 16(b) of the act: 

* + * . * 

“(3) Receeivers, trustees in bankruptcy, assignees 
for the benefit of creditors, conservators, liquidating 
agents, and other similar persons duly authorized by 
law to adininister the estate or assets of other per- 
sons” (Rule I6a-4, 17 C.F.R. § 240.16a-4). 


Provident was a liquidating agent or other similar person 
authorized by California law to administer the assets of 


its shareholders. 


On September 26, 1969, the Provident shareholders 
approved a plan of complete liquidation under which Pro- 
vident was to wind up its affairs and liquidate (Jt.Appx., 
pp. Av8, A99-A101). That plan provided for pro rata 
liquidating distributions to the shareholders leading to 
the “complete liquidation of Provident” within a twelve- 
month period following adoption of the plan (Jt.Appx., 
pp. AlO02, A103). It was expressly provided that “all dis- 
tributions made by Provident as such shall be made 
within the above-mentioned twelve-month period” (Jt. 
Appx., p. 104). And, as required by Rule 16a-4(a), all 
transactions complained of by Foremost took place within 
that twelve-month period and Provident was dissolved 
within that period (Jt.Appx., pp. AS2-A83). | 


Under California law, the shareholders’ approval of the 


plan of liquidation began the proceedings for the winding 


o4 


up of Provident (Cal.Corp.Code, §§ 4600, 4604). As re- 
quired by statute (Cal.Corp.Code, §§ 4603, 4605), a certifi- 
cate of winding up was filed with the California Secretary 
of State (Jt.Appx., pp. A108-A110) and notice of winding 
up was sent to all shareholders and all creditors (Jt. 
Appx., p. Alll). Under California law, Provident was 
under an express mandate to “cease to carry on business 
except to the extent necessary for the beneficial winding 
up thereof” (Cal.Corp.Code, § 4605). The California law 
also provides that: 

“After determining that all the known debts and 
liabilities of a corporation in the process of winding 
up have been paid or adequately provided for, the 
directors shall distribute all the remaining corporate 
assets among the shareholders and owners of shares 
according to their respective rights and preferences” 
(Cal.Corp.Code, § 5000). 


Thus, from September 26, 1969 forward, Provident 
existed for the sole purpose of liquidating and making 
distributions to its shareholders. The California law not 
only authorized but required the directors of Provi- 
dent to act for its shareholders’ benefit in the process of 
liquidation. In accord with this statutory mandate, the 
Foremost debentures were distributed pro rata as re- 
ceived and those portions of shares not distributed were 
held “as a separate fund for the sole benefit of the share- 
holders concerned pending sale or other appropriate dis- 
position” (Jt.Appx., pp. A120-A121). Prevident’s officers 
considered that their “sole duty was to get the assets of 


Provident into the hands of its individual shareholders 


as quickly as possible” (Jt.Appx., p. A83). 


—oeeeeeee 


333) 


Provident’s status as a liquidating agent antedated 
both the date upon which the purchase agreement be- 
tween Foremost and Provident became binding and the 
date of the receipt by Provident of the Foremost de- 
bentures. The purchase agreement was expressly condi- 
tioned upon approval by Provident’s Board of Directors 
and shareholders (Jt. Appx., p. A76; Purchase Agt. (fol- 
lowing Jt.Appx., p. AS4), p. 14, par. 7(e)). That ap- 
proval was given on September 26, 1969, after approval 
of the plan of liquidation (Jt.Appx., pp. A77-A78, A99- 
A101). No debentures were received until October 15 (Jt. 
Appx., p. A81). 


Foremost asserts that the exemption provided by Rule 
l6a-4 was intended only to apply to estates of limited 
duration (Foremost Br., pp. 55-56). Even if such a re- 
quirement could be read into the rule, it is met here. The 
plan of dissolution adopted by Provident required com- 
plete distribution and dissolution within twelve months 
of September 26, 1969, and dissolution in facet oecurred 
within that period (Jt.Appx.., pp. AS2-A83, A102-A107). 


Foremost also places great store in the fact that there 
Was no court supervision of the winding up and disso- 
lution unti! August, 1970 (Foremost Br. pp. 55-56). 
Rule 16a-4 does not require court supervision. To the 
contrary, its only requirement is that persons doing the 
liquidating he “liquidating agents” or “other similar 
persons” who are “authorized by law” to so act. Under 
California law, after the shareholders have elected to 
wind up and dissolve, the directors of the corporation are 


“authorized by law,” indeed commanded by law, to do 


56 


what is necessary to beneficially wind up and dissolve 
the corporation and to distribute the remaining assets to 
the shareholders (Cal.Corp.Code, § 5000). The directors 
continue to function as directors, but their scope of ac- 
tivity is severely limited. Once the election has been 
made, “the corporation shall cease to carry on business 
except to the extent necessary for the beneficial winding 
up thereof” (Cal.Corp.Code, § 4605). And the decision to 
wind up and dissolve can only be revoked by the share- 
holders (Cal.Corp.Code, $4606) or, if the winding up 
process is under the supervision of the Court, by order 
of the Court (Cal.Corp.Code, § 4607). Without shareholder 
revocation, the corporation is irretrievably bound to dis- 
solution and distribution and is acting only as a liquidat- 
ing agent, or other similar person, to and for the benefit 


of the shareholders. 


Foremost’s assertion that “Rule lGa-4 was not designed 
to exempt arrangements by which a party could declare 
itself a ‘liquidating agent,’ engage in securities trans- 
actions, and then cause the liquidating agent status to be 
revoked” (Foremost Br., p. 57) is beside the point. In 
this particular transaction a bona fide election to liqui- 
date and dissolve was made and carried out. If the 
hypothetical situation suggested by Foremost occurred, 
then the election to dissolve no doubt would be a sham 


and would be so treated. 


There is likewise no basis for Foremost’s assertion 
that Rule 1l6a-4 applies only to securities which have 
“devolved upon” a fiduciary (Foremost Br., p. 58). The 


rule clearly specifies that it applies to securities which 


o7 


are “held” and it savs nothing ahout the manner of their 
acquisition. Provident unquestionably did hold and sell 
the debentures within 12 months of the adoption of the 
plan of liquidation. 


llere, Provident and its directors were acting as liquidat- 
ing agents for Provident’s shareholders. The acquisition 
of the Foremost debentures as payment for Provident’s 
assets was an integral part of the plan of liquidation. The 
distribution of a part of those assets to the shareholders 
and the public sale of the remainder were expressly au- 
thorized and directed by the shareholders? and were 
within Provideit’s role as a_ liquidating agent. <Ac- 
cordingly, the transaction falls within the exemption from 
» 16(b) provided by Rule 16a-4. 


B. Provident did not have beneficial ownership of the de- 
bentures at the time of the purchase and the sale. 


1. Beneficial ownership at all times rested in Provident’s sharehold- 
ers, not in Provident itself. 


Section 16(b) applies only to a “beneficial owner” of 
securities (15 U.S.C. § 78p(b); emphasis added). Prior 
to the acquisition of the Foremost debentures, Provident 
did not own any security of Foremost (Jt.Appx., p. A73). 
The debentures were acquired solely to accommodate Prov- 
ident’s liquidation and, we submit, beneficial ownership 


at all times rested in Provident’s shareholders and not 


22 Approximately one half of the debentures were distributed 
pursuant to resolutions of the Board of Directors (Jt.Appx., p. 
A82). The sale of the other one half was undertaken with express 
authorization from the shareholders given prior to the sale by 
Provident (Jt.Appx., pp. A80-A81). 


58 


in Provident.?* Hence, any transactions subject to § 16(b) 
would be transactions by the shareholders, not by Provi- 
dent. 

The facts pertaining to Provident’s status as a liquidat- 
ing agent for its hareholders are set forth above. To re- 
capitulate briefly The earliest possible date upon which 
it could have been determined that Provident had aequired 
the Foremost debentures is September 26, 1969 (supra, 
p. 55). Yet, the election to wind up and dissolve preceded 
that acquisition (Jt.Appx., pp. AT7-A78, A95-A9S, AYD- 
A107). From the moment of the shareholders’ adoption of 
the plan of liquidation and election to wind up and dis- 
solve, Provident was committed either to distribute all as- 
sets to its sharcholders or to sell the assets and distribute 
the proceeds to its shareholders (Cal.Corp.Code, $9 4605, 
5000; see discussion supra, pp. 54-57). Provident acquired 
the debentures in its capacity as an agent for its share- 
holders and all transactions by Provident in the deben- 
tures were for its shareholders and for its shareholders’ 


benefit. 


Thus, Provident never had a beneficial interest in the 
Foremost dehentures. It was the shareholders who con- 
trolled the course of the liquidation and for whose benefit 
it was carried out, Accordingly, as of the time that the 


shareholders clected to wind up and dissolve Provident, 


23Contrary to Foremost’s arguments (Foremost Br., pp. 40, 45),

all beneficial interest in assets then owned or thereafter

2. In any event, Provident was not a beneficial owner of 10% or 
more of a class of Foremost’'s securities at the time of sale. 


Section 16(b) requires that a beneficial owner be such 
“both at the time of the purchase and sale” (Securities 
Exchange Act, § 16(b), 15 U.S.C. § 78p(b)). Assuming for 
purposes of argument that the date of the sale was Octo- 
ber 21, 1969 (see discussion, supra, pp. 49-52) and that 
beneficial ownership of the debentures initially vested in 
Provident, Provident nonetheless was divested of such 
beneficial ownership prior to the signing of the under- 
writing agreement on October 21. On October 13, Provi- 
dent’s Board of Directors directed Provident’s officers to 
distribute Foremost’s debentures to the shareholders (Jt. 
Appx., pp. A79, A120-A121). The resolution expressly 
declared that the debentures would be distributed pro 
rata as received and that those portions of shares not 
distributed would be held “as a separate fund for the sole 
benefit of the shareholders concerned pending sale or other 


appropriate disposition” (Jt.Appx., pp. A120-A121). 


The October 13 resolution did not fix a record or pay- 
ment date (see Jt.Appx., pp. Al11S8-A122). Under Califor- 
nia law, when a date is not fixed in a resolution which 
declares a corporate dividend, the dividend vests in the 
shareholder as of the date of the resolution and the board 
of directors has no power to revoke the dividend (Meyers 
ve. El Tejon Ol & Refining Co. (1946) 29 Cal.2d 184, LSS, 
174 Pi2d 1,3: Smith v. Taccker (1983) 133 Cal. App. 351, 


CS het 


doz, 24 P.2d 182). Although this rule is generally applied 


60 


io dividends declared by a going corporation, it is equally 
applicable to the dividends declared by Provident. Provi- 
dent could no more have stopped the liquidation and the 
distribution than a going corporation could revoke a de- 
clared dividend. Under the California law (Cal.Corp.Code, 
‘ 4606), the power of revocation rested in the sharehold- 
ers, not Provident. The sale of the debentures was ex- 
pressly authorized by the shareholders (Jt.Appx., pp. 
AS0-A81) and Provident acted as a liquidating agent in 
‘arrving out the sale (see discussion, pp. 52-57). The pro- 
ceeds of the sale were thereafter distributed to the share- 
holders (Jt.Appx., pp. AS82-A83). 


It is simply not true that Provident “repudiated” the 
October 13 resolution and “never carried it out” (Fore- 
most Br., p. 46). Approximately one half of the debentures 
were distributed to the shareholders. The sale of the other 
one half. and the distribution of the proceeds in accord 
with the October 13 resolution, was undertaken with ex- 
press authorization from the shareholders given prior to 
the sale (Jt.Appx., pp. AS0-A81). There is also no sig- 
nificance to the fact that there may have been liquidating 
preferences and creditors to be paid (see Foremost Br., 
». 47). Such conditions merely state the terms and extent 
of the shareholders’ beneficial ownership. One’s vested 
right in a fund may be subject to prior satisfaction of 


some other person’s rights. 


Therefore, even if beneficial ownership initially vested 
in Provident, that ownership was divested on October 13, 
1969. Hence, even if the sale is deemed to have occurred 
on October 21, Provident was not a beneficial owner at 


that time and section 16(b) is not applicable. 


For each of the foregoing reasons, we respectfully sub-

in contravention of such rules and regulations as the

ate in the public interest or for the protection of in- 
vestors” (48 Stat. 891).

rr i i 


REPLY BRIEF FOR THE PETITIONER 


As respondent Provident Securities Company’s answer- 
ing brief (hereafter ‘‘Provident’’ and ‘‘Res. Br.’’) would 
have it, this case should provide the occasion for this Court 
to re-examine and reverse, or rewrite the statutory lan- 
guage, not only in respect of the Stella doctrine, as to which 
certiorari was granted, but also as to many other presum- 
ably settled principles of Section 16(b) law, including but 
not limited to the definitions of ‘‘purchase’’, ‘‘sale’’, 
‘*beneficial ownership’’ and ‘‘equity security’’, the decision 
of the Second Circuit in Chemical Fund, Inc. v. Xerox 
Corp., 377 F.2d 107 (2d Cir. 1967), and the meaning of 


SEC Rule 16a-2. Insofar as the amicus brief of Gulf & 
Western Industries (hereafter ‘‘G&W”’ and ‘‘G&W Br.’’) 
is concerned, this reply brief constitutes our first oppor- 
tunity to deal with the several arguments that were not 
proffered by Provident but are advanced by G&W. 


ARGUMENT 
I 


The initial purchase of 10% of an issuer’s securi- 
ties is a Section 16(b) “purchase”. 

A. The Legislative History “Affords No Expla- 
nation of the Purpose of the Proviso”. 

Provident and G&W, like the alchemists of old, seek to 
transmute the dross of the alleged legislative history of 
Section 16(b)’s proviso into a treasure-trove of support 
for a construction of the statute which would render it 
largely ineffectual in dealing with abuses arising from 
transactions involving beneficial owners of 10% of the 
equity securities of issuers. Both have come late to the 
apparent conclusion that this Court was in error when it 
determined that the legislative history affords no explana- 
tion of the purpose of the proviso. Reliance Electric Co. v. 
Emerson Electric Co., 404 U.S. 418, 424 (1972).* 


At most, what Provident and G&W have extracted from 
the legislative history is that early drafts of Section 16(b) 


*It should be noted that G&W had not argued the point here 
involved in the Seventh Circuit in its regularly filed briefs, save to 
note the point in a footnote. Only when the Ninth Circuit decision 
in the instant case was filed did it seek leave to file 
briefs in the Circuit Court on this point. This history bears striking 
I Ce, VEEES CURIS GES to eng Gi gue Netwe Ce 


3 


(S. 2693 and H.R. 7852) may be read as requiring prior 
beneficial ownership of 5% before subsequent purchases 
and sales are subject to the statute. But there is no doubt 
that the language of the early bills, including the specific 
language on which Provident and G&W rely, was altered 
or deleted prior to enactment. The fact that Provident 
and G&W offer possible explanations for those changes is 
hardly affirmative support for their contention that the 
‘*clear’’ limitation of the prior bills survives the elimination 
of the language which made the limitation ‘‘clear’’.* What 
emerges from the entire discussion in both briefs is sup- 
port for this Court’s conclusion that the legislative history 
‘‘affords no explanation of the purpose of the proviso.’’ 
We have consistently maintained this position in our briefs 
to this Court with respect to the proviso, while arguing 
on the other hand that the general legislative purposes of 
Section 16(b) as a whole are only fulfilled by the construc- 
tion which we offer. (Foremost Br. 18-20, 25-32; Cert. Pet. 
14-15) However, if we, like our opponents, were to indulge 
in speculation as to why the language of the proviso was 
substituted, it would not seem unlikely that when Congress 
changed the 5% ownership requirement in the original 
bills to 10%, it decided to counterbalance the relaxation of 
* While of critical language would generally make 
any early bill, comments thereon, highly dubious guides to inter- 
preting an amended bill, this is particularly true here where their 
incipal draftsman admitted that the insider trading provisions of 
.2693 and H.R. 7852 were not well drafted. Hearings on S. Res. 
84, S. Res. 56 and S. Res. 97 Before the Senate Committee on Bank- 
ing and Currency, 73d Cong., 2d Sess. 6557-58 (1934) (Thomas 
Corcoran stated that the sale-repurchase situation “should have been 
provided for * * *”) ; Hearings on H.R. 7852 and H.R. 8720 Before 
the House Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, 73d 
Cong., 2d Sess. 133 (1934) (Mr. Corcoran observed that H.R. 7852 


was not limited to directors and officers who also own 5% of the 
stock and was “badly drawn” in suggesting such a limitation). 


4 


that provision by ensuring that the transaction by which 
one attains 10% beneficial ownership would constitute a 
statutory ‘‘purchase’’. 


G&W pays particular attention to the language in the | 


initial draft bills declaring unlawful purchases by insiders 
‘‘with the intention or expectation of selling’’ within six 
months, and argues that: 


‘*[t]he statute aims expressly at the person who buys 
stock [intending] based on side information to sell 
at a short-term profit and necessarily contemplates the 
statutory relationship, and imformational access, be- 
fore his purchase.’’ (G&W Br. 11) (emphasis sup- 
plied). 


Not the least of the defects of this argument is that the 
early bills specifically provided that intention to both buy 
anc sell within a six-month period would not be a sub- 
stantive element of the statutory liability. Moreover, even 
if Congress had chosen to make such intention a required 
element of liability, it does not follow that at any point in 
the drafting process Congress also assumed, as G&W sug- 
gests, that statutory ownership (5% at the preliminary 
stage discussed) would invariably have to be reached 
before the purchase. A person owning some shares, but 
less than the 5% statutory benchmark, could acquire inside 
information and thereafter make a second purehase in- 
creasing his ownership to the statutory level fully intend- 
ing, at the time of the second purchase, to exploit the in- 
formation by selling within the next six months. The un- 
lawful intention required under the draft legislation could 
well exist prior to or simultaneously with a purchase con- 
ferring the percentage of ownership required to invoke the 
draft statute’s sanctions. 


G&W’s argument also ignores the fact that manipulation 
by insiders was a subject of considerable Congressional 
concern at the time of Section 16(b)’s adoption. 8S. Rep. 
No. 792, 73d Cong., 2d Sess. 9 (1934) ; Hearings on S. Res. 
84, S. Res. 56 and S. Res. 97 Before the Senate Committee 
on Banking and Currency, 73d Cong., 2d Sess. 6559 (1934) 
(hereinafter ‘‘Senate Hearings’’). A person contemplat- 
ing influencing corporate affairs to his own advantage after 
acquiring a large block of equity securities might intend 
to sell within six months in order to profit from his manip- 
ulative activities. The pre-purchase intention to sell in 
such a case could well be based solely on the contemplated 
manipulation and not at all ‘‘on inside information’’. In 
short, G&W’s reliance on the language relating to an inten- 
tion, allegedly based on the prior possession of inside in- 
formation, to buy and sell within six months, language 
which was never enacted and indeed was never even deter- 
minative of liability in the draft bills, evidences an ex- 
tremely circumscribed view of Section 16(b), and one that 
cannot be said to reflect the intent of the Congress which 
enacted the statute. 


We note that the Stella case*—which both Provident 
and G&W argue was decided contrary to Congress’ intent— 
is more than twenty years old, yet no action has been taken 
by Congress to reverse its construction of Section 16(b). 
In Blau v. Lehman, 368 U.S. 403 (1962) the Court refused 
to apply Section 16(b) to partnership short-swing profits 
where one of the partners sat on the issuer’s board of di- 
rectors. It relied in part on the fact that a lower court 


* Stella v. Graham-Paige Motors Corp., 232 F.2d 299 (2d Cir.), 
cert. denied, 352 U.S. 831 (1956), a ing Stella v. Graham-Paige 
Motors Corp., 104 F. Supp. 957 (S.D.N.Y. 1952). 


6 


decision reaching the same result had been called to Con- 
gress’ attention in the SEC’s annual reports, despite which 
Congress had failed to amend the statute. 368 U.S. at 
412-13 and n. 13. Here too, Congress has not acted to 
amend the statute to reverse the decision in Stella and the 
eases following it, despite its knowledge of that decision 
through SEC reports.* See 18 SEC Ann. Rep. 78 (1953). 


B. The Statutory Policy Requires Application 
of Section 16(b) to a Purchase Conferring 
10% Beneficial Ownership. 


While the legislative history does not in explicit terms 
give guidance to the meaning of the language here at issue, 
nevertheless a construction of Section 16(b) exempting a 
purchase conferring 10% beneficial ownership will contra- 
vene the statute’s purpose of preventing insider trading 
abuses. It is the potential for abuse, not actual abuse, at 
which Section 16(b) is aimed. 


‘‘(T]he only method Congress deemed effective to 
curb the evils of insider trading was a flat rule taking 
the profits out of a class of transactioms in which the 
possibility of abuse was believed to be intolerably 
great.’’ Reliance Electric Co. v. Emerson Electric Co., 
404 U.S. 418, 422 (1972).

As was recently observed in a different context in Lewis

‘*The history of section 16(b) shows that Congress

(footnote omitted). 


Notwithstanding these unquestioned principles, the 
construction of the proviso contended for by G&W and 
Provident would render the statute inapplicable to all but 
the most unsophisticated transactions by 10% holders, con- 
trary to the manifest statutory purpose. Among the cases 
which would escape the statutory sanction are the follow- 
ing. In each example almost any percentage between 10% 
and 100% could be substituted for the ‘‘10%’’ used in the 
iiustrations. 

(1) A purchaser acquires 10% of the issuer’s securities 
from the issuer or one or more large stockholders on the 
basis of inside information obtained during negotiations 
leading to the purehase, or at some prior time, and sells the 
securities purchased at a profit within six months of the 


purchase. 

(2) A punehaser of 10% of the issuer’s securities ac- 
quires inside information within six months of the purchase 
prompting an immediate sale of his holdings at a profit. 


(3) A purchaser of 10% of the issuer’s securities uti- 
lizes his pesition to influence corporate affairs, selling the 
securities purchased within six months at an artificially 
inflated pri 


8 


(1) G&W vigorously attacks application of the statute 
to the first situation insofar as it relies on the possibility 
of obtaining inside information during negotiations looking 
toward a 10% purchase on the ground that ‘‘this theory 
is woefully inadequate in describing the likely means of 
achieving a stock interest * * *.’’ (G&W Br. 22 and n. 32) 
To be sure, some large purchasers (perhaps including 
G&W) undoubtedly do acquire their interests by processes, 
such as open-market purchase, that may involve no contact 
with the issuer or other insiders. But the negotiated pur- 
chase is certainly the more likely form for acquisitions of 
this magnitude (as well as the form of the transaction at 
issue here) and the fact that some large purchases do not 
involve negotiations between issuer and purchaser is an 
insufficient basis on which to refuse to apply a prophylactic 
rule to any of them. The principle enunciated by Judge 
Weinfeld in Lewis v. Arcara, [Current] CCH Fed. See. 
L.Rep. 195,238 (S.D.N.Y. July 18, 1975) is applicable here: 


‘‘Such an accommodation in the unexceptional cireum- 
stances of this case not only runs counter to the 
intended automatic application of the statute to re- 
capture ‘any profit realized’, but also affords the op- 
portunity to evade its purpose.’’ 95,238 at 98,253. 


In Champion Home Builders Co. v. Jeffress, 490 F.2d 611 
(6th Cir.), cert. denied, 416 U.S. 986 (1974), the insider 
apparently obtained actual inside information in the course 


of negotiations leading to his acquisition of 13% of the 
issuer’s stock. 490 F.2d at 618. 


The argument (Res. Br. 13-14, 29-30; G&W Br. 22-23) 
that the Court’s decision in Kern County Land Co. v. Occi- 
dental Petrolewm Corp., 411 U.S. 582 (1973) (hereinafter 


9 


*‘Kern County’’) precludes application of Section 16(b) to 
prevent exploitation of pre-purchase inside information has 
already been considered. (Foremost Br. 33-35) Suffice it 
to say that Kern County hardly stands for a blanket exclu- 
sion from the statute of cases in which information is ac- 
quired prior to the time that ‘‘substantial stockholdings”’ 
are acquired, and further that, contrary to G&W’s assertion 
(G&W Br. 23), there is no requirement in the statutory 
language that a right to purchase be ‘‘intertwined with un- 
fair access to information”’ in order for the acquisition of 
such right to be deemed a purchase under the statute. See 
hemical Fund, Ine. v. Xerox Corp., 377 F.2d 107 (2d Cir. 
1967) (purchase of debentures convertible into 10% of 
underlying common would confer insider status). 


Finally, G&W’s claim (G&W Br. 22) that interpreting 
the statute so as to deter 10% purchases based on informa- 
tion acquired prior to purchase would resurrect the deleted 
‘*tippee’’ liability provision is without merit. Any person 
to whom inside information is communicated by another, 
whether before or after acquiring insider status, could be 
called a ‘‘tippee’’. Section 16 has no application to ‘‘tip- 
pees’’ as such, but only to officers, directors and 10% 
holders whether or not they are actual ‘‘tippees’’. 


(2) Relying also on Kern County, Provident urges that 
‘*there can be no presumption of access to inside informa- 
tion until after such time as one has become an owner of 
more than 10% of an issuer’s securities’. (Res. Br. 14, 
29-30). But this argument speaks not at all to the second 
situation set forth above. Even if Section 16(b) presumes 
an inability to obtam inside information until 10% owner- 
ship is acquired, the fact remains that a 10% holder is able 


10 


to exploit information obtained as a result of his position 
by a single sale transaction. It is the position of the in- 
sider at the second or ‘‘closing’’ transaction which is crucial 


in determining whether there was a possibility of specula- 
tive abuse. See Brief for SEC as Amicus Curiae at 18-19, 
22, 24 and Supplemental Brief for SEC as Amicus Curiae 
at 5-8, Gold v. Sloan, 486 F.2d 340 (4th Cir. 1973), cert. 
denied, 419 U.S. 873 (1974). 


lt was precisely this consideration which led the court 
in Newmark v. RKO General, Inc., 425 F.2d 348 (2d Cir.), 
cert. denied, 400 U.S. 854 (1970) to apply the statute to a 
purchase conferring 10% beneficial ownership. 


‘‘The statutory reference to a ten percent beneficial 
owner rests on the presumption that an owner of this 
quantity of securities has access to inside information 
(footnote omitted). Although this presumption would 
not justify the conclusion that one who purchases a 
quantity of shares which makes him a ten percent bene- 
ficial owner has done so on the basis of inside informa- 
tion, the presumed access to such information resulting 
from this purchase provides him with an opportunity, 
not available to the investing public, to sell his shares 
at the moment most advantageous to him. Thus, a pur- 
chase of shares which makes the buyer an insider cre- 
ates an opportunity for the type of speculative abuse 
the statute was enacted to prevent.’’ 425 F.2d at 356. 


‘*That RKO’s heart may have been pure and its 
motivation noble matters not. The significant factor 
is whether RKO could have reaped a speculative profit 
from the ‘unfair use of information * * * obtained * * * 
by reason of [its] relationship to [Central].’’’ 425 
F.2d at 353, 


11 


And it was precisely this possibility which was absent under 
the peculiar facts of Kern County not only because the 
opposition between the offeror and target company manage- 
ment rendered ‘‘extremely remote’’ the possibility that the 
offeror could have obtained confidential information but 
also because both the occurrence and timing of the defensive 
merger ‘‘sale’’ were ‘‘out of [the offeror’s] hands.’’ 411 
U.S. at 598, 599. 


We note G&W’s quotation (G&W Br. 27) of the Eighth 
Cireuit’s hypothetical in Emerson Electric Co. v. Reliance 
Electric Co., 434 F.2d 918 (8th Cir. 1970), aff’d on other 
grounds, 404 U.S. 418 (1972) regarding a purchase of 51% 
of the issuer’s securities: 


‘‘Tilustrative of some of the mischief that would be 
permitted in spite of Congress’ action in enacting 16(b) 
if we accorded with Emerson’s contentions is an initial 
purchase of as large a block of stock as 51 pereent or 
more of a corporation’s stock, followed by a sale any 
time within six months by the stockholder who obvi- 
ously within that period could obtain much inside in- 
formation and also could influence, manipulate, or con- 
trol corporate transactions. The deterrence of such 
apparent potential mischief must have been within the 
contemplation of Congress.’’ 434 F.2d at 924. 


We simply cannot agree with G&W’s blithe assumption that 
such a case is not covered by Section 16(b). 


G&W rejects ‘‘the spurious post-purchase informa- 
tion theory’’ based in part on its analysis of the legislative 
history discussed above and in part on certain additional 
grounds purporting to show that ‘‘when such a theory of 
liability is tested, the structure of the statute breaks down.”’ 


12 


(G&W Br. 20-22) The reverse is true.* Moreover, this 
**spurious’’ theory received a much less hostile reception 
from the Court in Kern County than it receives from G&W. 
After determining that the period prior to the tender of- 
feror’s acquisition of 10% ownership did not present the 
potential for speculative abuse at which Section 16(b) is 
aimed, 411 U.S. at 596-97, the Court went on to consider 
whether abuse of inside information could have occurred in 
the period after 10% ownership had been obtained, con- 
cluding that the possibility of informational access during 
the latter period ‘‘seems extremely remote’’ in the context 
of a hostile tender offer. 411 U.S. at 598. This portion of 
the Court’s opinion certainly suggests acceptance rather 
than rejection of the ‘‘post-purchase information theory’’ 
in the more typical context involved here of cooperation 
between purchaser and seller. 


G&W’s claim that the ‘‘structure of the statute breaks 
down’’ in the post-purchase information case (G&W Br. 
20-21) is founded on a misconception of the purpose of 
Section 16(b). The statute was not designed to apprehend

and render liable in damages actual traders on inside in- 
formation: rather its purpose was to deter insider trading 
in the first instance by means of ‘‘a flat rule taking the 
profits out of a class of transactions in which the possibility 
of abuse was believed to be intolerably great,’’ Reliance 
Electric Co. v. Emerson Electric Co., 404 U.S. 418, 422 
(1972), without regard to ‘‘actual abuse of insider informa- 
tion,’’ Kern County at 595. Accordingly, G&W’s attempt 
to discredit the post-purchase information theory by show-

directed. (G&W Br. 20-21 and nn. 28, 29) The statutory 
recovery from an innocent insider whose transactions 
violate Section 16(b) would appear to be an even more 
‘‘eapricious, irrational penalty’? (G&W Br. 22) if it were 
intended to be measured against standards applicable to 
damage recoveries for actual wrongdoing, as in the cases 
inappropriately cited by G&W. But Section 16(b) does not 
purport to measure the actual value of inside information. 
It seeks instead to deter possible misuse of inside informa- 
tion, without assessing the actuality of wrongdoing, by the 
automatic forfeiture of an insider’s profit measured only 
by the net gain on prohibited matching transactions. 


(3) The policy of preventing insiders from influencing 
corporate affairs to generate short-swing profits for them- 
selves constitutes a third alternative ground for applying 
Section 16(b) to a purchase conferring statutory owner- 
ship. The fact that Section 16(b) was directed, at least 
in part, against such practices, S. Rep. No. 792, 73d Cong., 
2d Sess. 9 (1934) (examples cited of controlling insiders 


14 


formulating dividend policies productive of personal trad- 
ing profits) ; S. Rep. No. 1455, 73d Cong., 2d Sess. 67 (1934) ; 
Senate Hearings 6559 (statute aimed, inter alia, ‘‘at the 
general evil of officers and directors rigging their stock up 
and down * * *’’), has been recognized not only by this 
Court, Kern County at 592 n. 23,* but also by lower courts 
interpreting the statute, Emerson Electric Co. v. Reliance 
Electric Co., 434 F.2d 918, 924 (8th Cir. 1970), aff’d, 404 
U.S. 418 (1972); Blau v. Lamb, 363 F.2d 507, 515, 521 n. 
19 (2d Cir. 1966), cert. denied, 385 U.S. 1002 (1967); Adler 
v. Klawans, 267 F.2d 840, 845, 848 (2d Cir. 1959), and by 
Provident itself. (Res. Br. 12 quoting Foremost Br. 18) 
While other remedies may exist for manipulation, Section 
16(b) was designed as an automatic deterrent to such ac- 
tivities without the added requirements of proving a case 
under Sections 9 or 10 of the Exchange Act. 


Although G&W minimizes the manipulative power of 
10% shareholders, it is clear that Congress did not share its 
view.** Indeed, the very purpose of including substantial

C. Provident Has Failed to Distinguish 
the Pertinent Authorities. 

Provident argues that the District Court in Stella v. 
Graham-Paige Motors Corp., 104 F. Supp. 957 (S.D.N.Y. 
1952) did not ‘‘direetly address’’ the question whether a 
purehase conferring 10% ownership is comprehended by 
Section 16(b) (Res. Br. 17); in other words, did not ‘‘di- 
rectly address’’ the only question before the court and the 
one that it decided. G&W suggests that the Stella result 
would have been different had the case involved ‘‘an in- 
vestor with no previous relationship to the issuer,’’ (G&W 
Br. 29) rather than one who had been a 10% beneficial 
owner prior to the purchase in question, which re-estab- 
lished his 10% holding. But the Distriet Court never relied 
on the defendant's prior inside relationship to the issuer 
in support of its holding—and it is hard to see how it could 
have, since such relationship had ceased more than a year 
prior to the purchase in question (104 F. Supp. at 958)— 
and subsequent Second Circuit cases sustaining the court’s 
interpretation of the statute contain no such requirement. 
Perine v. William Norton & Co., Inc., 509 F.2d 114 (2d Cir. 
1974); Newmark v. RKO General, Ine., 425 F.2d 348 (2d 
Cir.), cert. denied, 400 U.S. 854 (1970). In Perme, there 
was no ‘‘prior insider relationship between [the defendant] 
and the issuer’’, 509 F.2d at 117, while in Newmark, con- 


17 


trary to G&W’s suggestion (G&W Br. 26-27), the existence 


of such a relationship was not essential to the court’s 
decision. * 


Cases holding that purchases by officers and directors 
prior to assuming office fall within Section 16(b) (Foremost 
Br. 23-24) are deemed irrelevant by Provident because, it 
is contended, the statute distinguishes beneficial owners 
from other insiders, as evidenced by the proviso at issue 
here. (Res. Br. 19-20) However, the decisions involving 
officers and directors uecessarily recognize that abuses with- 
in the purview of Section 16(b) can oceur where a purchase 
precedes attainment of insider status and it is difficult to 
see how this view of the statute, notwithstanding the pro- 
viso, is any less applicable to a beneficial owner whose pur- 
chase does not merely precede but confers insider status. 


These cases also speak to G&W’s legislative history 
argument that H.R. 7852 and S. 2693 **necessarily [contem- 
plate] the statutory relationship, and informational access, 
before his purchase’. (G&W Br. 11) Were they all wrong- 
ly decided? If not, a much larger question looms—why 
would Congress, without any apparent discussion of the 
point, require what G&W claims is the intended sequence 
of purchase of 10% before obtaining access to inside infor- 
mation in the case of beneficial owners, but depart from this
